#3455. New Scientific Analysis Suggests Jeffrey Epstein Was Murdered. His Brother, For One, Feels Validated.

One day in August 2019, Mark Epstein was having breakfast at a Virginia hotel when he looked at the TV and saw CNN reporting that his older brother, Jeffrey Epstein, had died by suicide in a Manhattan federal prison. As jarring as the report was, he had no reason to doubt it.

“I knew he wouldn’t want to live the rest of his life in jail,” Mark told Vanity Fair this week. “He had no children to worry about. Our parents were gone. He knew he didn’t have to worry about me.”

Mark says he finished his omelet and headed back to New York. Then, like so many other Americans, he started to become skeptical of the official narrative.

Over the last seven years, the endless conspiracy theories surrounding Jeffrey Epstein’s death have largely been relegated to the backwaters of YouTube and Reddit, while local and federal authorities have stuck to the suicide story. But this week there was a breakthrough. On Monday, Michael Freeman, a leading forensic scientist who testified for the prosecution in the trial of Derek Chauvin for the murder of George Floyd, issued the most legitimate challenge to date to the prevailing consensus.

Freeman presented his findings at a historic London legal society, saying, “The pattern and distribution and multitude of injuries are not explained by a suicidal hanging.” In a New York Times story published the same day as the presentation, Freeman told the publication that he had no view on who might have killed Jeffrey: “All I’m interested in is, how did this get so sideways?” Along with several global news outlets, including CBS and the BBC, the paper covered the presentation with a straight face even as it noted that Freeman’s efforts to publish his findings in a peer-reviewed journal had thus far been rejected.

The relationship between Donald Trump and Jeffrey Epstein has loomed large over the president’s second term.

In his thick Brooklyn accent, Mark Epstein, who has long been trying to prove that his brother was murdered while awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges, excitedly recounted this new development over the phone the day after Freeman’s presentation, which he attended.

“This crosses all party lines,” Mark said. “Most people believe he didn’t commit suicide. So it’s a mystery. People want an answer to that. I think now they have the answer.”

Mark emphasized that the story of the recent findings was not about him but rather about his brother’s death and Freeman’s work. It was Freeman who reached out to him, Mark said, based on what the scientist independently thought was shoddy work on Jeffrey’s autopsy, and Mark agreed to turn over all the records, reports, and photographs he had as next of kin.

“I want to make it really clear,” he said. “I didn’t pay for this. He’s never asked me for anything other than the information, which I gave him willingly. And he’s been studying this. As a matter of fact, the night before last was the first time I ever met him face-to-face.”

Still, Mark has made his suspicions both his calling card and his personal mission in recent years. After working in real estate investing and serving as the chair of Cooper Union’s board of trustees, he had his own business dealings came under some scrutiny as Jeffrey’s life and crimes dominated political and cultural discourse beginning in the late 2010s—Jeffrey allegedly housed models and employees in an Upper East Side building that was predominantly owned by his brother’s real estate holding company. In the years since his brother’s death, Mark has said that Jeffrey “definitely had dirt” on Donald Trump, and he became a minor fixation amid the Epstein files rollout on account of emails containing banter between him and his brother. (Trump has denied any prior knowledge of Jeffrey’s crimes and said that the release of the Epstein files “totally exonerated” him.) Mark has dismissed a suicide note purportedly written by Jeffrey as a fabrication.

Jeffrey’s death certificate initially said “pending further study” in regard to the cause of death, rather than ruling it a homicide or suicide, but the chief medical examiner ruled it a suicide days later. “All the pathologists I’ve spoken to,” says Mark, “they said, [if] an initial death certificate says ‘pending further study,’ you don’t get an answer usually for weeks or more because something’s being studied.” Mark hired the celebrity forensic pathologist Michael Baden to observe and evaluate the autopsy, and Baden previously stated that “the evidence points to homicide.” Federal officials’ handling of the matter in the years to come only amplified Mark’s concern.

“You know a suicide when you see one,” FBI director Kash Patel said last year while he was under fire for not producing any proof of the Epstein conspiracies he had been touting during his time as a mere conservative podcast personality, “and that’s what that was.”

“I actually laughed out loud when I heard that,” Mark said, “because I thought, How many suicides has this fucking jackass actually seen?”

So who does Mark think killed his brother?

“It’s like in a Mob hit,” he said. “You try to find who the hit man was, and then you try to find who ordered the hit.” The hit man, he figured, could only be someone among a limited number of people: prison employees and other prisoners who had been on Jeffrey’s security tier. “Then the question becomes,” said Mark, “who would have the ability to orchestrate this in a federal prison, and who would have the ability to have the DOJ cover it up?” He couldn’t think of anyone besides Trump. (Trump has not been accused of any wrongdoing in connection to Jeffrey’s death; in a 2023 interview with Tucker Carlson, when asked whether Jeffrey could have been killed, he said, “Oh sure, it’s possible. I mean, I don’t really believe—I think he probably committed suicide.”)

I thought Mark and I had developed some rapport over the conversation, particularly after I mentioned that I’d attended the same Coney Island middle school where he and his brother had been students; I emphasized that I was trying to listen to him carefully and take him seriously. But there was a bit more rancor in his tone after I said it was still difficult to believe that the Department of Justice could have successfully covered up the murder of the most high-profile prisoner in the world.

“If you don’t think that after what I just told you,” Mark said, “then you, sir, are a fucking idiot also.”

#3454. This Actively Exploited Chrome Vulnerability Is Putting Your Browser at Risk

If you've seen an uptick in security updates as of late, you're not alone. AI models have become very good at finding new security vulnerabilities throughout 2026. Researchers and hackers alike are increasingly relying on these models in their individual pursuits: Hackers want to find these flaws to exploit them, while researchers want to block hackers from doing so. Microsoft's latest Patch Tuesday update included more than 1,400 patches; meanwhile, Apple's latest security update fixed two iMessage flaws that let both bad actors and innocent parties alike access texts they shouldn't.

Whether you use a Mac or a PC, you probably browse the web with Chrome, or a Chromium-based browser. As it happens, Google's web browsing platform is the latest to receive an important security update—but it's far from the first important Chrome update of the year.

As reported by The Hacker News, Google released a new update for Chrome on Monday that patches nine security flaws. While all vulnerabilities are important to patch, one in particular is more serious than the rest: CVE-2026-125350, a use-after-free bug in Chrome's XML component.

Use-after-free vulnerabilities happen when the system frees up a memory location, but a program tries to access it anyway. It's a glitch in programming, but it offers bad actors an opportunity to break into your system. At worst, it allows arbitrary code execution, or, in other words, gives hackers the ability to run their own code in the app or system.

That's bad enough on the surface, but, unfortunately, Google confirmed that CVE-2026-125350 has an active exploit in the wild. The company is keeping other details close to the vest, but it's dangerous nonetheless. At least someone, somewhere, has used this flaw against a target, which puts all Chrome users (as well as users of Chromium-based browsers) at risk.

What's more, this isn't Chrome's first active exploit of the year—this is its eighth. The company is playing catch-up with hackers looking to target users of its browser, which makes sense, seeing as Chrome is by far the world's most popular browser.

If you're using Chrome on your computer, you'll want to update it as soon as possible. Make sure you're running at least versions 157.0.8103.50/.51 on Mac or PC, or 157.0.8103.50 on Linux. To check, click the three dots in the top-right corner of your Chrome window, then go to More > Help > About Google Chrome.

Other Chromium-based browsers may not have the update yet, but they are affected by this flaw. If you use browsers like Microsoft Edge, Opera, or Brave, keep an eye on your updates to install any of the latest patches.

#3452. The Rings Of Power Season 3's Best Storyline Redeems A Controversial Peter Jackson Idea

Spoilers are never late (nor are they early; they arrive precisely when they mean to), so don't read ahead without first watching Season 3, Episodes 5 and 6 of "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power."

Over halfway into its run, it's clear "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" Season 3 is spectacular whenever Sauron (Charlie Vickers) is on-screen. Indeed, this season is for the baddies, with the Dark Lord's menacing Nazgnagôl making their grand entrance and a thrilling civil war brewing in Númenor.

But it's not all doom and gloom, as Season 3 also introduces the brightest light of hope in Middle-earth: the elven golden retriver Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower). From the moment he shows up, it feels like he's been a part of the show from the start, fitting in perfectly as a strong, funny, flirty elf who has excellent chemistry with Galadriel (Morfydd Clark). Celeborn is the ultimate wife guy, and his relationship with Galadriel is the best romance we've seen in a Middle-earth adventure to date.

Nevertheless, there's trouble in Valinor for these two, as Celeborn has competition for Galadriel's heart. No, not Robert Aramayo's Elrond (despite them sharing a kiss in Season 2 to distract the orcs holding Galadriel captive), but Sauron, the Dark Lord on his dark throne in the Land of Mordor where the Shadows lie.

That's right: "The Rings of Power" Season 3 has finally turned "The Lord of the Rings" into a romantasy story, placing a love triangle at the heart of the saga of the One Ring. And while J.R.R. Tolkien purists may scoff at this, the show's love triangle is so good that it redeems the controversial romances from Peter Jackson's otherwise beloved "Lord of the Rings" films.

Peter Jackson's "Lord of the Rings" films are the most widely celebrated fantasy movies of all time and changed the genre forever. As such, it's easy nowadays to forget that Jackson's trilogy stirred up its fair share of controversy upon its initial release. After all, as faithful as they were to J.R.R. Tolkien's original books overall, those films also made some big alterations. That includes erasing the Scouring of The Shire from "The Return of the King" and removing characters like Tom Bombadil and Glorfindel, in addition to introducing a prominent love triangle.

In Jackson's movies, to jog your memory, a respectable amount of time is spent on Éowyn (Miranda Otto) falling in love with Aragorn (Viggo Mortensen), with even King Théoden (Bernard Hill) buying into their match and congratulating Éowyn on finding a good and honest man. Meanwhile, Aragorn keeps thinking about Arwen (Liv Tyler), who is about to leave Middle-earth for Valinor. In fact, the original plan was for Arwen to be at Helm's Deep alongside Éowyn and Aragorn in "The Two Towers," which presumably would've fueled their love triangle even further.

Things get even worse in Jackson's "The Hobbit" films. There, he and co-writers Philippa Boyens and Fran Walsh introduce Tauriel (Evangeline Lilly), an elf who develops romantic feelings for the dwarf Kili (Aidan Turner). In that case, it's Legolas (Orlando Bloom) who rounds out the love triangle, as he's still racist towards dwarves at the time.

Neither of these Middle-earth love triangles really work (especially not the latter), so it's hard not to be skeptical of "The Rings of Power" introducing yet another one. And yet, this ends up being the most compelling aspect of Season 3.

There are two things that make the love triangle in "The Rings of Power" work. The first is that the show is very clearly in on the joke, with Sauron often behaving like a teenager when it comes to his borderline hilarious fixation on Galadriel. That he even goes to the trouble of disguising himself as Galadriel and kissing Celeborn to get information out of him shows Sauron is not beyond being a little bi-curious.

Then there's the fact that the series has been building to this since Season 1, starting with Galadriel slowly falling for Sauron in disguise as Halbrand and being seduced by his promises of power. By the time Season 3 rolls along, she still has complicated feelings for him, as evidenced by her dreams and visions of Sauron waking up in bed next to her. Thus, when Celeborn re-enters her life, and Galadriel sees both men in front of her, there's a tiny bit of hesitation on her part.

And yet, Season 3 never suggests that Galadriel would actually leave her husband for the Dark Lord. Instead, it juxtaposes Sauron's jealousy with Celeborn's confidence. Specifically, in Episodes 5 and 6, Sauron gets visibly flustered when Celeborn talks about how much Galadriel loves him. In the end, it works just as well as the incredible romances in J.R.R. Tolkien's source material, proving that Middle-earth is not devoid of effective romantic storytelling.

Heck, the scene in Episode 6where Celeborn talks about making the elven smith that Sauron has been looking for tell him the secrets of the rings, just so he can hear about every minute the smith spent with Galadriel, is arguably the most romantic TV scene of 2026. Stream Season 3 on Prime Video, and see for yourself.

#3451. High-Protein Packaged Foods May Not Be As Healthy As They Look

Of the three major macronutrients—protein, carbs, and fat—protein has the best reputation, and it’s fairly well deserved. We need significant amounts of protein in our diet, and nothing particularly bad happens if we get too much. Dietary protein helps you build muscle, and if you’re trying to lose weight it helps stop you from losing too much muscle along with the fat. It also helps to make meals feel filling. Great! But.

Once the general public gets the idea that something is good for you, the companies that make packaged food start putting it in everything. Or, they make products where the good-for-you thing features prominently on the label, whether or not there is very much inside. So a lot of packaged food now boasts protein on the label. Here’s what you should ask yourself about those foods:

Take a close look here—sometimes a food will boast of a certain amount of protein per package but the package contains two or three servings. Other times, the protein per serving is correct, and we're supposed to be excited to have, say, 7 grams per serving. That's just not very much—and certainly not worth paying extra or choosing a less-delicious food just for those few added grams.

It’s good to know how much protein you need in your diet. If you’re not gaining or losing weight, and not doing very much exercise, a 150-pound person only needs about 54 grams of protein a day. (I've done the math for various body weights here.) If you’re working out a lot, or if you’re trying to gain or lose weight (yep, either way), that same 150-pound person will need more like 81 to 95 grams of protein per day. More is OK, but not necessary.

So if you’re trying to get 90 grams per day, 30 grams per meal is a reasonable amount to shoot for. Coincidentally, 30 grams is the amount of protein that tends to make a meal feel satisfying. You can do the math to figure out whether a protein-added product is going to be helpful in your day’s diet.

I think this is the most important question about protein-added foods. It’s not hard to get protein in a meal; meats, dairy, tofu, beans, and grains all tend to supply plenty. So what is this protein-added thing you’re considering, and are you eating it instead of a traditional meal?

Here’s an example. If I’m heading straight from the gym to run some errands, and I need something to substitute for a meal—yeah, this isn’t great planning, but sometimes it happens—a protein bar with 20 grams of protein is a step in the right direction. Much better than a candy bar, anyway.

But then there are things like this "protein mix" trail mix: 7 grams of protein with 200 calories. A double serving would be 400 calories and only 14 grams of protein. Hardly a great choice if your goal is just to add to your protein intake for the day.

And then there are the chips that my kid, for a time, couldn't stop eating. He loves Doritos and such; on a whim, we bought him some protein chips (yes, these are a real thing). Are they better for him than the equivalent amount of Doritos? Arguably, sort of yes. But then he started arguing that since they have protein, he should be able to eat them in place of dinner. We nixed that, but admit it: Are you having that same argument with yourself, feeling better about a snack food because it contains extra protein? If so, the marketing is working—you’re feeling good about your supposedly healthy choices, even though you’re just eating a bag of chips.

#3450. Switch 2 Is Getting an All-new Gamecube Controller

8BitDo has a wireless take on a beloved gamepad

Super Smash Bros. fans, this one’s for you. Peripheral maker 8BitDo just revealed the GC Bluetooth Gamepad, a wireless spin on the GameCube controller meant for Nintendp Switch, Switch 2, and Windows PC. It’s available in the GameCube’s iconic purple-and-orange color palette and features the "classic GC design and iconic button layout," according to its product description. The controller can connect wirelessly via Bluetooth 5.0 or a 2.4 GHz adapter, and has wired support via a USB-C cable. All three connection types work with the original Switch and Switch 2, while only wired and 2.4 GHz wireless connections work on PC. The controller goes for $49.99 and ships on Dec. 10, 2026.

Nintendo released its own wireless GameCube controller for the Switch 2 last year. It was closely modeled after the original gamepad, with a few small changes, like additional buttons for better compatibility with the Switch 2.

The most obvious reason that both Nintendo and 8BitDo created modern versions of the GameCube controller is that the Switch 2 supports certain GameCube games through a Nintendo Switch Online subscription. Specifically, the service has beloved titles like The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker and F-Zero GX. You can even play Wario World on there, for some reason.

Beyond that, GameCube controllers have remained surprisingly relevant over the years thanks to Super Smash Bros. fans. The controller is still popular because many players first got into the series through Super Smash Bros. Melee on the GameCube, which maintains an active tournament circuit. Nintendo even officially re-released the original wired GameCube controller for the Wii U as a tie-in for Smash 4. The company later released a USB adapter that lets the original GameCube controller work with the original Switch when playing games like Super Smash Bros. Ultimate.

Another reason many players likely want a modern wireless GameCube controller is to play emulated games on PC. While reviews described Nintendo’s GameCube controller for the Switch 2 as faithful to the original, players found it wasn’t compatible with the original Switch or Windows by default, limiting its use cases. 8BitDo’s version of the gamepad works with both of these platforms. Additionally, the 8BitDo version costs $20 less than Nintendo’s official release. We’ll find out whether the third-party peripheral matches the feel of the beloved GameCube controller when it launches next month.

#3449. Meta's VR Glasses Could Be The Future Of Home Viewing (But They Probably Won't)

In stark contrast to the dire straits that the movie theater industry was in just a few years ago, 2026 has been especially encouraging to those of us who adore going to the movies. A big part of why that's changed lies in the industry's embrace of unique Premium Large Formats, with numerous releases this year having been shown in formats like IMAX, 4DX, Screen X, Dolby Cinema, and so on. Along the way, screening on celluloid (70mm in particular) have become a draw unto themselves, and some cities are home to even more specialized formats, among them Las Vegas' immersive Sphere and the Cosm experience. And while the biggest draw to movie theaters will always be good films, it's clear that audiences also enjoy an experience they can't get elsewhere.

As usual, however, the tech industry isn't far behind to try and stoke the competition between theaters and home viewing. While most consumers have been content with things like big screen 4K TV's or even their handheld devices for watching at home or on the go, the latest attempt to leap forward from these is just around the corner, in the form of Meta's VR Glasses. It's important to note that these are not the latest version of the smart glasses that have existed on the market since 2021, as they're explicitly not designed to be used while engaged in other activity. Instead, they're a cutting edge virtual/augmented reality system intended to bring together multiple work and entertainment options while idle.

I recently had the opportunity to try these glasses for myself, and their potential, especially for home viewing, is amazing. That said, there are some restrictions to them which, unless changed, mean they won't be replacing our existing personal devices anytime soon.

Although virtual reality, or VR, has existed in some form for decades, it's mostly been utilized as a gimmick more than a viable first choice for media. Fortunately, the folks behind Meta VR Glasses seem to understand this. I got to see a clip from the recent concert doc "Billie Eilish — Hit Me Hard and Soft: The Tour (Live in 3D)" on the glasses, and the experience was like I was watching it on a movie theater screen. That is to say that the aspect ratio was exactly the same as its theatrical exhibition, and the 3D display was pitch perfect. Turning my head in any direction didn't move the "screen," but kept it fixed in front of me, as if it was a physical object in the space, which is a very smart design.

While the James Cameron documentary acted as a demo of how watching most films and shows on the glasses would go, the Meta employees next showed me what they're calling "Enhanced Cinema." Using a clip from "Avengers: Infinity War" in which Thor (Chris Hemsworth) constructs Stormbreaker, the presentation was almost exactly akin to the Cosm experience. This meant that the film was playing on a similar fixed "display" in front of me, while all around me (literally 360 degrees — I checked!) was the environment of the forge on Nidavellir. It's an effect that's totally immersive but not distracting, nor does it betray the original intent of the film itself. After being told that Meta has an exclusive license with the IMAX corporation to present movies filmed for that format on the glasses, I have no doubt that the device could brilliantly replicate those screens for home viewing, and that's incredibly exciting.

While the Meta VR Glasses are not intended to replace a smartphone or similar device, they do seem to do a lot of what those devices do, only bigger and better. From working on VR video games and multiple computer monitors at once to allowing you to watch sports games as they broadcast while seeing the view from courtside, the glasses seem almost too good to be true as a personal media device.

This is where the catches come in. For one thing, watching something with other people at the same time can only occur depending on the content. For another, though they're engineered to be used while stationary, the temptation for people to wear them in public while walking (or, god forbid, driving) exists, and it's quite troubling. Then there's the fact that the glasses seem designed to only work with whatever services and content Meta allows. This means that us physical media fans are SOL, and as with any all-digital service, the content available on the glasses could be subject to change (or disappear) at any time. That's a lot to ask for a device priced at $1,299.99 USD, which is about the same as a new iPhone.

Note: Following publication, a representative for Meta did inform us that the VR glasses will support playback devices that are compatible via a wired DisplayPort-over-USB-C connection, meaning that additional content (like physical media) that the consumer has control over may be viewable on the glasses.

Right now, Meta's killer app beyond the tech itself are its exclusive licenses, such as with IMAX and James Cameron's Lightstorm Entertainment. The only way it'll compete with devices already on the market is if it can consistently deliver the quality experiences I got to have with it while being as user friendly as possible. If the glasses prove they can be used at home and on the go as smoothly as an iPhone can now, then they could be a game changer. Until then, they're just a gimmick, albeit a really nice one.

#3448. Lux Pascal, Sarah Pidgeon, Ella Rubin, and More Glammed Up for Chanel’s Watches and Fine Jewelry Dinner

“That is the highest compliment you could give anyone!” Lux Pascal says after I tell her she looks like Megan Draper from Mad Men. We’re at Chanel’s Watches and Fine Jewelry holiday dinner, held at Daniel Humm’s new eponymous restaurant, Humm, in the West Village. Pascal is in a ’60s black modish leather minidress that she’s paired with a cat eye. On her wrists are Chanel’s Première Galon watch and Coco Crush bracelets, which, like her rings and earrings, are all dotted with diamonds. As I look around, most of the celebrities dressed by the brand are wearing looks that show off their French fine accessories. Ella Rubin, the Gen Z star of the hit teen TV show Sterling Point, has upgraded a simple pair of vintage Levi’s with a sleek black-and-gold Première Ribbon watch and several diamond rings. This is not a night for hidden gems.

The Pierre Yovanovitch–designed restaurant is a verified New York power room at the moment: There’s Derek Blasberg talking to Sarah Pidgeon about books—War and Peace gets a name-check—and Architectural Digest’s Amy Astley in a corner with Metropolitan Museum of Art board member Robert Denning. Indrė Rockefeller is here, as is stylist Vanessa Traina. In a feat of fun seating arrangements, the Chanel team has sat Rubin next to another young Ella: Beatty, the recent star of Monster and daughter of Warren Beatty and Annette Bening. (Although, with all due respect to those lovely Ellas, the two neighbors I’d most like to eavesdrop on are Devon Lee Carlson and Jack Harlow.) At the bar I hear two fashion people gossiping about industry hiring rumors: “Lauren Sherman says there’s two people in the running,” they whisper about some gig. I think I know what they’re talking about, but not enough to print it.

Laura Love and Devon Lee Carlson on November 17, 2026, in New York City (Photo by Dimitrios Kambouris/WireImage)

Guests mill about because there’s much to mill about: Humm’s filled his restaurant with dozens of notable, site-specific artworks. Louise Bourgeois supplied 24 watercolor paintings, as well as a fantastical sterling silver cast of one of her sculptures, situated by the bar. (Tonight it’s serving mezcal sours with guava and an apple brandy highball.) Francesco Clemente painted not one, not two, but four celestial murals across two months, with motifs of abstract stars, animals, trains, and clocks. On the walls in the main dining room are 12 pigment drawings by Roni Horn. Then there’s all the work by Rashid Johnson: In the lounge—which for this event doubles as a red carpet—hangs his painting Untitled Homes. With Yovanovitch, he also built a custom host stand cast in aluminum and painted red. It’s so textural that you can see the fingerprints, and a number of guests gather around it as the maître d’ explains Johnson’s artistic process like he’s a docent at The Met.

Chanel has decorated the tables with long taper candles and arrangements of deep fuchsia peonies and burgundy garden roses. Waiters serve Humm’s signature everything caviar bagels. When I think about ordering something other than the chicken, a waiter tells me not to. He’s right.

At the end of the night, after most guests are a few glasses of red wine (or martinis) deep, Pidgeon herself grabs a microphone. The event, as it turns out, has a surprise performer: girlsweetvoiced. “She captures something that’s very honest,” Pidgeon says of the emerging singer-songwriter, who then belts out a cover of Joni Mitchell’s “California.” Title aside, it’s been a very New York night.

#3447. Everything You Should Know About Black Friday 2026 Sales: Early Deals, Dates, and Retailers

As is often the case with major sales these days, retailers are increasingly blurring the lines between early deals and the official start of a sale. Black Friday sales appear to be becoming a month-long event, with early deals appearing in the first week of the month. If you haven't been paying attention, major retailers have already put out their plans and even started churning out deals. But you're still in time to make this upcoming Black Friday sale a great one. Here is everything you need to know to prepare you for the big sale.

Black Friday is always the day after Thanksgiving. This year, Black Friday starts at midnight on Nov. 27. Cyber Monday is the Monday following Black Friday, which starts at midnight on Nov. 30.

The major retailers doing sales are the usual: Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, Home Depot, and many others. Currently, Walmart has publicized its plans already and has early deals available. Best Buy is offering one of the largest Black Friday and Cyber Week sales, with multiple events and early deals. Target has a three-day event. Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Cyber Monday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

Unlike Spring or Summer sales, Black Friday doesn't focus on specific categories, which means everything is fair game for discounts. In previous years, we've seen tech, tools, fitness equipment, outdoor supplies and furniture, bedding, video games, kitchen appliances, and more. This is one of the best times to make a list of what you need. You're likely to find what you're looking for discounted, and probably at its lowest price it has ever been. If you'd like to avoid having to do all that work, we always vet all of our deals for you. Just follow our Black Friday coverage.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

Yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

Prime Day and Black Friday are the two best times of the year to get the best deals on most purchases. Of course, depending on what you're shopping for, you might find other opportunities throughout the year, but in general, Prime Day and Black Friday have the best sales.

#3445. Why Websites Show the Wrong Server Location When You Use a VPN

There are many reasons why someone might use a VPN, but most often, it’s to conceal your real geographic location or prevent websites from tracking your online activity. It can also be a way to get around location-based restrictions that stop you from accessing certain websites or platforms.

When you connect to a VPN server in the United States, websites are supposed to detect that your online traffic is originating from the U.S. That way, you can access online platforms that use IP filters to block non-U.S. traffic or circumvent regional censorship when travelling outside the U.S. But if you connect to a VPN server in the United States while you’re vacationing in Mexico, and a website thinks your IP address is from Brazil, that might not solve your problem and may even add unnecessary complications.

If you’ve encountered something similar with your VPN provider, there are several fixes you can try. Depending on why your IP location is being misinterpreted, one of these should help you access the internet from the server location of your choice.

IP geolocation isn’t infallible. Websites rely on third-party IP databases to look up your location based on your current IP address. Maxmind, which has one of the largest such databases in existence, claims that its GeoIP products have a 99.8% accuracy. Lesser-known providers with smaller IP databases may be far less accurate.

Websites can also use more than just your IP address to estimate your location. For example, they can send WebRTC requests to your browser or directly query your device’s GPS. Moreover, VPN providers often have physical servers in one country while their IP addresses are registered to another country, and this discrepancy can also create issues. Let’s take a closer look at each of these problems individually, so you can find the fix that works best for you.

WebRTC is an open-source technology that lets your browser reduce latency when engaged in high-bandwidth tasks like streaming or video calls. Based on the IETF standard RFC 8828, it lets a website choose between your VPN server and your real IP address so it can establish the quickest path to transmit large amounts of data and reduce wait times or buffering.

But the catch with WebRTC is that it exposes both your VPN server and ISP-assigned addresses to websites, which can reveal your real IP location and cause websites to reject your VPN server country. Firefox now comes with built-in protections to prevent WebRTC leaks, while Chrome and Edge support third-party extensions like WebRTC Control that you can use to eliminate these issues. To check if your browser is leaking your real IP address during WebRTC requests, you can use a free tool like BrowserLeaks.

Even when a browser isn’t leaking your real IP address, DNS resolvers may fetch inaccurate location information if their nearest servers are too far from your current location. For example, a user in São Paulo may be geolocated to Chile when using Google Public DNS because that’s where Google’s nearest resolvers are located.

If you toggle on DNS leak protection in your VPN app, this will force websites to use your VPN’s resolver to perform DNS lookups. That often solves the problem, but, again, you can confirm the fix worked through a service like BrowserLeaks or IPLeaks.

Websites rely on IP databases like Maxmind, IP2Location, IPinfo, etc. to look up your exact location, but these databases get outdated quickly and need constant updating. Most of these databases also correct errors on request, but that takes some time. Also, each website has its own rules for how often it queries IP databases for updates.

Even when locations are updated in the actual database, a website may be sitting with outdated information unless it actively has refreshed it recently. MaxMind recommends doing this at least twice a week, but that’s ultimately up to the specific website.

VPN providers often rely on virtual servers that use IP addresses registered in a different region than the server’s physical location. For example, ExpressVPN notes that it serves IP addresses in Bolivia, Ecuador, Peru, Uruguay, and Venezuela through servers located physically in Brazil.

While this is usually to help with the lack of local infrastructure or strict surveillance laws in the region, many databases and analytics tools will flag the discrepancy for websites, leading to confusion and inconsistency regarding your actual server location. In these cases, your best bet is to switch your VPN server or use a dedicated IP address by signing up for a paid add-on for your VPN.

Before investing in a specific solution, it’s better to do a thorough lookup to make sure why your IP address is pointing to the wrong location and whether a WebRTC or DNS issue, virtual servers, or something else is the cause. Here’s how I’d go about it, step by step:

We’ll start by recording your baseline IP address, country, city, and ASN. With your VPN disconnected, navigate to IPConfig.co on your browser to grab your default IP details. I like this tool because it’s free and uses echoip to pull your location data straight from Maxmind. If you prefer using Terminal instead of your browser, you can also run curl ifconfig.co/json to grab these details in plain text format.

Now connect your VPN server. Then visit IPConfig.co again to note down the changed details.

Make sure the Country and Timezone fields match your current VPN server location. Also make sure the ASN (organization) field does not list your home ISP.

In case these details do not match your VPN server, run a WebRTC leak test and a DNS leak test using BrowserLeaks. If either of these tests doesn’t return your VPN server’s IP address, you’ve found your culprit.

If both the leak tests come back clean but a specific site still gets your location wrong, the issue is likely originating from an outdated database or virtual server.

There’s no surefire way to solve IP location mismatches for good. But if it happens often enough to disrupt your internet use, you can consider switching to a different VPN server and getting a browser add-on that prevents WebRTC leaks. If that doesn’t work, I’d consider buying a dedicated IP address that isn’t based on a virtual server. While many IP databases like MaxMind or IP2Location also have ways to request a location correction, that takes a while to go through and isn’t worth the effort unless it’s a permanent IP address registered through your ISP.

#3444. Robert Pattinson Is the New James Bond—Revisit 007’s Style Legacy Here

There must be no male character across film history who has done more for menswear—and for the suit—than Bond, James Bond.

That is in part because the sartorial premise of Bond, the suave British spy, is remarkably simple: Presumably, all it takes to embody 007 is a black tuxedo, a sexy watch, and a pair of well-buffed dress shoes. And yet, as Daniel Craig, Pierce Brosnan, Sean Connery, and other dangerously handsome men have proven, a mere suit does not a 007 make. This is why, despite Bond being one of the most popular film characters of all time, you will rarely see ordinary men dare to take him on as a Halloween costume. There’s simply more to making Bond than a good tux.

Denis Villeneuve is set to direct the next era of the franchise, now under the creative control of Amazon MGM, and Robert Pattinson has been chosen to reincarnate the character conceived by Ian Fleming in 1953. In the announcement clip for Pattinson’s casting, the actor looks the part in a black tuxedo and white shirt, but it’s his eyes, which pierce through the camera rather than down the barrel of his gun, that do most of the talking and offer a suggestion of what Pattinson’s Bond may have to offer. Will he be a little darker and tortured, like his take on Batman? Or perhaps his Bond will be louche and somewhat pricklier.

A safer bet to make is that he will look good. One of the most enduring legacies of the James Bond franchise is how stylish both the character of Bond and the universe built around him have always been. Bond has appeared classic and timeless in style during each of the franchise’s eras, but hindsight offers a much richer perspective.

Pierce Brosnan, The World Is Not Enough, 1999.

As portrayed through the decades in the property’s famous title sequence, Bond is a silhouette—a classic, timeless silhouette. Fleming established the look in his development of the character when he made the suit his primary uniform. But it is Terence Young, the director of the first 007 films, who is responsible for the visual definition of Bond.

When Connery was cast as Bond for the first film, Dr. No (1962), Young, an avid wearer of suits himself, took him to his own tailor, Anthony Sinclair. We can credit Sinclair with developing the original silver screen Bond look: The suit was lighter in fit and tailoring than most other English suits at the time. The Bond suit had a soft shoulder and waist, but a strong, wide chest and a low button stance that elongated its wearer. Every Bond suit that’s followed has been measured to the standard of Sinclair’s work, and every Bond actor has had to compete with Connery’s charisma while wearing it.

Brosnan and his Brioni suits were indicative of the 1990s corporate look of the time. Craig wore Brioni too, but only for Casino Royale; Tom Ford created his subsequent suiting, which often stood out for the slim fit popular in the 2010s. Most memorable sartorially is Roger Moore’s take through the ’70s and ’80s, which often deviated from the sleekness that had come to define Bond by creating a little frisson with lighter, brighter fabrics and a bolder sense of playfulness.

The character of Bond, and the actor personifying him at a given time, have also become representative of a certain male standard: Connery in the ’60s, tan and athletic, or Brosnan in the ’90s, polished with lithe elegance. And then came Craig, whose casting was met with skepticism, to put it lightly. His arrival was marked by the image of the actor walking out of the ocean in tight swim trunks in Casino Royale. His strong legs, rounded shoulders, and sculpted, hairless chest cemented then and there the idea of what a leading man had become and would look like for the next two decades.

Daniel Craig as James Bond, Casino Royale, 2006.

Also synonymous with Bond are his watch and many vehicles. Most recently, Bond cars have all been made by Aston Martin, though Brosnan drove some spectacular BMWs. The official Bond timepiece since Brosnan’s turn has been Omega. But before such kinds of commercial partnerships were commonplace in Hollywood, Connery wore watches by Rolex, Gruen, and Breitling, while Moore wore pieces by Seiko.

With the news that Pattinson is taking on the mantle, an equally pressing question emerges: Who will be the first new Bond girl?

Some of the most memorable moments in the franchise’s history have been anchored by women. Halle Berry’s emergence from the ocean in an orange bikini and a white belt safekeeping a knife was only made better by the fact that this moment was an homage to the first Bond girl, Ursula Andress, and her ivory two-piece featuring a belt for her own weapon. Then there was Eva Green as Vesper Lynd in a slinky Versace dress in Casino Royale. But it didn’t get better than Grace Jones in A View to a Kill. As May Day, a fabulous femme fatale, Jones wore costumes designed for her by Azzedine Alaïa. How could anyone measure up?

Halle Berry and Pierce Brosnan, Die Another Day, 2002.

Roger Moore and Grace Jones, 1985, A View To a Kill, 1985.

Of course, we will have to see how stylistic choices play out in the 26th Bond film, which, like Bond movies of the past, will become emblematic of the era in which we live. It will also, as a creative project, have to contend with the way Hollywood operates today. The fact that Amazon now has full creative control over the franchise—the company acquired MGM, a co-owner of the Bond franchise rights, for $8.45 billion in 2022 and later struck a deal with the other co-owners in regard to creative authority—is the primary indication of that.

Pattinson will also be the first Bond with airtight fashion-brand deals. Craig was an Omega ambassador as an extension of his role as Bond, which made him a household name, and the 007s who came before him operated within a film industry that was not as closely connected to fashion.

Also unlike his predecessors, Pattinson is stepping into the role as a bona fide movie star who has appeared in three other major franchises (Harry Potter, Twilight, and Batman). He’s already one of the most prolific and bankable stars of his generation, and an undeniable part of being a movie star today is becoming the face of a franchise, a brand, or a product.

In September, Pattinson was announced as a global ambassador for Jaeger-LeCoultre, a Swiss watchmaker. But 007 has worn Omega watches onscreen for decades, a partnership between the brand and the franchise that dates back to the Brosnan years. If Omega’s partnership with the franchise remains for this new installment, it could present a potential conflict if Pattinson’s contract with Jaeger stipulates that he is not allowed to wear another brand’s watch onscreen or front related campaigns for competitors. It may sound like a banal preoccupation, as Pattinson has only just been cast, but there are millions of dollars at play, and actors today often make as much money from brand deals as they do from their turns onscreen.

Pattinson has also been an ambassador for Dior since 2013, serving first as a fragrance ambassador and subsequently as a face for ready-to-wear Dior Homme; he was originally tapped under Kris Van Assche, with his ambassadorship extending through Kim Jones’s tenure at the renamed Dior Men and now continuing with Jonathan Anderson at the helm of the French mega-brand. Will Anderson be providing his suits? The Irish designer has costumed films before, working with Luca Guadagnino on Challengers, Queer, and the upcoming Artificial. To design for the big screen would hardly be a stretch for him.

The real question is more existential: Should Bond wear high fashion? To return to the idea of the 007 silhouette, that in itself is counterintuitive to Pattinson saving the world in one of Anderson’s menswear takes on the famous Dior Bar jacket, with its nipped waist and slightly flared hem. And yet in this brave new world of brand deals, anything is possible.

#3443. 10 Years Ago Today: The Harry Potter Universe Expanded With A Star-Studded Spin-Off

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

"Harry Potter" is perhaps the defining franchise of the 2000s, but all good things must come to an end. That end originally came in 2011 with "Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows – Part 2" which had the biggest opening ever up to that point in cinema history. But creator J.K. Rowling and Warner Bros. weren't content to let the Wizarding World end there. Ten years ago, they expanded the universe with a star-studded spin-off.

Set decades before Harry Potter was even born, 2016's "Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them," which opened 10 years ago today, brought the action to America and focused on entirely new characters within the Wizarding World. Specifically Newt Scamander, played by Oscar-winner Eddie Redmayne. Redmayne had an unexpected inspiration for his performance, namely film icon Buster Keaton. The movie itself was loosely based on an in-universe textbook mentioned in the main series, with Rowling eventually releasing a version of the book, though it didn't contain a narrative.

The resulting prequel/spin-off takes place in 1926 centered on magizoologist Newt Scamander as he arrives in New York during a worldwide tour to research and rescue magical creatures. A mysterious magical being begins causing chaos in NYC, which threatens to expose the wizarding world to the muggles of Earth.

Redmayne was far from the only big star to secure a role in the spin-off. The stacked cast also includes but is not limited to Katherine Waterston, Dan Fogler, Alison Sudol, Samantha Morton, Ezra Miller, and Colin Farrell. "Fantastic Beats" also cast Johnny Depp as Grindelwald in a surprise appearance. Arguably the most important casting decision the movie made, with the benefit of hindsight.

J.K. Rowling wrote the script for "Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them" personally, which wasn't the case with the other "Harry Potter" movies. David Yates, who helmed the final four "Harry Potter" movies, was recruited to tackle the spin-off as well, providing a sturdy hand.

The majority of the core cast were on the upswing. This movie was expected to be a big break for all of them. In many ways, it was. "Fantastic Beasts" was dubbed a worthy extension of the Wizarding World in many reviews, with audiences tending to agree. Even if it wasn't effusive praise, it was good enough.

The movie was released in November 2016 and did quite well for itself, pulling in $816 million at the global box office. That was more than enough to convince Warner Bros. to double down, with four "Fantastic Beasts" sequels announced before the first one even hit theaters. Everyone involved fully expected this to be the long-term future for the "Harry Potter" franchise. What's perhaps most surprising about that, especially in light of the first movie's success, is the fact that the words Harry Potter don't appear anywhere in the title. All the same, audiences found it.

The train had left the station and everyone involved had every reason to believe, on paper, that people would show up for the sequels en masse. After all, the first installment scored well enough with critics and was the eighth-biggest movie of 2016 overall. Unfortunately, the future had different plans.

Warner Bros. and director David Yates wasted no time, with the second "Fantastic Beasts" installment dated for November 2018. Much of the cast returned, with new additions entering the fold. But in no small part due to forces beyond the studio's control, "The Crimes of Grindelwald" doomed "Fantastic Beasts."

The sequel pulled in more than $650 million at the box office, but made a lot less domestically and had to rely on international audiences to bail it out. Then there's the Depp of it all. Controversy started swirling around the actor due to his public feud with his ex-wife Amber Heard, involving accusations of domestic abuse. Depp later dropped out of the "Fantastic Beasts" franchise following a court case verdict. Mads Mikkelsen took over as Grindelwald in "The Secrets of Dumbledore," but the writing was on the wall.

The third installment made hardly more than $400 million globally, failing to break even theatrically. "The Secrets of Dumbledore" proved that the magic was gone, despite the appeal of Jude Law as a younger Albus Dumbledore in a lead role. The cast continued to be star-studded all along the way but, at a certain point, appealing casts only go so far. Especially in the 2020s when audiences are more content than ever to stay at home and stream something from the couch.

Controversy and middling results with diminishing returns eventually derailed "Fantastic Beasts." Ten years ago though, the spin-off arrived with a great deal of promise and a lot of potential. That potential just never proved out.

You can grab "Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them" on 4K, Blu-ray, or DVD from Amazon.

#3442. GTA 6's Completely Unrealistic Mountains Had to Be in the Game, Rockstar Says

GTA 6 takes some liberties with its world around Vice City

If you’ve ever spent time in and around Miami, Grand Theft Auto 6 is bound to delight you. Rockstar Games spared no expense in bringing the diverse world of Florida to life in digital form. Walk down the street in Vice City, and you’re sure to find an approximation of a bar you’ve actually been to. Head to the Leonida Keys, and you’ll find rows of houses on stilts. The attention to detail is impressive, but it also makes one odd detail about the map a little odd.

Go all the way north in Leonida, right up to Lummox County, and you’ll be able to go hiking and hunting in the mountains. As any Floridian will tell you, that’s not exactly reflective of the real Florida’s topography. Why take such a major creative liberty there when so much else about Leonida is grounded in realism? In an interview with Polygon, Rockstar North co-head Rob Nelson explained why GTA 6 takes players to the mountains.

Nelson said that one of the biggest challenges the team faced when designing the game was figuring out the map. Rockstar’s map team began working on the game in 2015, Nelson said, well before anyone else at the studio. While creating another city was easy enough for a team that has mastered that art, expanding to surrounding Florida locales was a tougher proposition. That’s because Florida is a very flat state.

The problem with depicting it as is, though, is that GTA players likely would have some expectations about what should be in a modern GTA map. GTA 5, for instance, built off of Los Angeles to create Los Santos. Because of that, the map has a lot of variety in elevation. That wouldn’t be possible if Leonida stuck too close to reality, so Rockstar ultimately decided to include some mountains to keep GTA 6 a little more consistent with GTA 5.

Though it may not be accurate, it’s a welcome addition to the map. As fun as it is to drive around Vice City, weaving around the same highways can get old. Lummox County offers a lot more open space for off-roading, biking, and other activities that just wouldn’t be possible in a city. For instance, when I found a bicycle perched atop a hill, I found myself racing down a natural BMX course that was built into the world. Every time I head up to Lummox County, it feels like I’m on vacation.

Crucially, it’s also the best date spot in the entire game. You can take Jason and Lucia out on impromptu dates throughout GTA 6, letting the couple play some mini-golf together or blow off steam at a shooting range. One of my favorite play sessions so far simply happened when I got the two in a truck and took them up north to a part of the map I’d never seen. We got out when we found a hiking trail and wound up stumbling into some ruins high up on a hill. It was a peaceful moment of discovery that the two got to share together. Moments like that are what make GTA 6 special, and Leonida’s intricate design is the thing that powers it all.

Rockstar’s magnum opus searches for love and catharsis in desperate times — and finds them

#3441. Hackers Now Want Your Browser Sessions More Than Your Passwords, but You Can Stop Them

There’s a very organized dark web supply chain that attackers use to trade in stealer logs. Russian Market has effectively replaced Genesis Market as the new storefront for black hat cybercriminals, although much of the market has also shifted to private channels on Telegram.

According to threat analysts at DarkOwl, approximately 180,000 stealer logs were sold on Russian Market in just the first half of 2025. What's more, Russian Market is a well-designed storefront that users can access even without Onion links or the Tor browser. That means anyone could go there and buy a bunch of stealer logs to start attempting account takeovers at scale.

Meanwhile, Flare Research estimates that this isn’t even close to the actual scale of the threat, because 90% of stealer logs now surface privately on Telegram. There, automated chatbots let scammers shop for stealer logs like it’s Amazon, with options to filter by country, app, and account privilege. Logs sell for anywhere between $5 and $500 a piece, depending on the estimated value of the target accounts.

The easiest way to go about this is to take a look through all your active devices and their locations in your account settings on most websites. If you see a device or location you don’t recognize, you are likely the subject of an ongoing breach. However, keep in mind that this may not always be a reliable method if you use iCloud Private Relay or a VPN. Still, it's generally best practice to log out of all active sessions every once in a while and perform a fresh login to invalidate any unauthorized sessions.

Reset the passwords on your email account, enable two-factor authentication for added protection, and sign out of all sessions before doing a fresh login. Your email inbox is the single point of entry for most attacks because that’s where most websites send their verification codes or magic links.

Sign out of all active sessions on every account that you suspect is compromised. This will log out any attackers who are currently on a hijacked browsing session.

Change your passwords on every platform in order of priority. Start with banking websites, cloud storage providers, and password managers first.

Look through each compromised account’s third-party integrations and app permissions. Revoke access if you can’t recognize an app, or it looks suspicious. Also make sure to rotate any API keys that you’re currently using, since those may have been compromised as well.

But while the initiative has already been open-sourced, no other major online provider has begun offering native support for it as of this article. That means DBSC’s security benefits are limited to Google services like Gmail and Docs, Chrome for Windows, and third-party websites that offer single sign-on (SSO) options for your Google account. We might see a wider rollout in the near future, though.

#3440. Avengers: Doomsday's PG-13 Rating Explained

We are a month away from potentially the biggest box office weekend of 2026, with Dunesday set to blow Barbenheimer out of the water as both "Dune: Part Three" and "Avengers: Doomsday" make their way into theaters. These movies are aimed at similar audiences, yet they're vastly different when it comes to their tones and approaches to adapting popular characters for the big screen. Indeed, where Denis Villeneuve's cinematic takes on the "Dune" books have so far been somber and introspective, the road to "Doomsday" has been paved almost entirely with nostalgia.

To be sure, between Robert Downey Jr. returning to the Marvel Cinematic Universe (this time to play Doctor Doom), the latest Avengers roster featuring multiple beloved characters from the MCU's past, and several actors reprising their roles from 20th Century Fox's "X-Men" films, "Doomsday" has had no problem catching the attention and interest of virtually every kind of moviegoer out there. After all, where "Dune: Part Three" can afford to target older audiences given the mature themes of its source material, "Doomsday" is aimed at everyone with a pulse and a heartbeat.

Hence, it's no surprise to learn that the new "Avengers" movie is now officially rated PG-13, just like almost every other previous film entry in the MCU since 2008 (save for "Deadpool & Wolverine"). Per FilmRatings.com, the film earned this rating from the Motion Picture Association (MPA) based on its "violence/action, bloody images, and language."

Just in case it needs to be said, "Avengers: Doomsday" was never going to be rated anything other than PG-13. The MCU's movies, in general, tend to feature too much intense action for any of them to garner a mere PG rating, yet they also tend to avoid going overboard into full-blown adult territory. At the same time, the explanation for its rating suggests "Doomsday" will make good on its promise of being one of the darker installments in the franchise.

Keeping that in mind, Marvel Studios and Disney were never going to allow a movie as costly as this one to get slapped with an R rating either, lest it severely limit the number of people who can pay to see it in a theater. And yes, "Deadpool & Wolverine" managed to become a massive success with an R-rating, but that was a different situation. Since the first two "Deadpool" films had been R-rated, it might've actually hurt the movie financially if it had tried to take the larger "Deadpool" property in a more family-friendly direction.

That's not to suggest that "Doomsday" won't be sufficiently dark or violent, though. Just too long ago, in fact, Sam Raimi pushed the PG-13 rating as far as humanly possible with 2022's "Doctor Strange In the Multiverse of Madness," the most gruesome Marvel movie yet. As you may recall, that film was filled with incredibly brutal death scenes, legitimate jump scares, and upsetting imagery that's not suitable for younger audiences. On the other hand, we can probably safely assume "Doomsday" won't push the envelope that far, given everything that's riding on it.

You can see what "Avengers: Doomsday" has to offer for yourself when it opens in theaters on December 18, 2026.

#3438. Aura's Second E-Ink Picture Frame Is Much Improved, and Much Cheaper

Last year, Aura released the Aura Ink, its first digital photo frame using an e-ink display rather than the LCD screens common to the other devices that made them the major player in the market (Aura customers have already uploaded more than one billion photos this year alone). When I reviewed the original 13-inch Aura Ink last year, I recommended it, with a few major reservations. Today, Aura announced its second-generation 10-inch Ink frame, and while I wouldn't exactly say they've solved every one of my issues, the new device is significantly improved—and much cheaper.

Most digital photo frames will remind you of an iPad with a decorative border around it. They're great for displaying hundreds of your photos with vibrant color, but not everyone loves the look, or the fact that these frames always need to be plugged in. An e-ink frame, on the other hand, uses a variant of the sort of low-power screen you'd find in a Kindle Colorsoft—less bright, but more paperlike, and much closer to the look of a traditionally printed photo.The Aura Ink is a great choice if you want a digital frame that looks more like a "real" photo and doesn't need to be plugged in and doesn't light up like a tablet (though it does have a light, it's really to make up for the fact that color e-ink screens don't reflect light very well, and thus can make your pictures look way too dark without an additional boost). You'll still get all the benefits of an LCD frame like the Aura Aspen, including the ability to load photos from anywhere using the versatile Aura app (you can now even text them directly to the frame), but you'll only need to charge it once every few months.

Now for the downsides: Where most digital frames allow you to flick between photos with a swipe, the Aura Ink is much more sluggish—switching from one photo to another takes about 45 seconds. While an LCD can match the colors in your photo exactly, e-ink uses a "dithering algorithm" to blend tiny pixels together to create the illusion of different hues ("millions" of them, according to Aura). In practice, this means up close, your pictures will look rather grainy, and the colors won't be nearly as bright as what you see on your phone screen.

All of that said, the Aura Ink is a great product, provided you know what you're buying, and the new 10-inch model offers some big upgrades over the 13-inch original released in 2025:

Resolution has been bumped up from 150 ppi to 200 ppi, so your images look more detailed and less grainy. (Though the difference is hard to capture in a photo, I can definitely see the improvement when comparing them side-by-side.)

Instead of the six base colors available on the older frame, the 10-inch Aura Ink blends nine different hues to approximate the colors in your images, offering greater color accuracy and improved contrast.

The transition effect when you move between photos has been updated to look more intentional—like waves of color moving across the screen versus a series of increasingly intense flashes.

It's a heck of a lot cheaper: $349, versus $499 for the 13-inch model—though that's still significantly pricier than Aura's most popular offering, the 10.1-inch Aura Carver, which starts around $200 less.

I write a lot about e-ink devices, from e-readers to tablets, and my common refrain, especially with color devices, is that they're great at what they do, but you should understand what they do before you plunk down your money. The Aura Ink will never look as bright and colorful as an LCD frame, and if you want a frame that can switch between images every few minutes or even play video, you'll need to look elsewhere (to maximize battery life, Aura recommends swapping photos on the Aura Ink no more than 12 times per day).

But if you want to display photos that look more like the ones that hung on the walls of your childhood home, in a frame that doesn't need to be plugged in all the time, you'll probably dig it, provided you can stomach the $350 price tag.

#3437. Avengers: The Kang Dynasty's Scrapped Doctor Doom Twist Explained By Marvel's Kevin Feige

As we march ever closer to "Avengers: Doomsday," it's easy to forget this movie was supposed to look very different. The original lead-in to "Avengers: Secret Wars" was supposed to be "Avengers: The Kang Dynasty," as directed by Destin Daniel Cretton (who had already helmed "Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings" for Marvel and would go on to direct "Spider-Man: Brand New Day").

Kang the Conqueror (Jonathan Majors), a time traveler who hails from the 31st century, appeared as the main villain of "Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania." A post-credits scene debuted the "Council of Kangs," or all of Kang's variants from a multiverse full of different timelines. But "Quantumania" earned unenthusiastic reviews upon its release in February 2023, and worse, Majors was arrested for assault the following month. (He was found guilty, and then fired by Marvel/Disney, in December 2023.)

Yeah, not exactly the launching pad you want for your next Thanos. Cue a pivot, and the announcement at San Diego Comic-Con 2024 that "Kang Dynasty" had been reworked into "Avengers: Doomsday," featuring Robert Downey Jr. returning to Marvel but as Doctor Doom, not Iron Man, as well as the return of "Infinity War" and "Endgame" directors Joe and Anthony Russo.

Now, this all seems like a "break glass in case of emergency" situation. But Marvel Studios President Kevin Feige, sitting down with Empire Magazine, now claims that even before "The Kang Dynasty" became "Doomsday," Kang was planned to be a red herring for Doom:

"People think there was a cause-and-effect with Jonathan's issues, and that certainly accelerated some things. But the Doom of it all was well underway before that. [...] It probably would still have been called 'The Kang Dynasty,' but it would have been a set-up for Doom, midway through that movie."

Kevin Feige, noting the "very delicate" situation with Jonathan Majors, told Empire that "[Marvel] didn't want to rush into any rash decisions in terms of employment." He acknowledged the changes to "The Kang Dynasty" started after the bad reception and underperformance of "Quantumania," noting:

"'Quantumania' was not received the way we would have liked. There are many elements of that that we're proud of, the Kang performance being one of them. But we were changing [The Kang Dynasty] even at that point."

Reading between the lines of Feige's claims, it would appear that once Majors was fired, the studio decided to push forward with Doom as the villain from the start instead of recasting Kang. But is this credible? I'll admit my first thought while reading this was, "Yeah, right!"

In his Empire interview, Feige appears to say the plans to bring in Doom to supplant Kang happened after the release of "Quantumania" but before Majors' arrest. "Quantumania" was released on February 17, 2023, and Majors was arrested on March 25, 2023. That seems like a pretty slim window to rework "The Kang Dynasty."

In November 2023, Variety reported that — at the annual Marvel Studios retreat held that past September — studio leadership was actively discussing how to move forward with Kang. ("Marvel is truly f***ed with the whole Kang angle," an insider was quoted as saying.) Apparently, the Marvel brain trust discussed replacing Kang with another villain, Doom specifically being named, as well as bringing back Avengers who died in "Endgame," like Robert Downey Jr. as Iron Man, to gin up excitement. As we now know, that's basically what Marvel did.

During a November 2023 appearance on the "Hot Mic" podcast, journalist Jeff Sneider claimed that Doom would appear in the then-upcoming "The Fantastic Four: First Steps" (which he did) as set up for him to show up in "Avengers: Secret Wars." However, Sneider said in that same interview that, "It'd be inaccurate to say [Doom is] the villain."

But Doom is the villain of Marvel Comics overall. The only reason the Marvel Cinematic Universe waited so long to use him is because 20th Century Fox held the film rights to his character. Once the Disney and Fox merger was completed in 2019, and Doom became available to Marvel Studios, Doom had to be high on any list of characters being considered for inclusion.

The "Secret Wars" comics — both the 1984 original and the 2015 pseudo-remake — also feature Doom as the main villain. In both, he attains godlike power and rules over a domain called Battleworld. If you're adapting "Secret Wars," the thought of using Doom has to cross your mind.

Kevin Feige's claim that Doom would take over "midway" through "The Kang Dynasty" also aligns with supposed leaked plot summaries for "Doomsday," which assert that Doom initially presents himself as an ally before revealing his true intentions. If that's accurate, it appears the movie still has the broad structure of "The Kang Dynasty," just with no Kang.

On the other hand, "Secret Wars" (especially the 2015 one) is a culmination of Doom's character. Rushing right into him becoming a God Emperor of Battleworld, without him being the villain in a "Fantastic Four" movie first? Yeah, that sounds like something that was "accelerated," per Feige.

"Avengers: Doomsday" releases on December 18, 2026.

#3436. 2026's Most Viral Movie with 97 Rotten Tomatoes Score Sets Streaming Date

You are not ready for what Nathan Fielder has in store

In recent years, Nathan Fielder has rightfully earned a place as one of the most provocative figures in modern comedy. Most recently, the actor, filmmaker, and pilot (it’s a long story) co-directed You Can See Everything, a three-hour, brain-bending documentary about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes and her partner Billy Evans in the days before Holmes began her 11-year prison sentence for defrauding investors.

Despite this seemingly obscure premise, the A24 movie has exceeded all expectations, grossing an impressive $93 million on a $7 million budget to become the 10th highest-grossing documentary of all time. The film has received widespread critical acclaim, with a 97% Tomatometer score and an even more impressive 97 average review score on Metacritic. Audiences are equally enthusiastic; the movie has a 95% user score on Rotten Tomatoes.

According to WhenToStream’s sources, You Can See Everything is coming to Video On Demand (VOD) and digital platforms on Nov. 24, 2026. This would put the movie on streaming right before Thanksgiving; one can hope it leads to many awkward Turkey Day meals. While we don’t know how much the movie will cost to rent or buy, it will likely be priced between $19.99 and $24.99 to rent, as has become standard for early digital releases. You Can See Everything is still in theaters in the U.S. and hasn’t opened worldwide yet. It’s coming to the U.K. on Nov. 20, and to France on Dec. 30.

It’s difficult to explain what makes You Can See Everything so mesmerizing without spoiling its bizarre twists and turns, but the gist is that the movie pitches itself as one thing, before slowly spiraling into something else. Fielder once again shows his ability to squeeze the absurdity out of people and situations, as he did on Nathan for You and The Rehearsal, leading to increasingly ridiculous, self-referential circumstances built around deception and performance.

The movie intersects with many contemporary issues, including the increasing right-wing radicalization of tech bros, and grows increasingly meta until it eventually calls into question whether documentaries can really uncover the “truth” at all. There’s a lot going on, and it’s best to see the madness unfold yourself.
