#3435. What Happens If We Break Letterboxd?

Earlier this month, the Trylon in Minneapolis gave audiences six chances over three days to see “Kanał,” Andrzej Wajda’s 1957 film about Polish resistance fighters retreating into the sewers of Warsaw. After opening night, programmer John Moret saw enthusiastic reviews on Letterboxd.

The next evening, he says, ticket sales picked up.

Moret could imagine the calculation for somebody still on the fence: “Oh, these people I trust went to go see this movie, and they loved it. And it’s just playing for two more days.”

On November 5, the New York Times reported that its parent company was in exclusive talks to buy Letterboxd for roughly $330 million. Under the deal being discussed, the popular film-logging site would likely keep operating on its own but use the Times Company’s advertising technology. Related Stories How GKIDS Home Releases Are Creating the Fandom They Want to See in the World IDA Documentary Awards 2026 Nominations: ‘You Can See Everything,’ ‘Concrete Land,’ and More Earn Nods

For theaters like the Trylon, what matters is whether cinephiles who went on opening night can still reach those who might go tomorrow. In 2026, that handoff is working remarkably well on Letterboxd.

Five days before “Kanał” opened, Ken Russell’s “The Devils” sold out at the Trylon on election night. Moret also co-founded the national Programmers’ Jam with Bret Berg, theatrical sales director at the American Genre Film Archive, and Dan Halsted of Portland’s Hollywood Theatre. When the Jam met in Los Angeles in May, Berg told IndieWire that programmers had access to more restorations than ever before; plus, more places to show them and a new audience coming through the doors.

We helped declare it the Golden Age of Repertory programming this spring. And when we spoke with Berg again this month, he said Letterboxd still drives “the FOMO of needing to be conversant in a movie of the moment.” For at least a few days in Minneapolis, that movie was “Kanał.”

Berg can see why a press company might be a good home for Letterboxd. He also remembers what the last sale made plain to him: Something cinephiles had spent years building was ultimately “just an asset to be bought and sold.” In the r/Letterboxd thread about the talks, one commenter saw an upside to a newspaper owning a site that rates movies. They also worried about paywalled features and ads, but liked the prospect of a ratings system free of “studios putting their fingers on the scale.”

If you come home from seeing a rep movie and write what you thought about it, your friends get a recommendation, the theater gets a little local press, Letterboxd itself gets something to put an ad next to, and as a matter of historical record? Years later, a “Kanał” fan who’s never even been to Minneapolis can land on the same page and read what it was like to see it with your crowd.

That’s a powerful engine for word-of-mouth, particularly among the very online. Moret keeps his own movie diary in a paper notebook these days, and told us he actually stopped posting what he watched on Letterboxd for a while because Trylon customers kept asking if that meant he was going to program it. “Sometimes a guy just wants to watch a movie,” he said.

Moret still regularly checks Letterboxd after screenings and uses that data to help shape his local scene. “I can see that night exactly how they responded,” he said. Moret said he’s seen Trylon patrons meet theater volunteers and follow them on Letterboxd afterward. He’s also heard from people who knew one another by their Letterboxd handles before they started going to showings together. Their community has real taste, and Moret’s job is to help subtly steer that momentum in exciting artistic directions.

He did have an ulterior motive for December’s Dede Allen series.

Moret explained to IndieWire that he wanted to show “Mike’s Murder,” James Bridges’ 1984 mystery starring Debra Winger as a bank teller trying to find out who killed her tennis instructor, and realized a Letterboxd user could make a pretty good list out of movies you didn’t know shared an editor like Allen. So, he put multiple of the craftsman’s offerings on the calendar — effectively allowing Trylon visitors to use a popular classic like “Dog Day Afternoon” on December 11 as an avenue toward “Mike’s Murder” on December 18. (Of course, both play in 35mm.)

On the supply end at the American Genre Film Archive, Berg reads the reviews from one town with the next town in mind. A joke review with thousands of likes might tell him very little about who’d pay to see a movie. But five people leaving a one-off screening at a DIY microcinema and feeling compelled to write about it could tell him quite a lot.

For someone deciding which films in the archive’s catalog deserve another look, that’s “some interesting free data,” and even Berg comes across movies he’s never heard of. Three and a half stars on Letterboxd is enough to make him give one a closer look. Then, he wants to know what kind of time people had. “How many audience moments are there? That’s what I care about.”

For a horror movie, he might be counting jump scares. With Herzog, he’s thinking about how many iconic images there are. (Referencing Les Blank’s “Ship of Dreams,” I personally suggested that the nation craves the sight of a steamship being pushed up a mountain. “Oh, it’s true,” Berg said.)

Berg also named Spectacle in Brooklyn and Whammy! in Los Angeles as places where he could count on hearing from a few people whether a movie made an impression. He said he can look for the same things he would on any research viewing, but with the added benefit of a crowd that makes a significant difference. Was everybody there to see a new restoration? How full was the room exactly?

Berg could always pick up the phone and ask someone like Moret how a screening went in Minneapolis. But Letterboxd gives them both a way to see and respond to the same information, connecting what happens in one theater to what programmers are noticing hit elsewhere.

Berg also thinks about who’s had the chance to write film books previously, and who has been taken seriously as a critic on a national stage. He singled out trans critics among the writers who can find an audience on Letterboxd without first persuading an editor to commission a review. In the end, the person who finally gets you to watch a movie might write three sentences half a century after the original reviews ran. They might also be the only person you encounter who’s heard of it.

If the people writing those Letterboxd reviews scatter across half a dozen sites, Berg could still go looking for them but it would take longer. And if Letterboxd imploded altogether, he’d expect “a return to gut feeling” that wouldn’t be bad — but might give the audience less of a voice.

Berg has some experience with the decision to leave. He still uses Vimeo for his day job, but the price helped persuade him to move his own project, Museum of Home Video, to a cheaper service. Finding another place to stream was manageable, and the Letterboxd equivalent of that transition is doable for most users too. First, it would mean finding another place to put your film log and reviews. Then, you’d have to find the people whose retro picks and ideas got you to sign up in the first place.

In that same Letterboxd Reddit thread, one person was already looking for the exit. “Any other apps people know about with similar list-building functionality?” they asked.

Andrew Masyk, the founder of rival tracking site Simkl, says its importer can bring over your watchlist, ratings, and the full text of your reviews, and custom lists can come over using a separate tool. That said, the comments and follows stay behind. “People have to find each other again, and that’s the hardest part of moving,” he wrote.

Masyk has every business reason to make switching easy. Even so, he figures people who have spent years keeping a movie diary on Letterboxd are mostly inclined to stay put. “What moves people is the product changing under them: core features going behind a paywall, heavier ads, or getting your data out becoming harder.” His test for a buyer is whether they keep that exit open. “The export button matters more than who owns the company,” he wrote.

Yes, the export button can save a Letterboxd review but the friend who used to see it in their feed still has to find it — and that can get more difficult long before anyone actually leaves Letterboxd. If a buyer gave sponsored posts more room in the feed, for instance, you could still log every film you see while missing the three sentences from a friend that would’ve gotten you to your local theater in time.

If Letterboxd breaks, the Trylon loses one way to fill a seat, and a programmer in another town loses one way to tell whether “Kanał” might fill a few seats there, too. As for regular film fans? Hear about “Kanał” on Monday, and you can go. Hear about it on Wednesday, and you’ve missed the boat.

#3434. The Next Major Fantasy Franchise Has Been Brewing For Over 30 Years

Every new fantasy movie wants to be the next "Lord of the Rings," and every new fantasy TV series wants to be the next "Game of Thrones." But both mediums are littered with the corpses of projects that failed to capture the zeitgeist. That includes perfect little gems like "Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves" (whose box office underperformance remains a crushing shame) and "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" (which has proven it's not easy to be "Game of Thrones" for a "Lord of the Rings" audience, even with a billion dollar budget).

Recently, you may have noticed a new fantasy franchise waiting in the wings. Well, "new" isn't the proper word, perhaps — millions of people are very familiar with it. But rather, new to the people who made "Lord of the Rings" and "Game of Thrones" a crossover success. I'm talking about Magic: The Gathering, the long-running fantasy card game that's been draining wallets and firing up imaginations since its debut in 1993, which is now poised to make the leap to the big and small screens with two different projects.

The first of them is a Netflix animated series called "Planeswalker" from showrunner Terry Matalas, who's already a geek favorite thanks to his strong work on "Star Trek: Picard" season 3 and Marvel's "VisionQuest." The second is a live-action feature film starring Maya Hawke from Legendary Pictures and Matt Johnson, the eclectic filmmaker behind titles as divergent as "Blackberry" and "Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie." It's the kind of two-pronged attack that suggests the timing is right for Magic, the biggest fish in its fantasy tabletop pond, to leap into the mainstream ocean.

Magic is about to have its crossover moment, and I think it has the goods to back it up.

Despite being an avid tabletop gamer and RPG player for over 20 years, I'm new to Magic, having only started playing and collecting this year to prepare for the new "Star Trek" set. However, the game got its hooks in me something fierce, and what was intended to be a brief dalliance has transformed into a new hobby/obsession/addiction.

I was initially drawn to the gameplay and its time-tested mechanics: simple to learn, hard to master, and infinitely flexible to match the style you find most entertaining. But the more time I spent in gaming shops, reading the flavor text at the bottom of a particularly dangerous card, noticing recurring characters across years of art, or chatting with people who have been collecting and playing for decades, I found myself increasingly interested in the world behind the game. Specifically, I was drawn to how the game's definition of fantasy was malleable, willing to blend traditional sword-and-sorcery with traditional folklore, gothic horror, science fiction, nautical adventure, and even zany swings like weird Westerns and multidimensional racing. If there's a creative itch to be scratched, the "planeswalkers" who anchor the narrative will surely expose a new world that will do the job nicely.

It's a universe where anything feels possible, starring varied and instantly recognizable heroes and villains who can travel between vastly different worlds as they journey on epic quests. It's a grand canvas with 33 years of history, characters, lore, and storytelling to build upon. There's more than enough for a movie series and TV show to draw on while still having enough to branch out indefinitely from there.

Following the formal announcement of "Planeswalker" at MagicCon, I asked the clerk at a local gaming shop if he was invested in Magic: The Gathering's world or if he just liked playing the game. He was emphatic: the gameplay hooked him, but the world and the characters and the expansive narrative is what kept him coming back. He spoke of the characters and their world with a reverence I've seen others bring to "Star Wars" and similarly rich universes.

The thin line separating the corners of various fantasy fandoms has eroded. The countless fans who line up for Sarah J. Maas novels and the nerds who crack open Magic booster packs aren't quite a circle, but it's a Venn diagram with a lot of overlap. The kind of weirdo fantasy that is Magic's bread and butter is now mainstream. The timing has never been better to open the door to the people devouring fantasy in other mediums and make it clear that the world of Magic: The Gathering is for them, too.

In recent years, Magic has (sometimes controversially) brought in outside franchises like Final Fantasy, Marvel, and yes, "Star Trek," to entice new players to play the game via their "Universe Beyond" label. I can attest firsthand that this works. But Magic is a great game and a rich world. The main draw for new fans shouldn't be just familiar IP on a Magic card. It should be the original world, fleshed out over three decades, itself. That's where a first-rate movie or show can do the heavy lifting.

The people who go to movie theaters every week and scroll the Netflix Top 10 every night may not realize that Magic offers a world as deep as Middle-earth or Westeros. The film and TV show must treat this universe itself as the main event, the reason to hit play or buy a ticket. A Magic: The Gathering series or movie will need more than just its players to be a true success ... and all of those new viewers pulled into a compelling fantasy epic become potential new players once they realize the game offers more of what they see on their screen.

If this film and this show are good (and they've certainly rounded up some promising talent), the Magic universe could be the next obsession for fantasy movie and TV fans. Even those who have never stepped into a gaming shop in their lives.

You are a Dutton — or you might as well be. You understand that some things are worth protecting at any cost, and that the modern world's indifference to history, to land, to legacy, is not something you're willing to accept quietly. You lead from the front, you carry your family's weight without complaint, and when someone threatens what's yours, you don't escalate — you finish it. You're not cruel. But you are absolute. In Yellowstone's world, that combination of ferocity and loyalty doesn't make you a villain. It makes you the only thing standing between everything that matters and everyone who wants to take it.

You thrive in the chaos of high-stakes negotiation, where the money is enormous, the margins are thin, and the wrong word in the wrong room can cost everyone everything. You're a fixer — the person called when a situation is already on fire and needs someone with the nerve to walk into it. West Texas oil country rewards exactly what you are: sharp, adaptable, unsentimental, and absolutely clear-eyed about what people want and what they'll do to get it. You're not naive enough to think this world is fair. You're smart enough to be the one deciding who it's fair to.

You are a Dwight Manfredi — someone who has served their time, paid their dues, and arrived somewhere unexpected with nothing but their reputation and their wits. You adapt without losing yourself. You build loyalty through respect rather than fear, though you're not above reminding people that the two aren't mutually exclusive. Tulsa King is for people who are still standing when everyone assumed they'd be finished — who find, in an unfamiliar place, that they're more capable than the world gave them credit for. You don't need a throne. You build one, wherever you happen to land.

You carry the weight of a system that is broken by design, and you do it anyway — because someone has to, and because you're the only one positioned to do it without the whole thing collapsing. Mike McLusky's world is for people who are comfortable operating where there are no good options, only less catastrophic ones. You speak every language: law enforcement, criminal, political, human. That fluency makes you invaluable and it makes you a target. You've made your peace with both. Mayor of Kingstown belongs to people who understand that keeping the peace is not the same as being at peace — and who do the job regardless.

Thornton isn’t eligible for a raise yet because he originally inked a three-season deal to star in the show. Should it be renewed for Season 4, he’s in line for a massive payday.

#3431. Tilda Swinton, Mark Ruffalo, Jacques Audiard, and Others Join in Protest of Jafar Panahi’s Prison Sentence

The film community is marshaling to support Oscar-nominated, dissident Iranian filmmaker Jafar Panahi, who was given a prison sentence of five years and one month by the Tehran Revolutionary Court back in October.

A letter initiated by the International Coalition for Filmmakers at Risk (and shared with Variety) so far features more than 200 signatories “deeply concerned by reports of the new prison sentence of five years and one month issued by the Tehran Revolutionary Court against Iranian filmmaker Jafar Panahi, in absentia.” Panahi returned to Iran in the spring following the end of Neon’s awards run for his Cannes Film Festival Palme d’Or winner “It Was Just an Accident,” nominated for Best International Feature and Best Original Screenplay at the 2026 Academy Awards. Related Stories What Happens If We Break Letterboxd? How GKIDS Home Releases Are Creating the Fandom They Want to See in the World

Actors and filmmakers who’ve signed the letter include Mark Ruffalo, Tilda Swinton, Jacques Audiard, Kleber Mendonça Filho, Catherine Breillat, Bertrand Bonello, Alice Braga, Arthur Harari, Asif Kapadia, Lucrecia Martel, Rob Epstein, Rodrigo Teixeira, Apichatpong Weerasethakul, Geeta Gandbhir, and many more. Festival leaders who signed the letter include Berlinale director Tricia Tuttle, New York Film Festival artistic director Dennis Lim, Venice’s Alberto Barbera, Telluride head Julie Huntsinger, and others — many of whom have hosted Panahi’s films across the last four decades.

Previously, Panahi was sentenced to one year in prison and a two-year ban on leaving Iran in December, in absentia. The new October 2026 sentence carries additional penalties, as the letter notes, including confiscation of his assets, freezing of his bank accounts, a two-year travel ban, and a two-year social media ban.

Panahi has a long history of legal entanglements with the Iranian government, which his films have criticized, including numerous imprisonments, a temporary house arrest, and being barred from participating in filmmaking activities. These punitive actions have frequently forced Panahi to make his films in secret or structure them around his filmmaking process or legal status — such as in the 2022 Venice prize winner “No Bears.”

Panahi’s bank accounts were frozen around the October sentencing, according to Panahi’s attorney Mostafa Nili. Panahi could not be reached in October for the sentencing, according to reports, despite being present in Iran as recently as September.

“In March 2026, the 66-year-old Mr. Panahi courageously decided to return to Iran, aware of the risks but having always spoken of his deep love for his country, and for his desire to stay and work there. In October 2026 he learned of the new court verdict against him after his bank accounts were frozen, his lawyer, Mostafa Nili, said in a statement to the Iranian press. The new charges against him remain unclear, but appear consistent with repeated efforts to intimidate him into ceasing his filmmaking. The case will now go to regional court, and the sentence can be appealed. This requires resources, but all of Mr. Panahi’s accounts have been blocked,” the letter states.

“We stand in solidarity with Mr. Panahi and all Iranians facing persecution for their work at the hands of their own government. We call on the Tehran Revolutionary Court to rescind all actions to penalize and imprison Mr. Panahi and to abide by the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights to which the Iranian government is a signatory.”

See the letter in full here. The Cannes Film Festival issued a similar letter in protest earlier this week.

#3430. The Rings Of Power Season 3's Incest Storyline Is A Big Change From The Books – And It Could Have Been Much Worse

One does not simply walk into spoilers. This article discusses major plot details up to "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" Season 3, Episode 6.

When it comes to a story as sprawling and complex as "The Lord of the Rings," not all adaptation changes are made equally. Throughout three seasons of "The Rings of Power," showrunners J.D. Payne and Patrick McKay have given us plenty to choose from. Some, like the arrival of Gandalf (Daniel Weyman), make perfect sense — although technically he's not meant to be involved in the action until centuries later in the timeline, you can understand why the series' creatives would want to speed things up a bit. Others, like the decision to keep Galadriel (Morfydd Clark) and her husband Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower) apart for so long, took longer to come into focus.

While many of the headlines will center on the deception of Charlie Vickers' Sauron and his breakthrough in figuring out how to forge the One Ring, an under-the-radar twist revealed itself all the way in the west on the island kingdom of Númenor. For several episodes, we've watched rivals and royal cousins Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle) and Míriel (Cynthia Addai-Robinson) come closer and closer to outright conflict over the throne. How they resolve this may seem to line up with author J.R.R. Tolkien's original telling, but the circumstances vary considerably.

Now we know why the Prime Video series changed things up. In the latest episode, their attempts to negotiate and avoid bloody civil war reach an impasse ... until Pharazôn finds an unexpected solution. Actually, make that a proposal. Yes, this is the moment "The Rings of Power" takes a page out of the "House of the Dragon" playbook. And it could've been much worse.

"The Lord of the Rings" may have a reputation as cozy, comforting fantasy with its plucky Hobbits and kindly old wizards, but don't look past the abject darkness at the heart of the story. J.R.R. Tolkien never shied away from the shortcomings of individuals throughout his tales — in fact, as a Catholic, he emphasized them. But all it takes is a cursory look at the lore and mythology preceding his most famous novels to realize just how much Middle-earth has in common with the likes of Westeros in "Game of Thrones."

Don't believe us? Look no further than how "The Rings of Power" begins to resolve one of its biggest storylines in Season 3. After several episodes of Númenor coming perilously close to tearing itself apart, we're left on an unsettling cliffhanger. The usurper Pharazôn suggests that he and Míriel repair this rift through an incestuous political marriage. It's clear from the look on Míriel's face that this is a measure of last resort, but everything about her arc thus far implies that she'll end up putting the greater good of the kingdom over her own desires (which, remember, are more romantically inclined towards Lloyd Owen's noble Elendil).

Still, this is far tamer than how Tolkien originally tells it. While the appendices found at the end of "The Return of the King" are light on details, other sources (like "The Silmarillion") explain how Pharazôn looked enviously upon the rightful heir Míriel, forced his cousin into marriage against her will and against all the laws of the land, and took power. Compared to this, "The Rings of Power" gives Míriel far more agency.

Those who know their J.R.R. Tolkien ought to be well familiar with where "The Rings of Power" is going next. (For those who don't, be advised this next section dives into major potential spoilers.) With only two episodes to go in Season 3 and the bulk of it likely taking place on the mainland, the Númenor plot will soon need to resolve itself. Míriel must still actually agree to Pharazôn's terms and avoid a costly battle, thus allowing their combined forces to look outwards and send their armada to assist the beleaguered Elves attempting to resist against Sauron.

But it's what comes next, almost certain to unfold in Season 4, that concerns us the most. With their power soon to be consolidated in an uneasy alliance, Míriel and Pharazôn will eventually have to contend with that pesky Dark Lord. According to the various texts, this is the pivotal inflection point that puts us on a path towards the inevitable Fall of Númenor. According to Tolkien's original writings, Númenor's entrance into the war has disastrous consequences. Granted, their fearsome army quickly overwhelms Sauron's own and leads to him being taken back to the island as a prisoner, but that's where all the troubles begin. Eventually, Sauron worms his way into Pharazôn's ear and convinces him to set his sights on the Valar themselves — a desperate gambit to stave off death among Mortal Men and seize the eternal life that's been denied them.

None of this ends well for Númenor, but we're getting ahead of ourselves. The final two episodes of "The Rings of Power" Season 3 stream November 25, 2026, on Prime Video.

#3429. PlayStation Network Outage Hits On GTA 6 Release Day Eve

PS5 users are reporting widespread technical issues as GTA 6 rolls out

What happens when a potential 250 million people try logging into a server at the same time? Problems, that's what. Thursday, Nov. 19 is the official release day for Grand Theft Auto 6 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X, and it appears Sony's platform, commonly known as PlayStation Network, is already buckling the day before under enormous demand for the world's most hyped game.

Many PS5 users tried to plan ahead by preloading the game starting on Nov. 10. Sony surely anticipated potential issues — the company has publicly treated GTA 6's release as if it were a first-party game — but that did little to prevent outages. Players around the world are facing messages like "Sony services are busy," "Too many failed connection attempts," or a mishmash of different errors. Though Sony's official status tracker currently lists the network as healthy, websites like Down Detector are seeing a sudden jump in reports related to the service. Most PS5 players say they're experiencing login issues with the PlayStation network, but there are also many reports of PSN server connection issues and update and download hiccups.

Whether you've seen codes like WS-116449-5, CE-34861-2, or WS-37505-0, they all point to the same thing: PlayStation's servers are facing serious strain.

GTA 6 is the follow-up to one of the most successful video games of all time, so the number of people trying to log in at once and download the game is likely massive. In the United States, it's the early afternoon — so many GTA fans probably just got off work and are all trying to do the same thing.

Though GTA 6 is not a multiplayer game that requires an online connection, players must download the title and its mandatory updates before they can enjoy it. This would have been the case even if GTA 6 had been printed on a disc — seemingly all major games require a day-one download for new patches or security reasons, like the recent PS5 jailbreak situation. This means that millions of people are trying to download hundreds of gigabytes of data at the same time, which was never going to end well.

There's no timeline for when PlayStation's servers might stabilize — and by extension, GTA 6 — but given the importance of this release, Sony are undoubtedly working on it.

Grand Theft Auto 6 officially launches on Nov. 19 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X.

#3428. 'GTA 6' Runs Best on This Console

Grand Theft Auto 6 might just be the most anticipated game of all time. It's been 13 years since Rockstar dropped GTA 5, and after years of rumors, leaks, and official announcements, the sixth mainstream installment in the series is nearly here. In fact, anyone who pre-ordered the game digitally can now pre-load it onto their console, if you want to ensure you're ready to play the second the game comes out.

Now, few of us will buy a game console specifically for GTA 6—unless you don't already have a current-generation PlayStation or Xbox. (The PC version of the game isn't expected until at least early 2027.) But, as it turns out, there's one specific console that can run GTA 6 better than the rest.

Rockstar confirmed as much in a post on Tuesday, which was meant to spread the news about pre-loading the game. But, interestingly, it spurred a discussion about the performance of the game itself, as well as which consoles are best to run it.

No matter which console you play GTA 6 on, Rockstar says that the game will only target 30 fps (frames per second). That's decided slow for a mainstream game in 2026. GTA 5 also shipped at 30 fps in 2013, but newer consoles can run it at higher frame rates. In fact, most games that launch on the latest generation of consoles can run at 60 fps, if not higher. While it's certainly not a dealbreaker, it is interesting that Rockstar's latest game can't run at a faster frame rate even on the PS5 Pro or the Xbox Series X.

To that point, Rockstar called out the PS5 Pro specifically in its post, announcing, "The PlayStation 5 Pro offers breathtaking visuals, with improved clarity through PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) and ray-traced shadows only available on PlayStation 5 Pro."

PSSR is Sony's AI upscaler, similar to options like DLSS from Nvidia, which uses AI to add extra graphical information to games in real time. That allows developers like Rockstar to run the game at a lower resolution to save on processing power, but still boost the visuals to reach a higher perceived resolution. As such, it's not as ideal as running the game at a higher resolution natively, but it can help improve the visuals without pushing the hardware beyond its limits. Meanwhile, ray-tracing offers realistic lighting effects and can also be graphically intense.

While PlayStation and Xbox players alike will be stuck at 30 fps, it seems only PS5 Pro gamers will be able to play the game with ray-tracing effects and AI upscaling. It's surprising that Xbox Series X players don't have similar benefits, as the hardware is more powerful than Xbox Series S. Rockstar didn't specify why only the PS5 Pro gets these upgrades.

In the post, Rockstar also announced that the PS5 version of GTA 6 takes advantage of other PlayStation-exclusive perks, like high-fidelity haptic feedback in the DualSense controller, spatial audio rendering using the PlayStation's Tempest 3D audio, as well as improved load times—though Rockstar didn't specify what those load times would be. These perks apply to all PS5 consoles, not just PS5 Pros. Rockstar goes so far as to say that GTA 6 plays best on PlayStation 5 consoles.

That's not to say that Microsoft's consoles are totally left out of the perks. Rockstar says that GTA 6 will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming on both Xbox Series X and S, as well as Xbox One. In addition, both PlayStation and Xbox gamers can play GTA 6 using Remote Play, so no one has to physically play on their console if they want to game on the go.

Again, there's no reason to go out and buy a specific console for GTA 6, so long as you have something that can run the game. After all, PS5 Pros are difficult to find, especially without wildly overpaying. But it's interesting that Rockstar has managed to give Sony's consoles the extra perks here, particularly since the company hasn't explained why that is.

#3426. ‘Gentle Monster’ Review: Léa Seydoux Learns the Truth About Her Husband in Marie Kreutzer’s Tough Study of Child Sex Abuse

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on May 15, 2026 during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. Netflix will release the film on its streaming platform on Wednesday, November 18.]

Marie Kreutzer’s “Gentle Monster” opens with virtuoso musician Lucy Weiss (Léa Seydoux) sitting at the piano in her Munich apartment and plunking out a stilted but affecting cover of Charles & Eddie’s neo-soul classic “Would I Lie to You?”

This is before her Austrian husband Philip (Laurence Rupp) — a documentary TV producer of marginal success — comes home in a burnout panic that spurs them to permanently relocate their family to a cottage in the German countryside. Before the authorities bang on their door with a warrant for Philip’s arrest, forcing Lucy to ride the elevator up to the clearly designated “child porn” floor of the local police station in order to learn the facts of his case. Before she begins to wonder, in rage and terror and desperate layers of self-protective doubt, whether the father of her young son Johnny (Malo Blanchet) might actually be capable of preying on other kids, or even his own.  Related Stories Tilda Swinton, Mark Ruffalo, Jacques Audiard, and Others Join in Protest of Jafar Panahi’s Prison Sentence What Happens If We Break Letterboxd?

Among other things, this tough and unflinching social drama is a study in how painful it can be for a rhetorical question — like “Would I lie to you, baby?,” for example — to sour into the stomach-churning stuff of an urgent mystery. For the terms of a relationship to change faster than the facts of the matter are able to keep up with, let alone the feelings that might attend to them. “There is no ‘off button’ for pedophilia,” someone explains to Lucy at one point. There isn’t an “off button” for love either.

Perhaps that’s why Lucy was able to ignore the signs for so long, some of which the audience is given the chance to see in a dark and disquieting flashback that Kreutzer cleverly interjects during the movie’s second act. Perhaps, despite the less intimate nature of their relationship, that’s why Kreutzer herself was so inclined to believe the male lead of her previous film (“Corsage”) when he privately disputed the rumors that he was guilty of similar crimes. Actor Florian Teichtmeister ultimately pleaded guilty to possessing more than 76,000 child sexual abuse files, more than half of which showed children under the age of 14.

While Kreutzer surely laments that situation on several different levels, this is neither a penitent film nor a self-exculpatory one (its origins trace back to before the production of “Corsage,” when the director read a newspaper article about a pedophile ring in North Rhine-Westphalia). It’s safe to assume that most people will feel sick to their souls on Lucy’s behalf, but “Gentle Monster” — its title pointedly depriving us of Lucy’s natural doubt — doesn’t make any overt pleas for sympathy, just as it doesn’t render Philip as the kind of demon that anyone might see coming a mile away.

In the context of such a terrible crime, Kreutzer is naturally less concerned with right and wrong than she is with the way that even the most sordid type of abuse is able to disguise itself in domesticity. If victims are our friends and neighbors, then it stands to reason that perpetrators are too.

Hard-nosed and realistic as far as these things go, “Gentle Monster” only makes a few concessions to movie logic. The first and most obvious of those is that Lucy is a fantastically chic public figure of some renown, a Jacob Collier-like pianist known for deconstructing famous pop songs written by men — everything from George Michaels’ “Freedom” to The Cure’s “Boys Don’t Cry.” The latter bop proves especially instructional, as Lucy is fascinated by the fact that men are so much more honest about their emotions in music than they are in real life. Her mission is to take apart their words and question the meaning behind them, a semi-credible gimmick that Seydoux is able to sell on the strength of her confidence alone.

It’s true, of course, that men should never be trusted, but Lucy will soon find that her own feelings are just as liable to lead her astray. First, she convinces herself that relocating to the sticks might fix whatever’s going on with Philip — a choice that inspires her mom, played by an underwritten Catherine Deneuve, to crack that, “For a female artist, there’s only one thing worse than having children: moving to the countryside.” Then, once Philip is brought up on charges, Lucy does what she can to downplay the evidence of his deviancy. All fathers take videos of their sons, after all. Most of them don’t shoot on 8mm film or frame close-ups of their kids for the length of a portrait sitting, but Philip still imagines himself as an artist (which explains why he seems to be so cucked by his wife’s success), and he’s prone to saying things like “Faces say so much only after you’ve looked at them for some time.”

There are no histrionic scenes in which Lucy screams at people for doubting her husband’s innocence, and Seydoux’s implosive performance makes it seem as though — a little less with every passing detail she discovers — Lucy is only mad at herself for believing Philip’s rationalizations. He was doing it for a documentary. He only uploaded a video of Johnny to earn trust from the pedophile community. He was just acting as a fence for illicit content because he felt emasculated by his lack of income. Whatever he can say to convince this woman that it’s easier to blame herself for overreacting than it would be to contend with the true nature of his crimes. Nothing much really happens in this movie after Philip’s initial arrest, but the world viscerally shudders under Lucy’s feet every time one of her husband’s alibis falls apart.

Lucy’s image of Philip — the one she loves and clings to — is like a song that’s stuck in her head, and deconstructing that song turns out to be a challenge of a different sort. Her only potential ally in that process is special investigator Elsa Kühn (Jella Haase), who’s caught more pedophiles like Philip than she can count. As unmovable as Lucy is unmoored, the working-class Elsa is defined by the relative calm with which she navigates her own personal crisis: a senile father who keeps harassing his nurses.

The obviousness with which Kreutzer introduces Elsa into this story as a foil is offset by the uncertainty of the character’s purpose. On the one hand, Elsa could also be seen as collateral damage — as another casualty of a man whose inner life has betrayed the role he was meant to play in his family. On the other hand, Elsa’s permissive reaction to her father’s abuse introduces a less gendered hypocrisy into the mix, as the lack of sympathy she feels towards Lucy is undercut by her refusal to confront the rot in her own house.

In a film that refuses to “resolve” any of its drama, or to glibly suggest that there’s anything constructive we can do about any of this aside from staring it in the face, Elsa’s subplot is left to awkwardly jut out from the side of the central story, a semi-effective distraction from the fact that Lucy has little to do but wait for the other shoe to drop and worry if she can contain the social blowback. “Gentle Monster” doesn’t quite get that far, as Kreutzer limits the drama to a slow drip of despair, its queasy suspense rooted in the question of how sick the revelations about Philip will have to get before Lucy is finally able to see him for what he is — to hear the man behind the song, so to speak.

And so the ugliness of pedophilia itself, rather than the specifics of how Lucy comes to grips with it, assumes center stage as Kreutzer’s primary subject. Full of feeling but starved of an outlet for it, Lucy is gradually woven into the fabric of Judith Kaufmann’s widescreen framing, which invites natural beauty into this grimdark story at the same time as it makes its subject feel inescapable. The world assumes the texture of a gilded cage; life goes on, some of it as sparkling as her in-laws’ picturebook summer house in the Austrian Alps, but Lucy remains trapped in the discordant hell that surrounds her, and that no one else can seem to hear. If only she had always known how to listen so closely.

“Gentle Monster” premiered at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival.

#3425. One of the Best Comic Anti-Heroes of All Time Is Officially Getting His Own Netflix Series

Just about everyone loves a good antihero. Morally gray protagonists who are more than willing to engage in decidedly unheroic actions for the greater good have become more and more popular on-screen as audiences seek out more challenging and interesting characters. Comics, in particular, have birthed some of the most beloved leads of this kind, from Marvel's Punisher, Deadpool, and Wolverine, to John Constantine from DC, and Todd McFarlane's legendary Image Comics icon, Spawn. Just as it once introduced viewers to Jon Bernthal's rendition of Frank Castle, Netflix is now bringing another storied antihero to life from the pages of an independent classic that's been around for over 40 years.

The streamer has officially announced a new animated adaptation of Matt Wagner's long-running Dark Horse Comics noir title, Grendel. Accompanying the news is a new image giving a taste of what the series' gritty portrayal of New York could look like once it hits the screen, with the vigilante himself standing front and center. Bobak Esfarjani, the Emmy-winning producer of Apple TV's breakout horror comedy hit Widow's Bay, among other things, has been tapped as writer, showrunner, and executive producer. This project will be the latest addition to Netflix's ever-growing catalog of adult animation, which, to this point, has taken on games like Devil May Cry, Castlevania, and League of Legends and even ventured into the cinematic realm of King Kong with Skull Island.

First published in 1982, Grendel follows Hunter Rose, a successful author who becomes a masked vigilante after the love of his life is horrifically murdered. He dedicates his life to seeking vengeance, tearing through "street gangs, the elite, and New York City’s supernatural underworld" to find and put an end to her killer. During his quest, however, the opportunity to pursue a real life arises, forcing him to make a choice that could either save him or inevitably turn him into the very monster he's been hunting the whole time. Wagner issued an official statement praising the new project as a faithful embrace of his original comic from the storytelling to the action, writing:

"It’s incredibly exciting to see my creation finally make this leap to the animated screen! Netflix’s dynamic new series retains the source material’s dark adult themes and also brings a fresh and thrilling approach to the narrative. This is Grendel as I’ve always wanted to see the character portrayed — a hyper-kinetic level of action, bracing explosions of violence, and a poignant, engaging storyline.”

Handling the animation for Netflix's Grendel series is Bobbypills, the studio best known for their work on James Gunn's DC Creature Commandos series. They're familiar partners to Netflix, having previously been involved with Adi Shankar's Ubisoft mash-up Captain Laserhawk: A Blood Dragon Remix. Chris Tongue, Tim Wiesch, and Jay Komas also serve as executive producers for Dark Horse Entertainment, joining Lydia Antonini and Wagner. In a separate statement, Esfarjani expressed his gratitude and excitement to the entire team working with him on the comic adaptation, adding:

“Being able to bring a character as iconic as Grendel to life has been a true thrill. Having the support of Matt Wagner, my great EPs, and the awesome team of Netflix, has made it all the more exciting, and partnering with Bobbypills Studio has made it all a true joy.”

Stay tuned here at Collider for more on Netflix's Grendel adaptation as it comes together.

#3424. Lifehacker's Pick for the Best TV to Gift in 2026 Isn't Actually a TV

Welcome to Holiday Office Hours From the Labs, a collaborative multimedia project in which Lifehacker, CNET, ZDNET, and Mashable harness the power of our product testing laboratory and our editors' expertise to offer the best gift-buying recommendations possible. In this episode, we're talking televisions.

I recently did a deep dive into TV development history, checked out what was on shelves for 2026, and I concluded that the best gift TV you can give this year is, actually, a pair of sunglasses. The XBX by XReal video display glasses are basically a TV you can shove in your pocket. Check them out:

I looked past traditional sets for a couple of reasons. First, because as much as we all love a great show or movie, who actually buys someone a TV set as a gift? More importantly, there's the nature of television itself. Since it was invented in the late 1920s, television quality has been measured by how big the screen is and how clear and bright the picture is, but in 2026, a nothing-special 4K television delivers an image that is pixel-invisible to a typical viewer, and most of us don't have living rooms big enough to need a display bigger than 65 inches. I think the innovation in the space is going to come from the form factor and the use case, and what better form factor is there than a pair of sunglasses?

These glasses deliver the equivalent of a 142" TV viewed from across the room. It's hard to compare resolution to traditional TVs—technically, the display is 1080p in each eye, but because the TV is just millimeters from your eye, it looks much clearer than that. The peak brightness is 1,600 nits, bright enough for most rooms, and there's a totally opaque shield if you need it. The refresh rate is a crisp 120Hz. They support HDR10 and real-time SDR-to-HDR upscaling, offer billions of colors, and it's all in a package that weighs only 62 grams.

Then there are the use cases. It can act as a separate monitor for your computer; you can watch a different show than your roommate without bothering them; but most of all, these are great for flights. There is no situation in life that calls for a big screen TV more than a cross-country airplane flight. Slip these on with a pair of headphones, and you can fly to Boise in your own private, virtual theater.

They plug right into any device that supports USB-C video, there's no battery to remember to charge, and they cost less than $300. In other words: They're the perfect TV gift for the holidays, even if they aren't technically a TV.

#3423. Friday The 13th (2027) Movie Cast, Title And Everything We Know So Far

For 17 years, sex-crazed teenagers with a penchant for getting high and/or drunk have had a veritable field day. Jason Voorhees, horror's deadliest and most dedicated moralist has been nowhere to be seen. It was starting to look like the only thing that could vanquish Jason for good was a protracted lawsuit, but now, Horror, Inc., which controls the rights to the machete-wielding killer, has moved forward with a new installment titled "Jason." Barring more legal shenanigans, he's set to slay anew on August 13, 2027.

Horror, Inc., Jason Universe, and Cineverse announced the news in a press release, which includes the announcement of the new film's final girl, Natalie Alyn Lind as Lauren. You might know her from "Dutton Ranch" or the X-Men television series "The Gifted." I find it kinda curious that they're revealing the final girl so far ahead of time. It's typically not hard to identify who's going to be the last girl standing, but there have been some reasonably decent fake-outs in previous movies (I thought Barbara Howard's virginal Sara in "Friday the 13th: The Final Chapter" had a shot at surviving the night). I dunno, maybe they're planning to pull the rug out from under us and kill Lind off early.

The other major announcement is that stunt coordinator Schuyler White will don the hockey mask as Jason Voorhees. Horror, Inc.'s "franchise steward" Robbie Barsamian believes White has the build and presence to be the "most intimidating" Jason ever. Per Barsamian, "[White] approached this theatrical feature like the role of a lifetime, packing 30 pounds of solid muscle onto his 6'5″ frame and studying the iconic Jasons who came before him so that he feels like an unstoppable force of nature." We'll see about that.

"Jason" wrapped production today after a fairly brief shoot that started in October. It's directed by Steve Miner, who helmed "Friday the 13th Part II" and "Friday the 13th Part III" (in which Jason first slipped on the mask, pictured in the images above). In a recent interview with The Wrap, Barsamian gave fans an idea of what to expect. "This is the scariest and most brutal movie we've ever made," he said. Okay then.

He went on to say, "We made sure to hold onto all the core elements that make Jason and 'Friday the 13th' what it is. Innovative kills, practical effects, scares and that classic slasher energy, but we really raised the bar across the board. The kills in this film are easily the most creative, brutal, bloody and visceral we've ever done."

As for the fresh meat, the probable victims include Matt Corney ("High School Musical: The Musical: The Series") as Asher, Lilia Buckingham ("Hocus Pocus 2") as Madison, John Owen Lowe ("Unstable") as Jake, Summer Madison ("The Summer I Turned Pretty") as Emily, Selena Turner ("Will Trent") as Olive, Matthew Keoni Sato ("High School Musical: The Musical: The Series") as Lucas, Brook Sill ("Stranger Things") as Zoe, Guillermo Diaz ("Scandal") as Rick, Johnell Young ("Wu-Tang: An American Saga") as Frank, Sencere M. Brown ("Homage") as Chase, and Bryan Gael Guzman ("Nickel Boys") as Dylan.

When it comes to raising the bar on kills, I can't help but wonder if they'll try to measure up to the gloriously grotesque mayhem unleashed by Johnny in "In a Violent Nature." Horror fans have become accustomed to new levels of brutality. We'll see if the old pro Miner can recapture the slasher magic.

#3421. The 10 greatest games to never get a GOTY nomination

The Game Awards announced its 2026 nominations yesterday, though not without controversy. Grand Theft Auto 6 — a game that isn't even out yet — leads the pack with eight nominations, including Game of the Year. No indies managed to get a GOTY nomination this year, despite the release of acclaimed games like Mina the Hollower and Big Walk. Several blockbusters — including Polygon favorites like Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave and Pokémon Pokopia — were also snubbed for the night's biggest award.

While there's a lot to be said about 2026's Game Awards snubs, some of the greatest games of all time never received a GOTY nomination. While the games below may have been nominated (or won) in other Game Awards categories, they never got their fair shot at Game of the Year honors.

Where to play: PlayStation 4, Windows PC, Xbox One

Dark Souls 3 was a gorgeous, somber conclusion to FromSoftware's groundbreaking Dark Souls trilogy. By speeding up the pace of combat, Dark Souls 3 bridged Bloodborne and Elden Ring, streamlining an already iconic gameplay loop. To close out its trilogy, FromSoft proved it had complete mastery over the gameplay style it innovated years earlier.

Despite widespread acclaim, Dark Souls 3 was not nominated for Game of the Year in 2016, only getting a nod for Best RPG. Fans should take comfort in the fact that 2016 was an absolutely stacked year, though, with Overwatch, Doom, and Inside all competing for top honors. There's also the fact that very difficult games face an uphill battle in the GOTY race.

Where to play: Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, Windows PC, Xbox One

Outer Wilds is hard to categorize. At once an open-world explorer, an action adventure title, and a puzzle game, it dropped a traditional combat focus in favor of rewarding curiosity and knowledge. Couple that with a tightly written story, and you have one of the most immersive, combat-free gaming experiences of the decade.

Outer Wilds faced even stiffer competition than Dark Souls 3. 2019 was a competitive year, with Control, Death Stranding, Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice, Super Smash Bros. Ultimate, The Outer Worlds, and the Resident Evil 2 remake fighting for top honors. Several other great games, like Disco Elysium, Fire Emblem: Three Houses, and Star Wars Jedi: Fallen Order also failed to secure nominations. So, for an indie game — which tend to build popularity via word of mouth — Outer Wilds was always a deserving but unlikely nomination.

Where to play: Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, Windows PC, Xbox One

NieR:Automata this relatively obscure spin-off of Square Enix's Drakengard series to mainstream audiences. Its intricate, existential story and seamless transitions between bullet-hell, hack-and-slash, and side-scrolling gameplay left a mark on millions of gamers worldwide.

Automata lost the nomination race to games like Breath of the Wild, Super Mario Odyssey, and Horizon Zero Dawn — games with enormous mainstream appeal. Though Automata was a breakout critical and commercial success for its franchise, it still came from a relatively niche series. What's more, the game's heavy philosophical themes and dozens of endings may have been a bit opaque for voters.

Ghost of Yotei, the highly anticipated follow-up to 2020 GOTY nominee Ghost of Tsushima, is about as cinematic as a game can get. With influence from filmmakers like Takashi Miike (13 Assassins) and Shinichiro Watanabe (Cowboy Bebop), Ghost of Yotei even has a game mode inspired by the work of Seven Samurai director Akira Kurosawa. And, it shows off its stunning graphics and cinematic influences without compromising on fluid, intense gameplay.

Ghost of Yotei earned seven Game Awards nominations in 2025, including Best Direction, Narrative, Audio Design, Action/Adventure Game, and more. So many people were confused about how a game that, apparently had some of the best direction, design, action gameplay and storytelling of the year could miss out on a GOTY nomination. Polygon's Oli Welsh even said "you could have grown it in a lab to win Game of the Year." Unfortunately, Ghost of Yotei paid a sequel tax — critics thought it didn't distinguish itself from Ghost of Tsushima quite enough.

Donkey Kong Country: Tropical Freeze deserved better. It's an absolute masterclass in platformer design, with carefully themed levels and gimmicks that feel purposeful. Developers mastered a sense of momentum, getting players to chain satisfying rolls, jumps, and precise landings. Also, everything is set to an absolutely classic soundtrack by composer David Wise.

Tropical Freeze came out in 2014, the first year of the Game Awards, alongside titles like Bayonetta 2, Dark Souls 2, and Dragon Age: Inquisition. So, it didn't quite fit in with the kind of vibe the early Game Awards honored. Also, Tropical Freeze was initially a Wii U game. While a Nintendo Switch port has brought the game to platformer fans nationwide, the commercial failures of the Wii U hindered its success.

Where to play: Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, Windows PC, Xbox One

Considered one of the best games of the 2010s, Hollow Knight dropped players into a vast, rich world with minimal guidance. Since 2017, millions of gamers have uncovered Hallownest's secrets, pieced together its tragic history, and died a lot. (It's a hard game!)

Hollow Knight didn't make a ton of headlines when it first came out. Like many other indie titles, it spread slowly via word of mouth. So, it lacked the kind of blockbuster momentum that can propel a game to a GOTY nod. Hollow Knight received an indirect nod last year through the nomination of its sequel Hollow Knight: Silksong, which lost out to Clair Obscur: Expedition 33.

Where to play: PlayStation 4, Windows PC, Xbox One

Konami and Bloober Team's Silent Hill 2 revisits one of the greatest psychological horror games of all time. It faithfully recreated the suffocating atmosphere and emotional weight of the 2001 original, while upgrading its gameplay to modern survival horror standards. Stronger performances and updated graphics made the terror and tragedy of Silent Hill 2 accessible to a new generation of gamers.

But horror games can be a tough sell at The Game Awards. Though high-profile blockbusters like Resident Evil 2 have been nominated, the only horror-adjacent game to bring home GOTY was The Last of Us Part II in 2020. Silent Hill 2 was also a remake; remakes are rarely nominated and have never won GOTY.

Fire Emblem: Three Houses was the best-selling mainline Fire Emblem game of all time, catapulting the series into Nintendo flagship status. Its iconic route split drew players into an intricate tale of war, love, and betrayal. It also sparked years upon years of discourse and fan arguments, which continue to this day. That ought to count for something.

Like Outer Wilds, Three Houses faced stiff competition amid a stacked 2019 gaming lineup. Also, Three Houses was a bit rough around the edges, particularly graphically. Couple that with a monastery hub that can feel repetitive (and the fact that you need to play the game four times to get the full story), and it's easy to understand why Three Houses failed to secure a GOTY nomination. That doesn't make it hurt less, though.

Where to play: Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 4, Windows PC, Xbox One

Yakuza 0 took on a lot. It features two protagonists, a high-stakes crime drama, over-the-top combat, and a quirky sense of humor, all without losing the series' integral "cool factor." It succeeded with flying colors, telling an emotional story about two iconic characters while leaving room for an all-important disco mini game.

When it was released overseas in 2016, Yakuza 0 was hampered by what Parasite director Bong Joon Ho called "the one-inch tall barrier of subtitles." Without an English dub upon release (it would eventually get one via its 2025 Director's Cut release), Yakuza 0's viral popularity was a slow burn with Western audiences. Once it launched on Steam in 2018, Yakuza 0 nearly doubled its past sales, and is now the best-selling game in the series. It may be the game that inspired a thousand memes — and took the Yakuza series into the mainstream — but it wasn't an overnight blockbuster.

Where to play: Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 5, Windows PC, Xbox Series X

Of course, this list would not be complete without Mina the Hollower, one of the most baffling GOTY nomination snubs of this year. Its intricately designed levels took an insane amount of effort, rivaling any AAA game out right now. That effort resulted in one of the year's best games, a loving homage to early Zelda games, the Game Boy Color, and Gothic horror.

While it received a nod for best indie game, Mina the Hollower was left off an indie-free GOTY nomination list. Though it was, critically speaking, one of the best received games of the year, it looks as though The Game Awards voters focused on mainstream blockbusters this year. It's also very, very hard, which may have dulled its mass appeal.

#3420. What to Expect From Best Buy's 2026 Black Friday and Cyber Monday Sales

Best Buy has announced the following events:

#3418. ’Pride and Prejudice’s 10-Part Spin-Off Is the Perfect Binge Before Its Christmas Special

Taylor Vollman is a contributor at Collider. She has long quipped, “T.V. is my name, TV is my game.” Fortuitous initials aside, at the heart of a tired joke is a simple truth — she has a lifelong passion for television. And along with it, an affinity for movies, music and pop culture.

After working in marketing for years, she wanted to sharpen her skills and went on to graduate with a master’s in journalism from Georgetown University. Taylor has since pursued entertainment writing and reporting.

Jane Austen is a preeminent romance author, with an impressive catalog of novels that are still relevant centuries later. Pride and Prejudice was her second novel published in 1813 and continues to be her most successful, repeatedly adapted for stage, screen, and page. It documents the at-times fraught romance of Elizabeth Bennett and Mr. Darcy, who must overcome misconceptions and differing stations in life to find happiness. But BritBox’s breakout hit of 2026 shifted its focus, instead turning to Elizabeth’s overlooked middle sister, Mary.

The Other Bennet Sister is based on Janice Hadlow’s 2020 novel of the same name, adapted for screen by Sarah Quintrell. Ella Bruccoleri stars as the socially awkward, but endearing titular character as she ventures to define herself separately from her critical family. With just 10, roughly half-hour-long episodes, it is the perfect weekend binge ahead of the upcoming release of its Christmas special.

As the last unmarried sibling, The Other Bennet Sister follows Mary Bennet as she sets out on a journey of self-discovery and romance. She is the bespectacled middle sister of Pride and Prejudice’s Elizabeth Bennet, often finding herself as the odd-woman out in their sibling set of five. Lacking the same wit, beauty, and coordination as her siblings, her negative self-image is reinforced by the highly critical Mrs. Bennet (Ruth Jones). Not only does she vocalize her worry that Mary could hinder proposals for her other daughters, but she actively thwarts perfectly serviceable matches. Mary explains her central issue in the opening lines of the series, which mimic the opening lines of the book. “It is a sad fact of life that if a young woman is unlucky enough to come into the world without expectations, she had better do all she can to ensure that she is beautiful. To be poor and handsome is misfortune enough, but to be penniless and plain is a hard fate, indeed,” says Bruccoleri.

With the assistance of some helpful extended family members and newfound friends, she journeys to London for work before finding herself caught up in a love triangle between Laurie Davidson as Mr. Ryder and Dónal Finn as Mr. Tom Hayward. Other Pride and Prejudice characters continue to reappear, including Charlotte Lucas (Anna Fenton-Garvey) and Mr. Collins (Ryan Sampson). Mary finds herself at odds with Caroline Bingley, played by Ted Lasso’s newest star Tanya Reynolds, who sees her as a rival in a dwindling marriage market.

The Other Bennet Sister struck a chord with audiences, recontextualizing characters from a beloved novel and giving a long-neglected figure her due. Mary’s constant pursuit of identity feels modern, despite the period setting. And with her family so often overlooking her, her ability to claim her own happiness feels like a true underdog story.

The Other Bennet Sister will show what comes after love and marriage in its upcoming three-episode Christmas special. BritBox released the trailer for the new installment, catching up with Mary as she struggles with her new identity as a married woman and the accompanying expectations. “As Mary Bennet, I’d often spoke my mind freely,” she says in the trailer, before adding she now feels “lost.” This backslide into insecurity comes as a shock to audiences who watched her work so diligently to become self-assured throughout Season 1. She’s not the only one feeling lost amid big life changes, with Mary’s frenemy Caroline Bingley seeking help ahead of giving birth to her first child.

Caroline isn’t the only returning character. The trailer shows not only Mrs. Bennet, but Mary reuniting with her sisters played by Poppy Gilbert, Maddie Close, Grace Hogg-Robinson, and Molly Wright. Mr. Ryder, Charlotte, and Varada Sethu as Ann Baxter are also set to return, with Nerys Amber Stocks joining as Lucy, Mary's new housemaid.

After the success of The Other Bennet Sister, BritBox announced it will apply the same treatment to other Jane Austen novels in its Austen Untold anthology. The Other Elliot Sister is up next, shifting the focus to Persuasion’s Elizabeth Elliot. Austen’s posthumously published final novel focused on Elizabeth’s younger sister Anne as she reconnected with her first love. Similarly told across 10 episodes, Quintrell is returning to adapt Hadlow’s upcoming novel of the same name.

Production on the series is expected to begin in 2027. “Elizabeth Elliot is an intriguing figure at the edges of Persuasion - someone we know just enough about to wonder what might be going on beneath the surface,” Jane Tranter, CEO of Bad Wolf, explained in a press release. “We’re delighted to be returning to the world of Jane Austen with the BBC and BritBox, and to bring another overlooked character to the centre of her own story as part of Austen Untold - an exciting new anthology that gives us the chance to explore Austen’s world through the eyes of characters whose stories have yet to be fully explored.”

There's currently a renewed interest in the works of Jane Austen, with the recently released film adaptation of Sense and Sensibility and Netflix's upcoming Pride & Prejudice miniseries. So now is the perfect time to binge The Other Bennet Sister, especially with its upcoming Christmas special just weeks away. The feel-good show will only take five hours to watch, so it is perfect for a weekend or even a long night in. And it’s just the start, with BritBox promising more stories centering Austen's overlooked characters.

An unusual period drama heroine navigates societal expectations on a journey to London from Meryton in Regency-era England.

#3417. 10 Google Privacy Hacks Everyone Should Know

Your Gmail account doesn't just have one email address. In fact, it has unlimited addresses, but you need a hack to utilize them. When you're signing up for a new service, you can add another word to your email address, as well as the "+" symbol, to create an alias. For example, if your email is "[email protected]," and you're signing up for an Amazon account, you can use "[email protected]" as your email address. The email will still end up in your main inbox, as if you simply used [email protected]. Not only can this trick turn one Gmail address into an unlimited number of addresses, but it also helps you identify who sold your email address to spammers, because those emails will have the alias in the "To" field.

Gmail's web view has a crucial security feature that lets you view session logs. This feature is inexplicably buried at the bottom of the inbox, and the font size is tiny, so it's easy to miss. To find it, log in to Gmail on the web, and scroll to the bottom of your inbox. Click the Details button in the bottom-right corner, below "Last account activity." This will show you a pop-up that lists the devices, apps, and locations you've recently logged in from. This makes it easy to see if there's been any suspicious activity in your Google account, and you can click the Security Checkup link in the pop-up to review this data. Just note that if you use a VPN or a service like iCloud Private Relay, you might not recognize your own device's location. To check if unwanted apps have access to your Google account, you can visit this settings page.

Google wants to show you personalized search results, which initially feels very helpful, but it also ends up trapping you in an algorithmic bubble. The best way to break out of your search bubble is to periodically use other search engines, but if you wish to stick to Google, you can disable personalized search recommendations in Google Search and the Play Store on Android. Go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized Recommendations and Play Personalization.

Google tracks your web and app activity by default, which includes your search history, voice data (if you use the speak-to-search feature), and activity from sites, apps, and devices that use Google services. However, associated information, such as your location data, is also saved to your Google profile, which you might not assume gets included in "Web & app activity." Fortunately, you can disable this tracking by going to this settings page, scrolling down to "Web & App Activity," and turning off all options in this section.

Google's Timeline feature saves your location in Google Maps to create a map of places you've visited. This is useful if you want to keep track of your recent stops; however, Google can use Timeline data to help businesses see how effective their ads were, or how likely you are to visit nearby stores. Its confirmation page confirms this: "Depending on your settings, activity saved as history in your Google Account, including ad interactions, may also be connected to Timeline data to help nearby businesses estimate the likelihood that people will visit their stores. No personal information is shared with businesses."

Timeline isn't enabled by default, but in case you enabled it a while ago, and are no longer using it, you can turn it off by going to this settings page. Click Turn off, and delete your activity to remove Timeline data from your Google account.

You can't fully escape Google's ads or tracking, but you can disable personalized ads to stop the company from using your account data to show ads. To do this, go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized ads.

While Google claims that it isn't using your emails to train AI, the company does offer AI features that make your emails feel more robotic than human. One of these is "Smart Reply," which offers email reply suggestions such as "Got it. See you soon." I can type that on my own, and I feel uncomfortable with Gmail analyzing the contents of my emails and replies to offer suggestions that I wouldn't use anyway. You can disable this by going to Gmail Settings > General, or by visiting this settings page. Scroll down to "Smart features," and turn off the checkbox next to it. This will disable Smart Compose, Smart Reply, suggestions for pending replies and follow-ups, spelling, grammar, and autocorrect.

A physical security key is a great security upgrade. It's a physical barrier that prevents most ways to hack into your account remotely. Even if someone discovers your email ID and password, and has access to your two-factor authentication code, they won't get in without physical access to that key. You can check out Google's support page for physical security keys for more information on compatibility and setting up your security keys.

Google uses data from Gmail and Google Drive to target ads, which means that your emails, files, and photos could be used for monetization. To stop this, you'll need to disable Personal Intelligence. To turn it off, visit this settings page, and click Turn off Personal Intelligence.

#3416. Here’s a HomeView feature that should come to every Apple device

This week, Apple started shipping the HomeView, its first display made for the smart home. On the HomeView, there’s one particularly nice feature that I’d love to see make its way to all Apple platforms: Ambient Dark Mode.

On iOS, iPadOS, and macOS today – the only flexibility you have on dark mode is whether or not it automatically switches on towards night time. While this is generally helpful and certainly appreciated, it isn’t super granular. Of course, you can adjust the time when it switches, but generally speaking its just a one time toggle.

With HomeView, you can enable ambient dark mode. In display settings, once you enable automatic dark mode, there’s the usual two settings you’d see on other Apple platforms: sunrise to sunset, as well as a custom schedule. HomeView takes it a step further with ambient mode, where the ambient light sensor determines whether or not you should be in light or dark mode.

Of course, a sunrise to sunset schedule generally works for most cases. However, if you’re up late at night with your lights turned on, you still might prefer light mode in an instance where macOS would generally be in dark mode. Similarly, if you wake up later in the day with your curtains shut, at say 11am, you might not want to immediately see light mode on your phone the second you open your eyes.

There are tons of good reasons for why someone would prefer ambient light-based automatic light and dark mode switching. HomeView software is the first Apple platform to enable this, and I’d love to see it come to iPhone, iPad, and Mac starting next year with OS 28.

#3415. Garmin Cyclists Can Now Make Themselves Appear on Waze in Real Time

Cyclists who ride with Garmin gear can now appear as live, moving icons on the Waze driving app, and nearby drivers will receive an alert to slow down and watch for them on the road.

For riders already using Garmin devices, opting in costs nothing and adds a new layer of safety, particularly on roads where drivers may not expect cyclists. The feature is rolling out now, but you should be aware of its limitations.

Riders can simply opt in once through Garmin Connect. After that, sharing starts automatically when an outdoor cycling activity begins and stops when the ride ends. While a ride is underway, Waze users near the cyclist see a cyclist icon move along the road and receive a Live Cycling Alert reminding them to slow down and stay aware.

The feature runs on LiveTrack, Garmin's existing live location-sharing tool, which lets friends and family follow a rider's real-time location, speed, course, and more. Garmin says this collaboration extends that peace of mind to motorists, giving them greater awareness of their surroundings.

Garmin notes its location sharing is temporary and session-based. The rider's name, identity, and route are hidden, and no personal information is shared or displayed in Waze. Drivers see only an anonymous icon and the alert.

You'll need a few things to get this feature up and running:

A compatible Garmin Edge bike computer or Garmin watch

A phone running Garmin Connect with a data connection

An outdoor cycling activity (the feature doesn't apply to indoor rides)

The good news is using the feature is free: LiveTrack costs nothing on compatible Garmin bike computers and watches, and Waze is free for drivers.

This new feature is a great safety perk, but there are real-world caveats worth considering:

This feature is for Waze only. Alerts reach drivers only when Waze is open on their phone. Google Maps, which has far more users, is excluded, so a large portion of the drivers you share the road with won't see you this way.

It depends on your phone's signal. Your position travels from the Garmin to your phone, then to Garmin's servers, then to Waze, and finally to the driver's phone. On a patchy rural signal, a few seconds of lag could put the icon on the wrong side of a bend from where you actually are. A rider who leaves their phone at home or whose phone loses signal simply won't show up on a Waze map, as a ride without a data connection is invisible to Waze.

Finally, remember to treat this safety feature as an extra perk, not a guarantee. At the end of the day, it isn't a replacement for bike lights, bright clothing, and defensive riding.

#3414. Indie App Spotlight: ‘Milton’ lets you turn your old iPad into a home dashboard

Welcome to Indie App Spotlight. This is a weekly 9to5Mac series where we showcase the latest apps in the indie app world. If you’re a developer and would like your app featured, get in contact.

Apple finally released its new HomeView this week, a smart display that serves at the center of your home. What if you don’t want to buy a new product though? Milton is an app for older iPads running iPadOS 17 and later that can serve a similar purpose.

Milton offers a customizable dashboard that allows you to put your most important tiles front and center. It can show your calendar, chores, shopping lists, weather, the clock, a photo frame, a to do list, and so much more. Everything you include will show on the family iPad, but it can also sync to iPhones if you want to check something remotely.

There’s one neat feature that’ll be fun for families: a points system. If your kids complete chores, they can be awarded points and as a parent you can set goals for what kids can earn with enough points. This system can be used to encourage kids to complete chores or follow routines. Parents can also sign off on the chores to ensure kids aren’t just tapping the complete button.

It also serves as a nice recipe guide. If you take photos of cookbooks, Milton can parse through what you captured and provide a step by step guide for cooking. If you don’t have certain ingredients, it can quickly be added to your shoping list.

This only scratches the surface of what Milton can do. You can read their website for the rest.

Here’s why Josh, the developer, decided to build Milton:

I’m a software engineer, and my partner is an oncology pharmacist. She wanted one place that kept our household organised: the calendar, the chores, the shopping, what’s for dinner. Skylight is expensive, and the iPad apps that do this charge a subscription every year. We wanted something that fit our lives, connected us as the Apple family we already are, and didn’t cost families a fortune.

Like most families, we had an old iPad lying around. We put it in a case with a magnet, stuck it to the fridge, and that became Milton.

Milton provides a very generous free offering on the App Store. The core organizer features are all available out of the box, but if you want to add more people to the app, sync across devices, or share the app with other family members (for their personal devices), you’ll need to purchase Milton Individual for $4.99 (one time purchase) or Milton Family for $14.99. Milton Family automatically shares with your iCloud family sharing group.

It’s rare for a short film to be named one of IndieWire’s favorite movies of the fall festival season. But last year, we couldn’t resist adding “DISC” to our roundup of must-see films. Directed by rising filmmaker Blake Winston Rice (who previously made “Tea” with Michael Gandolfini, another short that we championed) and co-written by Victoria Ratermanis, the film premiered at the 2025 Toronto International Film Festival before screening at more than 50 festivals worldwide. Now, just in time for the Best Live Action Short race, IndieWire can debut the full film as this month’s Vimeo Staff Pick.

“DISC” stars Ratermanis and indie filmmaker Jim Cummings as two conference attendees whose drunken hookup turns them into unexpected partners in crime when an inexplicable twist of fate turns their world upside down the following morning. We won’t spoil the unique premise, but an official synopsis reads: “After a one-night stand during a work conference, a man and woman wake to an unexpected crisis.
