#3412. 10 Movies Like ‘Interstellar’ You Should Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Christopher Nolan’s 2014 megahit Interstellar has it all: big sci-fi ideas, cool robots, ugly crying, and a Matt Damon character in need of rescuing. Grounded in the intensity of the human experience, this story of humanity’s potential extinction and the sacrifice of one man to save it doesn’t just deliver exotic planets and thrilling spaceship maneuvers; it also provides all the feels as Joseph Cooper (Matthew McConaughey) sacrifices everything he has in an effort to save the entire human race. It’s one of the best science fiction films ever made, with Nolan’s signature complexity, time manipulations, and emotional wallop. If you love this movie, here are ten more that offer a similar viewing experience.

If you loved both the special effects in Interstellar that make space travel feel viscerally thrilling (and terrifying) and the mind-blowing concepts, this is the film for you. Stanley Kubrick’s 1968 epic (written by sci-fi master Arthur C. Clarke) traces humanity’s development from mildly smart apes to spacefaring capitalists who discover a mysterious obelisk on the Moon that sparks a mission to Jupiter. While it operates in a colder emotional key than Nolan’s film, 2001: A Space Odyssey absolutely delivers on the epic side of things (and the cool—if slightly deranged and deadly—artificial intelligences). Stream 2001: A Space Odyssey on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re looking for more existential missions with somewhat reluctant heroes in space, Project Hail Mary is your next stop. When the Sun begins to dim due to the interference of an alien entity, scientists identify the one nearby star that isn’t being similarly affected. Brilliant molecular biologist Ryland Grace (Ryan Gosling) winds up forced to go on what is assumed to be a fatal, one-way mission into deep space to try to find a way to save humanity, unexpectedly assisted by a charming alien he names Rocky. It’s got the same emotional volume and big ideas as Interstellar, and fans of Nolan’s film will love it. Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+ or Philo, or rent it on Prime Video.

Part of what makes Interstellar so compelling is the stakes: The human race is slowly dying, and a handful of people must make incredible sacrifices to save it. That’s the vibe of Sunshine, set in a future where the Sun is dimming and a spacecraft is dispatched to deliver an enormous bomb designed to reignite the Sun’s fusion cycle. But the mission is the second attempt after the first ship vanished mysteriously seven years earlier, and when the new crew stumbles on the derelict wreck of the first mission, things quickly descend into violence and madness—but the crew remains determined to save the world, no matter the cost. Rent Sunshine on Prime Video.

Interstellar works in large part because of the emotional dynamics at play. McConaughey’s character leaves his children behind and is forced to witness them growing up without him, missing out on their lives and saddled with the knowledge that they resent him despite the necessity of his mission. Arrival is a First Contact story focused on language—linguist Louise Banks (Amy Adams) is drafted into an effort to understand the strange, complex language of the aliens. As she slowly builds to an understanding of how the aliens communicate and perceive time itself, her own heartbreak and loss come into play, giving this film a similarly devastating emotional punch. Stream Arrival on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Family dynamics and the toll of lonely space missions fuel Ad Astra, a film with the same emotional core as Interstellar. Twenty-nine years ago, famed astronaut Clifford McBride (Tommy Lee Jones) led the Lima Project, a space station around Neptune searching for intelligent life. Thirteen years ago, Earth lost contact with him. When bursts of energy emanating from Neptune threaten to end life on Earth, his son, Roy (Brad Pitt), is dispatched to try to make contact with his father. It’s an epic journey with a powerful climax that will satisfy fans of Interstellar in every way. Stream Ad Astra on Netflix or rent it on Prime Video.

Ridley Scott’s prequel to Alien has its flaws, but if you’re looking for a sense of epic spacefaring adventure in the same key as Interstellar, it’s perfect. When two scientists discover a star map apparently left behind by ancient aliens, they secure funding from the Wayland Corporation to organize a space expedition to the indicated planet. Accompanied by a colorful crew and the android David, they discover an apparently abandoned outpost of the species dubbed the Engineers. The story wrestles with questions about humanity’s origins, purpose, and potential—but this being an Alien film, things quickly turn horrifying. Rent Prometheus on Prime Video.

Adapted from Carl Sagan’s 1985 novel, Contact follows astronomer Dr. Ellie Arroway (Jodie Foster), who becomes involved with an effort to decipher a signal originating from the star Vega. The signal turns out to be a set of instructions for constructing a one-person spacecraft of some kind, and Arroway is eventually selected as the candidate to take the journey. There’s a sense of courage in the face of the unknown that’s similar to Interstellar, as well as the thrill of strapping into a spaceship and pressing the ignition. Plus, there’s the added bonus of seeing one of the greatest trick shots in cinematic history. Rent Contact on Prime Video.

Stanislaw Lem’s 1961 novel Solaris explores what Lem saw as the impossibility of ever understanding a truly alien life. The two major adaptations—Andrei Tarkovsky's 1972 version and Steven Soderbergh’s 2002 take starring George Clooney—are both worth watching, but Tarkovsky’s film is a masterpiece of psychological horror. The story is set mainly aboard a space station orbiting a planet covered in what appears to be a sentient "ocean" and chronicles the strange haunting and inexplicable experiences of the humans living on the station. If your favorite part of Interstellar is the ending when things get trippy and weird, you’ll probably love Solaris. Stream Solaris on HBO Max, Plex, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

The story of a mission to Jupiter’s moon Europa to search for intelligent life, Europa Report has the same sense of terrifying excitement that accompanies Interstellar’s missions to the different candidate planets. Leaning into the fragility of life in an environment not designed to support it, the mission crew face a steady stream of loss and danger as they work to catch sight of alien life on the frozen, deadly moon, ultimately faced with making terrifying sacrifices in order to provide humanity with the answers that it seeks. Stream Europa Report on Netflix, Kanopy, or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

A film based on a 1956 epic science fiction poem written by a Swedish Nobel Laureate might seem like an unlikely match for fans of Interstellar, but it’s actually perfect. As the Earth becomes uninhabitable, humanity begins launching ships to colonize Mars. When one such ship, the Aniara, is damaged and veers irreversibly off course, the passengers and crew are faced with the knowledge that they will sail off into the void without hope of rescue. Within a few years, despair has driven some to suicide and madness, while others cling to the possibility that they might yet find a way back. The film offers a different perspective on the existential crisis of humanity’s extinction, exploring the worst-case scenario to its bitter, bleak end. Stream Aniara on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

#3411. 6 Superhero Movies From the 2020s That Are 10/10 Masterpieces

With how prominent superhero movies have been for decades upon decades, one would think they'd eventually slow down—but no, they're still going and stronger than ever. With some amazing superhero movies released thus far in the 2020s, and some of them being among the highest-grossing movies of all time, it's hard to believe that superhero films will be going anywhere anytime soon.

Whether they come from the land of Marvel or DC Comics, there have been some astounding superhero adventures audiences have gone on in this new decade. While it may not be over just yet, what viewers have been treated to so far is more than worth noting. There are been some truly excellent projects that one could easily consider 10/10 masterpieces in one way or another.

If there's a superhero movie that flew under the radar of most, it is 2023's Blue Beetle. Directed by the excellent Angel Manuel Soto, starring the ever-lovable Xolo Maridueña, Blue Beetle ended up being a movie that—for those who went out to see it—was critically well-received. The title almost feels like Sam Raimi's Spider-Man for the DC universe, and that's helped it become very memorable.

The story of Jaime Reyes is such a strong one, filled to the brim with relatability. Following the young man as he comes back from college and struggles to find a job to help his family, he eventually comes across the Scarab through a freak incident, and dons the powers of the titular Blue Beetle. It's a true coming-of-age story that is a great watch from minute one to the final second. In a time of multiversal superhero movies releasing yearly, the likes of a blockbuster superhero movie like Blue Beetle felt like a true breath of fresh air in 2023.

James Gunn is a great filmmaker—this much has been clear for quite some time—and the general audience really became acquainted with his work in 2014 with the release of Guardians of the Galaxy. This Marvel trilogy became what he would most prominently be known for quite some time—until he became the co-head of DC Studios a short time after. So, with the release of this trilogy-capper, people knew Gunn had to really knock it out of the park to impress the audience.

Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3 is a great example of how to satisfyingly wrap up a trilogy, and give almost all of the primary characters a genuinely happy ending. Everyone gets a good conclusion to their character arcs, and it leaves the fans feeling like there's a true full-circle to the story that began in Guardians of the Galaxy. While he teases major deaths a good couple of times throughout the runtime, the Guardians all get a happy ending of some sort. When the standard for finales is typically leaving viewers with a heartbreaking death, getting to see these fan-favorites make their way out and end their journeys with a happy celebration is heartwarming.

Four powers, and four completely different kinds of person behind them. Here is what you would wake up with, what it would cost you, and why the MCU keeps handing it to somebody exactly like you.

You get the power that is really about taking the hit so that nobody else has to. Strength in the MCU always lands on people who were already carrying too much, which is exactly why it suits you.

You get the power that never switches off. Spider-sense is a gift and a nervous system on permanent alert, and the people who get it in these films are always the ones who were already worrying about everybody.

You get the quietest power in the building, and quietly the most useful. Invisibility comes with force fields for a reason, because the people who prefer not to be seen are usually the ones holding a shield around everybody else.

You get the biggest and least comfortable power on the list, the one that runs directly on feeling. Chaos magic is not really a superpower in the MCU so much as an emotional state with consequences attached.

For quite some time, Batman in cinema has been portrayed in a couple different ways, but not one that really hones in on his detective side (he's considered The World's Greatest Detective for a reason). Fans of the Big Bat finally were treated to a film that does just that in 2022, thanks to director Matt Reeves and superstar Robert Pattinson. The Batman is a crime noir that follows The Dark Knight in his second year as he attempts to solve the crimes of a new serial killer known simply as the Riddler (Paul Dano).

The Batman being so detective-focused is something that pleased a plethora of fans, and it allowed the story to be beyond engaging. Reeves' direction bleeds style and personality, making the movie feel one of a kind, and like a Gotham City that audiences have never experienced in previous Batman media. Pattinson does a stellar job bringing this loner hero to life in a way that truly gives him an amazing duality.

It's safe to say that the 2020s have treated James Gunn pretty well (until recently, that is). Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3 isn't the only smash hit he got to have in the 2020s. Another one of his best comes in the form of DC's The Suicide Squad. No one could have ever expected him to bring this franchise out from the grave it was exiled to after Suicide Squad, but he did.

This 2021 title is not only hilarious and visually vibrant, but has such a distinct heart and soul at the center of it. Much like Guardians of the Galaxy, James took these misfits and turned them into fully fleshed out, three-dimensional characters that are so easy to fall in love with. Granted, he managed to make the Guardians of the Galaxy MCU fan-favorites, so this seems in line with his previous superhero movie track record.

If one were to ask almost anyone, they'd say that Spider-Man: Brand New Day is the Spider-Man movie that people have been waiting about a decade for. After the conclusion of the trilogy that began with Spider-Man: Homecoming, fans were happy, but craving something different—a more grounded, street-level Spider-Man story. That is exactly what Spider-Man: Brand New Day is.

This project is so phenomenal and beloved that it has quickly become one of the highest-grossing movies of all time—landing in the current top three. The new director, Destin Daniel Cretton (known for Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings), did an exceptional job taking all the issues people had with the previous movies, and improving on as many of them as he could. Not only that, but it acts as the official introduction to the MCU's Jean Grey (Sadie Sink), and does so in a manner that feels natural and unforced.

There's absolutely no denying that Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse's release in 2018 changed the film medium forever. So, when it came to getting a sequel, it was hard to believe they could create something that could live up to the immense legacy that the 2018 title set. But, come 2023, audiences would soon see that Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse more than lives up to the legacy of the first film.

This sequel takes everything people loved about the first and expands upon those things. New art styles are introduced for new Spider-People, an incredible cast comes together to bring these characters to life, the attention to detail is off the charts, and the screenplay exceeds expectations. It is a living and breathing trolley problem that tests the protagonists in every single scene. There's no question that the trilogy-capper, Spider-Man: Beyond the Spider-Verse, has a gargantuant mountain to climb when it comes to following this film up.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3410. The Apple Watch's New 'Siri Recap' Feature Is Even Creepier Than I Expected

The “Siri Recap” feature that Apple announced in September is finally available in a developer beta, and I’ve spent the last 24 hours with the feature turned on. It’s even more unsettling than the “Live Rewind” feature that launched at the same time. It listens to all my conversations, and produces summaries that are both helpful and deeply creepy.

I have a button in the watch’s Control Center that can turn the recapping abilities off, but if I forget to do so, Siri listens to everything. I’ll get a recap of my entire evening, presented in roughly hour-long chunks, including things I would have completely forgotten I had even heard about.

The recaps somberly mention silly memes my kids were laughing about, and make major bullet points out of offhand remarks from brief conversations. If a conversation sticks to a single topic, I’ll often get a reasonably good summary of it, with specific facts and numbers highlighted; but just as often, Siri will get confused and mix up several topics or completely mishear a name or phrase.

Apple has four features that it considers part of “audio intelligence":

Music recognition, better known as Shazam. We’ve had a version of this on the Apple Watch for a long time now, although it has some improvements and now identifies music automatically.

Sound recognition, which can notify you about doorbells and babies crying. A version of this launched in 2020 as an accessibility feature.

Live Rewind, which gives you an on-wrist transcript of the last 15 seconds of detected speech.

Siri Recaps, which summarizes entire conversations for you to read on your phone.

Live Rewind had the flashiest demo from the Apple event: A server rattled off the day’s specials at a restaurant, and then the Apple Watch-wearing diner checked his watch to see a readout of exactly which dishes had just been mentioned. The utility is both obvious and kind of unnecessary: Why wouldn’t you just ask the server to repeat the list while they’re standing right there?

I haven’t found myself using Live Rewind, except out of curiosity about how the feature works. I discovered that it doesn’t pick up song lyrics very well, and also that by the time I think to check what was just said in a conversation, more than 15 seconds has passed since the part I was unsure about. I haven’t yet found a reason to use it for real.

But Siri Recaps? Those are both useful and unsettling. I enabled the feature, and decided to test it out later. But since it was on, it dutifully listened in as I picked up my son from school and gave him an update on an ailing family member’s health. We stopped by the library, and along the way we chatted about a variety of things: holiday travel plans, library policies, and the possibility of humans living in space in the future. Siri was listening to it all.

At least for now, the feature is only available in a developer beta, so sign up for that now if you want to try it. You'll need an Apple Watch Series 12 (or Ultra 4) and an iPhone 16 or better, excluding the 16e. (I have a 16 Pro, so I'm good.)

After you're updated to 27.3, go into the Watch app, tap Siri, and turn on Siri Recap. You can set a schedule for when it should listen (for example, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., if you want it on for the work day but off for the evening). You'll need to set a passcode on your watch, and you'll be guided through a step to upgrade your audio connection. The control center on the watch will have a button you can use to turn Siri recaps on and off at will. To read your recaps, go to the Siri app on your phone.

But still: I feel weird publishing the contents of these recaps, because they do contain things that people said to me in what they assumed was a private setting. I had the feature on when I attended a choir practice, and Siri recapped the brief chats I had with other choir members before and after practice. (Interestingly, it did not recap any of the quiet conversations I had with fellow sopranos while the tenors were rehearsing their part. I’m not sure if the watch was unable to hear us over the music, or if Siri is programmed not to listen when music is being played.)

Because speakers aren’t identified, it seems Siri doesn’t know what to do when there is a disagreement. A human note-taker would jot down that Person A made a point in favor of something, and person B made a point against. But when my son and I disagreed about how likely space colonization might be in the future, the recap didn’t reflect the separate positions that were put forth. It summarized the conversation as including “debating the feasibility and timeline of human space colonization and asteroid mining,” which isn’t exactly accurate, but close enough.

When it comes to the content of the discussion, the recap notes a bullet point of “skepticism regarding permanent space colonies within the next 100 years.” It didn’t include my reasons for being skeptical, and didn’t mention my son’s opposing viewpoint at all. If I were using this recap to jog my memory of the conversation, it wouldn’t be all that helpful.

Details are sometimes egregiously incorrect. After a discussion about a family member’s health, the recap had notes on the prognosis of “father.” The family member we discussed is not anybody’s father. Names in general seem to be a problem; I recommended a book to my son, and the recap includes notes about the content of the book, but not its title. The book’s author appears in the introduction to the recap (sort of a summary of a summary), but not in the content of the recap itself where the book is mentioned.

I should probably turn Siri recaps off. It seems wrong to let people chat with me without letting them know that their conversation is being ... well, not technically recorded, but basically recorded.

But it’s so tempting to leave it on so that I can review my day. Some of the details in the recaps are useful, like the dates that were discussed as options for a holiday party. The recaps will be deleted in about a week (unless I save them to the notes app), so if I want to remind myself of a conversation a few days ago, I should be able to scroll back through my recaps and find it.

I would be a fool to rely on the recaps, though. The most important points of a conversation are often left out; Siri doesn’t know what’s actually important, and there’s no way to guide it as to what to pay attention to. Specific details can be wrong, as I mentioned. There’s also no way to control when a “conversation” starts or stops, unless you are turning the recap feature on and off from the watch.

And there’s more: Not only are names usually omitted (wait, who did she say I should ask about that project?), the few identifiers that make it into the recap, like names of events, are often wrong. Subjects of discussion are often conflated in really unhelpful ways: My husband mentioned paying for certain course registrations for one of our children, and later I talked to that child about an unrelated exam. The recap got all of these things mixed up with each other and was wrong about pretty much every detail. About all the recap could usefully do is to remind me that something about AP U.S. History was discussed. Reading the recaps can be like reliving your day entirely in the passive voice.

#3409. ‘Elsinore’ Review: Andrew Scott’s Towering Performance as a Dying Actor Can’t Overcome AIDS-Movie Awards Bait Clichés

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on September 5, 2026 during the 2026 Telluride Film Festival. Focus Features will release the film in theaters Friday, November 20.]

There’s no question Andrew Scott, the 49-year-old Irish actor, has earned his position as one of the finest contemporary actors going. He’s in demand, but choosing wisely, and in roles that slyly play off his own status as an out gay man (a rare thing indeed) but with something off-center beneath, often a secret. He played Tom Ripley, one even more sociopathic than Matt Damon’s own iconically calculating Adonis, to devastating effect in the sinister Netflix series “Ripley,” there more explicitly grappling with the Patricia Highsmith character’s ambiguous (but was it?) sexuality. He played the Hot Priest who turned down a chance at heterosexual, secular love in “Fleabag,” of course, and starred in “All of Us Strangers” as a lonely adult orphan living in a glittering tower, bracing himself for romantic intimacy with Paul Mescal. Related Stories Jim Cummings Wakes Up to a Post-One-Night-Stand Crisis in ‘DISC’ — Watch the Short ‘Artificial’ Trailer: Andrew Garfield Stuns in Luca Guadagnino’s Sharp, Shocking, Funny Portrayal of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman

I also saw him playing up to nine roles in Anton Chekhov’s “Vanya” onstage in New York City last year as men and women of all sorts, showing an actor who can shimmy between genders and across ranges. He has the unmistakable warmth of someone you should trust, but with intrigue behind the curtain of many of his performances to suggest that maybe you shouldn’t. He’s that good.

Scott has now taken on what will, to this point, I suppose, go down as “the role of a lifetime” in director Simon Stone’s rueful, pained, and unremarkable new film drama “Elsinore” as Scottish actor Ian Charleson, who died of HIV/AIDS complications while portraying Hamlet at the National Theatre in London in 1990. Charleson’s story is unlikely to be one most are familiar with. Even the most public of deaths among the most publicly gay of people often still remain in hiding, though Charleson wasn’t out himself. He resisted pressures from his inner circle to announce his disease amid a stage run that miraculously lasted 24 performances. Actors then were afraid of damaging their reputations. It’s not that different now, even as many advancements have made HIV/AIDS feel locally like a plague of the past.

A blond-headed Scott throws himself valiantly into the role of Charleson with the urgency and commitment of any of his best work, but the problem isn’t his: It’s that the movie surrounding him dulls the greatness of his performance with its conventional storytelling, and over-complication in post. “Elsinore” is one of those movies where you can feel the filmmaker — here, Stone, known for both stage and screen — actively laboring to “open up the play” with the opportunities of film. But “Elsinore” was never a play. Instead, it’s a movie where every emotional beat worth lingering on, especially Charleson’s swan-song performances as Hamlet, is churned into a frenzied montage of editing that won’t let the material take a breath. Or the audience sink in.

Charleson played an Olympian athlete in the Best Picture-winning 1981 film “Chariots of Fire,” and an Anglican priest in the next year’s Best Picture topper, “Gandhi.” That was after playing an outré bisexual in the 1978 film “Jubilee,” directed by his former lover, the very openly gay director Derek Jarman, who died of AIDS in 1994. Aside from a handful of film credits, including one alluded to in “Elsinore” as Dario Argento’s giallo “Opera,” Charleson otherwise kept to the stage. Scott’s Charleson at one point in this film opines about how much more satisfying stage work is for an actor without an editor there to chop you up to pieces.

Stone, working from a screenplay by Stephen Beresford (himself a playwright), does not follow his protagonist’s lead. Every thoughtful consideration of Kaposi’s sarcoma lesions, or the retching of blood into buckets under the care of dutiful practitioner Dr. Margaret Johnson (Olivia Colman) to show the terrible realities of the disease, is whipped into what feels like a feature-length trailer. The best scenes out of the “Hamlet” production detailed here are tossed into a rushed montage near the movie’s end that gives us no sense of what we are promised is a performance of enormity. (The play in 1990 was directed by Richard Eyre, later the filmmaker behind features like the campy diva battle “Notes on a Scandal.” He’s played in “Elsinore” by Johnny Flynn.)

A couple of things are going on: “Elsinore” triggers in a watchful gay viewer’s senses the signifiers of what would be the AIDS awards-bait movie of serious gravitas. Tom Hanks’ Oscar-winning performance in “Philadelphia.” Ed Harris in “The Hours.” Everyone who came out of the cringey “Dallas Buyers Club” with Academy Awards in 2014. There are others, though more lost to time. We become suspicious of this device, especially when paired with great acting. Is HIV/AIDS being exploited in the package of a would-be Oscar hit? Or are we showing young queer audiences how it was, how we got to where we are, and how where that is still isn’t perfect? It can be both, but the structure of “Elsinore” tips toward the former.

Then, there’s a veritable, cheeky who’s-who of British gay literati and luminaries lingering about “Elsinore’s” 1989 London milieu that’s irresistible in theory, but often drab in execution. There’s Eyre, of course, and Jarman (David Dawson, as excellent and tender and wounded here as he was in his screen breakthrough “My Policeman”). The afterburn of his relationship with Charleson lingers affectingly, though. After some drinks, he invites Charleson home, but they instead part with one of those tacit kisses shared by people who once loved each other but can’t make it work anymore. There’s too much history here. The lingering scorches of Charleson’s secret affairs and friendships with various (and out) men make for the best parts of “Elsinore,” but there’s no life to the telling. (Joe Locke plays a young man also ailing in Johnson’s AIDS clinic alongside Charleson.)

The pallid grayness of Mike Eley’s cinematography is probably supposed to mimic the finality of HIV/AIDS taking hold, but there’s no passion aesthetically to counterbalance what becomes absolute misery onscreen to watch. I’m not in the business of comparing one gay social drama to another, but Robin Campillo’s 2017 Cannes-winning French drama “Beats Per Minute” imbued an albeit more activist-oriented story of ACT UP fighting against AIDS suppression in Paris with such heat and spectacle. Watching someone die of AIDS in a room becomes a bore unless anyone is given a reason to keep on living.

That reason is, of course, supposed to be Charleson’s performance in “Hamlet,” which is relegated to a whirlwind sequence at the movie’s end after many pained rehearsals where he refused to drop out (and where Johnson encouraged him to). Scott has a mesmerizing hold on his scenes, and he’s compelling to watch in his repartee with Colman as Johnson, who treated the disease at a time when it was most stigmatized. She named her groundbreaking HIV testing clinic after him; that’s how much he impacted her. We are told how much Charleson mattered to people, but never shown it. Which unfortunately shuffles off “Elsinore,” named after the Danish town where “Hamlet” was set and where its main character died, off to the realm of HIV/AIDS movies seeking prestige over deep feeling.

“Elsinore” premiered at the 2026 Telluride Film Festival. Focus Features releases it starting November 20.

#3408. Beats 360 vs Studio Pro: Here’s which Beats headphones you should buy

In September, Apple introduced the new Beats 360 headphones, the first overears from Beats since the Beats Studio Pro in 2023. That said, the older Beats Studio Pro still remain on sale at a lower price point – so it begs the question, which Beats headphones are more worthwhile?

One of the biggest differences between the two will be the price. The Beats Studio Pro, since they’re older, are regularly available on discount. Currently, you can pick up Beats Studio Pro for $199-249 on Amazon, compared to Beats 360, which aren’t discounted from their $349 launch pricing.

Despite being older and cheaper, the Beats Studio Pro have a couple advantages over the Beats 360. On top of the fact that they’re $100-150 cheaper, you may very well still want to consider them.

The biggest advantages, in my view, have to do with the form factor. The Beats Studio Pro can fold down into a much more compact size, whereas Beats 360 don’t fold at all. This means it’s easier to carry around the Beats Studio Pro.

Beats Studio Pro also offer a headphone jack, whereas Beats 360 don’t have any sort of wired audio at all, even over USB-C. This means Beats Studio Pro are easier to use in environments where bluetooth audio isn’t convenient, such as with a game console or on an airplane.

One of my favorite things about the Beats 360 is that they offer UltraPlush cushions you can swap into, but those cost extra. Beats Studio Pro by default come with UltraPlush cushions, so you can have a more comfortable experience out of the box.

Of course, Beats 360 are newer, so by default they do a number of things better. That includes:

Out of everything on this list, I’d say clearer transparency, stronger noise cancellation, and automatic device switching make the biggest difference. In my testing, its hard to hear with the transparency mode on the Beats Studio Pro, so I end up taking the headphones off to have conversation. With Beats 360, that isn’t the case.

As for noise cancellation and automatic device switching, I feel that if you’re buying Beats for the sake of having Apple headphones, you should buy the ones that offer true automatic device switching – and those are the Beats 360. Noise cancellation is more of a personal preference, but if you value having the best noise cancellation, the Beats 360 are noticeably better.

Lastly, the Beats 360 do have the customizable design going for them. While customization is more aesthetically pleasing, it also has an advantage longer term – when the earcups start wearing down over the years, you can quickly replace them on the Beats 360.

While it’s hard to overlook the fact that Beats Studio Pro come in at a much lower price point, I’d generally say that if you want a great pair of headphones that offer an Apple experience, you probably shouldn’t buy the Beats Studio Pro. The Beats Studio Pro are a fine pair of headphones for the price, but you certainly aren’t getting all of the same ecosystem creature comforts that Beats 360 offer.

That said, Beats 360 simply do not offer a headphone jack or a foldable design, and if those things matter to you, then Beats Studio Pro might still be the way to go. Beats Studio Pro also offer a ton of different color options that aren’t available on Beats 360, while costing $150 less.

#3407. 10 Hacks Every Reddit User Should Know

If you're looking for discussions, recommendations, or advice online, it's hard to avoid Reddit. From mainstream sports to niche crafts, it does seem that there's some kind of Reddit community for everyone. (And if there's not one, you can make one yourself.) If you're using Reddit, here are 10 hacks you should know about to improve your experience on the site.

Reddit used to let everyone view your post and comment history, but in recent years, you can make your profile private. You can hide your posts, comments, and the subreddits you're a part of. If you want to do this, click your profile icon once you've logged in to Reddit, and go to Settings > Profile. Alternatively, you can follow the direct link to Reddit's profile settings page. Click the drop-down menu next to Content & Activity, and select Hide all. You should also turn off Online Status on the same page to stop people from seeing when you're using Reddit.

Old Reddit lets you use the site's classic design, and I prefer it to the more modern UI. Old Reddit looks dated, but it doesn't have infinite scrolling, distracting animations, and a bunch of features designed to increase the time you spend on the platform. It's no wonder that Reddit is making it harder to access this version of the site. As long as it's around, you should switch to Old Reddit for a cleaner reading experience. You can do that by going to Reddit Settings > Preferences and enabling Default to Old Reddit. You can also visit old.reddit.com, though you'll need to sign in for access

Many subreddits use custom themes that range from beautiful to borderline unusable. If you want a more consistent UI across the site, you should disable these custom subreddit styles. Go to Reddit Settings > Preferences and turn off Use community themes. If you're using Old Reddit, click the preferences button in the top-right corner, and under "display options," disable allow subreddits to show me custom themes.

A multireddit is a feed that shows posts from a customized group of subreddits. You can think of it as a way to break out of Reddit's algorithms, and create your own Reddit feed. I use multireddits to follow all sports-related subs I'm interested in. I even have one for gaming, and one for fountain pens. It's a great way to create interest-specific feeds, and if you make them private, no one else can see them. To create one, click the Create custom feed button in the left pane in new Reddit. In the Old Reddit design, click the Create button in the left pane. Be sure to select the Private button to keep it from showing up for others. You can add as many subreddits as you like to the list, and bookmark the feed to access it whenever you wish to.

Reddit has recently adopted an Instagram-like experience for its feeds. It removed the ability to sort posts by new, controversial, best, etc., and instead offers "For You" and "Following." If you dislike this change, you can bypass it. I use Reddit on mobile Safari, and I recommend an extension called Sink It for Reddit. It can automatically redirect you to Old Reddit, and there's a feature that optimizes it for mobile, which brings back the old sorting options. You can also use third-party apps such as RedReader for Android, or RDX for Reddit on an iPhone or iPad to restore the old sorting options for Reddit posts.

After all these years, Reddit's built-in search still leaves something to be desired—at least, on the surface. To find posts on Reddit faster, use search filters on the site. For instance, adding "title:" to your search will limit the results to post titles, and boolean operators such as AND, OR, and NOT also work for advanced searches on the site.

#3406. Skydance to Combine Warner Bros. Television Group and Paramount Television Studios as One Big Studio

The corporate shakeups keep coming at Skydance, this time to the TV department. Warner Bros. Television Group and Paramount Television Studios are being combined as one big studio under Skydance, with WB’s Channing Dungey and Paramount’s Matt Thunell serving as presidents of the combined studio.

The new studio, which officially launches in early 2027 (the two entities will keep operating independently until then), will be known as Warner Bros. Television Studios. The entire studio will report to George Cheeks, co-chair and Chief Content Officer of Skydance TV. As previously announced, Dungey also serves as Chair of Skydance Global Cable Media, with oversight over all 50+ WB Discovery and Paramount cable brands. Related Stories IDA Documentary Awards 2026 Nominations: ‘You Can See Everything,’ ‘Concrete Land,’ and More Earn Nods A24’s TV Division Is Quietly Having as Strong a Year as Its Film Team

Together, Dungey and Thunell will lead all of scripted and unscripted programming, overseeing all creative departments. They will also oversee BET Studios and Warner Bros. International Television Production’s studios around the world.

CBS Studios will continue to operate independently, headed by President David Stapf, who also reports to Cheeks. CBS Studios International, Skydance Sports Entertainment and See It Now Studios will operate under the CBS Studios umbrella.

The new Warner Bros. Television Studios will be home to more than 120 active television series and some of the industry’s biggest global franchises, including “Harry Potter and The Philosopher’s Stone” (HBO), “The Pitt” (HBO Max), “Ted Lasso” (Apple TV), “Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage” (CBS), “Reacher” (Prime Video), “Marshals” (CBS), “Landman” (Paramount+), “Emily in Paris” (Netflix) and the upcoming series “Neuromancer” (Apple TV).

Yesterday, Skydance made some big changes to its film side of the business, appointing Don Granger and Kira Goldberg to lead Paramount’s Motion Picture Group and Jesse Ehrman to lead Warner Bros. #3405. Cross Season 3's Return Timeline On Prime Video Gets Huge New Update From Series Creator

EXCLUSIVE: A major new Cross season 3 production update has been revealed that gives insight into when the crime thriller might return to Prime Video.

An adaptation of James Patterson's Alex Cross books, the TV show debuted in 2024, with Aldis Hodge playing the titular detective who investigates horrific and fatal crimes. He's also dealt with losing his wife and doing whatever it takes to discover the truth behind her murder. After two seasons, production on Cross season 3 began back in April.

In an interview with ScreenRant's Brandon Zachary for The Greatest, Cross creator, showrunner and executive producer Ben Watkins revealed that filming has now wrapped on the eight-episode third season.

"We're in post-production," he revealed, before adding that the cast and crew had to come back for two additional days of filming "because we always film in DC." Around that same time, he was "writing page revisions" before cameras rolled again.

Watkins has also watched "some rough cuts of the scenes they did" and is "so happy" with what he's seen so far. "We just finished filming that," he added. "We're just finishing the editing of the episodes. We've even started scoring the episodes already."

The past several weeks have been "crazy" for Watkins, who explained that, aside from Cross, he's been conducting research for The Greatest, his new Muhammad Ali biopic series, so that he'll be ready to go if Prime Video orders a second season. Speaking of the famous boxer, Watkins was also in Louisville, Kentucky, to attend The Muhammad Ali Humanitarian Awards.

Ben Watkins: "This is how crazy life is right now. We're in post-production on season 3 of Cross, but we had two more days of filming because we always film in DC. I was in Louisville at the humanitarian awards for the Ali Center on Saturday and Sunday, and then I'm doing research for if we get season 2 [of The Greatest], so we brought writers with us while we're doing that. Then I'm on the flight in. I'm writing page revisions for the last two days of filming of Cross season 3, and Aldis Hodge and Isaiah Mustafa are coming in there, Coby Bell is in there, and it was really surreal because I'm in this moment where The Greatest has just dropped. I'm so blessed by that, and then Cross is so near and dear to my heart, and I'm on this text chain with my Cross team, getting everything going in DC. I've just seen some rough cuts of the scenes they did. I'm so happy. We just finished filming that. We're just finishing the editing of the episodes. We've even started scoring the episodes already."

Even though Cross season 3 is now in post-production, a release window has not been revealed by Watkins or Prime Video yet. However, the timelines for the previous installments could shed light on a possible premiere date.

The first season of Cross was in production from January to May 2023 before being released on Prime Video a year-and-a-half later in November 2024. Then the cast and crew returned to film season 2 from April to September 2024 before it premiered in February 2026, which meant there was a post-production gap of one year and five months.

Based on those trajectories, Cross season 3 could premiere on Prime Video in spring 2028. That is a long wait, of course, but it would align with the schedules of the first two seasons if that's when the show does end up returning.

Hodge's Cross co-stars in the most recent season were Matthew Lillard, Jeanine Mason, Wes Chatham, Alona Tal, Isaiah Mustafa, Juanita Jennings, Samantha Walkes, Melody Hurd, Caleb Elijah and Johnny Ray Gill. Ethan Embry, Ron Perlman and Robin Givens have joined the cast for the upcoming third season.

Cross, which has received largely positive reviews from critics throughout its run so far, introduced a billionaire named Lance Durand (Lillard) earlier this year, as Alex and Kayla Craig worked together to protect him from a killer, who was later revealed to be Luz.

The Cross season 2 finale showed Luz escaping after jumping from a bridge and Alex quitting after finding out that the FBI had been covering up Durand's potential crimes. This sets up a major shakeup and new conflicts for season 3, which is now in post-production.

#3403. 10 Hacks Every Hulu User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you don't like the content Hulu is suggesting for you, you have several options to curate your recommendations. "Disliking" a show or movie removes it from your Home view and You May Also Like entirely, so the only way you'll see that content is if you search for it. You can dislike on the Details page if you're watching on your TV or use the thumbs down on mobile or web. (The "Like" button will obviously influence your algorithm in the opposite way). If your "Continue Watching" queue is cluttered with shows you started but didn't like enough to finish, you can remove them from your watch history as well as the My Stuff list. This, too, will allow content to remain searchable but not suggested in other areas of the app.

If PIN protection is enabled, users must enter a four-digit PIN when switching between profiles on a single account. This is intended as a parental control feature, since it's available on non-Kids profiles and can keep children from accessing more mature content on an adult's profile. However, you can also enable this feature to keep other users from seeing your viewing history and preferences or influencing your algorithm by watching their content under your profile (accidentally or on purpose). To set up a PIN, log into your account on Hulu's website, select your profile, and go to Manage Profiles > Parental Controls. You'll have to choose a PIN and enter your password to confirm the changes.

Another approach to protecting your profile and algorithm is to set up separate profiles for specific use cases, such as when you have guests or if you host watch parties for certain shows. This keeps content from influencing your recommendations and prevents other viewers from seeing what's in your watch history or saved content (especially if there are things you want to keep private).

If you find that subtitles and captions are too bold—or not visible enough—you can change the font, color, size, and style from the default so they enhance your viewing experience rather than detracting from it. Hulu allows you to adjust the color and opacity of the font, background, and window so you get the right contrast, and you can also select the specific font and font scaling. On your streaming device, go to Settings > Subtitles & Captions, then hit the back button on your remote to save your preferences. You can update these settings on mobile and desktop as well.

If you have a long list of shows and films to watch but can't decide what to start next, look for the "Expiring Soon" badge to see which titles are leaving the service in the next two weeks. Badges display the number of days remaining, so you can determine what to prioritize and whether it's worth diving in based on how much time you have to finish before the expiration date. Go to "My Stuff" to monitor saved titles that are expiring soon.

If you've been watching Hulu under an account shared with family or friends and need to switch to your own subscription, you can transfer your profile to keep your watch history and settings intact instead of starting from scratch. You can initiate a profile transfer on a TV-connected device. Note that account holders have to approve transfer requests within seven days, and once expired, transfer requests cannot be resubmitted—so be sure to let the primary user know that you've made the request.

If you've shared your Hulu login information with friends or activated your account on devices you don't own, you may want to regularly audit where your account is being used and remove any that don't need access. This includes TVs in Airbnbs and hotels. If you stay logged in, unauthorized users may have access to your Hulu account and personal data. You can see activated devices (and their activation date) under Your Account > Watch Hulu on Your Devices > Manage Devices. Click Remove next to old or unrecognized devices.

Hulu has an offline mode that allows you to download shows and movies to watch when you don't have a network connection. This is useful for traveling or when you know your wifi or cell service will be limited. Downloads are only available on supported iOS and Android devices, which means you may have to consider how much space your content takes up. You can select High for video quality if you want maximum resolution, but you may want to choose Standard if you are short on storage. This option is available under Downloads > Settings > Video Quality on iOS and Account > Settings > Downloads > Video Quality on Android. Note that once you click play on downloaded content, you have 48 hours to watch it before it expires—so don't start it unless you are ready.

If you have a Hulu + Live TV subscription, you must designate a "Home" network, which determines the local channels included in your plan. You can update your location up to four times within a 12-month period, but this limitation is meant to prevent viewers outside a household from sharing a subscription. Hulu does allow you to stream live TV on mobile when you're away from your home network (within the U.S.) as long as you access your account on that network every 30 days. If you travel often, check in with your mobile device frequently to avoid being locked out when you're away. Note that you can still watch streaming content with no restrictions.

#3402. CBS’s Forgotten ‘NCIS’ Action Series Replacement Doesn’t Have a Single Bad Episode 17 Years Later

NCIS is one of the biggest television franchises in CBS history. The network still airs the flagship series, which recently reached its milestone 500th episode, along with the spin-offs NCIS: Origins and NCIS: New York. These spin-offs add healthy variety to the NCIS franchise: the former focuses on the early days of Mark Harmon's Gibbs, while the latter and NCIS: Los Angeles center on the adventures of NCIS agent Sam Hanna (LL Cool J). Some argue that NCIS set the stage for military thrillers like Reacher and The Terminal List, but another series followed in this franchise's footsteps in the early 2000s.

That series is The Unit, created by famed playwright David Mamet. True to its name, The Unit focuses on a group of soldiers operating within the titular "Unit" — or "Delta Force," as it's most commonly called. In addition to having Mamet and Shawn Ryan (The Night Agent) as producers, The Unit features a top-tier ensemble cast, including Dennis Haysbert as field leader Jonas, Max Martini as his second-in-command Mack, and Robert Patrick as commanding officer Thomas Ryan. It also featured enough action and stakes to rival, or even exceed, what NCIS brought to the table.

The genesis of The Unit lies in a meeting that David Mamet had with former soldier Eric Haney, who previously served in Delta Force. Haney wrote about his experiences in the novel Inside Delta Force: The Story of America's Elite Counterterrorist Unit, and said that part of the reason why CBS eventually greenlit a series based on his book was that then-president Les Moonves loved the blend of military action and personal drama that shaped the characters' lives. Haney also chose a television format because he didn't like how war movies tend to handle the act of war.

“One of my purposes for writing the book is I was so disgusted with the normal Hollywood portrayal. It was cartoonish, one-dimensional. It’s the Arnold Schwarzenegger, Sylvester Stallone film portrayals of this Neanderthal-like person who speaks in monosyllables and slaughters the whole world and there’s no repercussions, there’s no cost involved.”

The Unit wasn't afraid to show the darker side of the missions Jonas and his crew underwent. Not only do these soldiers have to undertake rescue missions and assassinations, but they also have to keep the details of said missions secret, since no one can know about their operations. This takes a toll on the soldiers—especially in their married lives, since their spouses are often left in the dark. In fact, part of the series' drama lies in the dynamic between Jonas and his wife Molly (Regina Taylor); he deeply loves her, but his commitment to the military often drives a wedge between the duo. There's a reason why the series was initially dubbed "Desperate Housewives meets G.I Joe."

While The Unit lasted four seasons, it was nearly canceled in its prime because of the 2007 Writers' Guild strike. That led to Season 3 being cut in half, and Season 4 dealing with scheduling issues since it was competing for attention with football season. Rising costs also meant that CBS wouldn't be able to produce a fifth season, which would have seen a new generation of soldiers signing onto the Unit. Ironically, part of the reason The Unit gained such a strong following is that it often aired after NCIS. Both series shared a military background and a strong ensemble cast, making them a major draw in CBS's stable of procedurals.

Despite the issues surrounding its back half, The Unit ended on a strong note, with its titular group of soldiers stopping a terrorist plot and one of their members getting married. While NCIS remains the strongest franchise in CBS's lineup, The Unit proved you couldhit all the same notes while delivering its own unique mix of action and drama.

#3400. ‘I Play Rocky’ Star P.J. Byrne Isn’t a Scene-Stealer — He’s Something Better

You might not always remember his name, but you know P.J. Byrne. A master of “hey, I love that guy!” roles, the actor is often classified as a scene-stealer, thanks to standout turns in everything from “The Wolf of Wall Street” and “Babylon” to “Coyote vs. Acme” and “The Rainmaker.”

Byrne is funny, yes, but also energetic and an eager scene partner. He improves his projects not by simply showing up and grabbing some quick guffaws, but by really doing the work, learning his characters inside and out, and making it a priority to truly understand his directors. In his own words, he’s not stealing scenes; he’s elevating them. He doesn’t ever want to be the best thing in a film or show — he wants his process to help everything be better. Related Stories ‘Elsinore’ Review: Andrew Scott’s Towering Performance as a Dying Actor Can’t Overcome AIDS-Movie Awards Bait Clichés Jim Cummings Wakes Up to a Post-One-Night-Stand Crisis in ‘DISC’ — Watch the Short

He brings that same approach and ethic to his latest turn as iconic super-producer Irwin Winkler in Peter Farrelly’s crowd-pleasing semi-biopic “I Play Rocky.” Farrelly’s film tracks the “only in Hollywood!” making of Sylvester Stallone’s smash hit “Rocky,” a true underdog story that hinges on the constant rejection of the then-unknown star, who was intent on starring in the film he had written. Stallone’s quest is aided by the support of Winkler and his partner Robert Chartoff (also an excellent Toby Kebbell), who went so far as to mortgage their own homes to make “Rocky” a reality.

Well, it paid off — for both the eventual Best Picture winner “Rocky” and Farrelly’s own film, which also features a massive star turn from Anthony Ippolito as Sly. Sure, there’s lots of drama in the film (Stallone’s physical toll stands out), but Byrne consistently brings his signature good humor and big laughs to Winkler, without ever making the Hollywood icon feel too big or crazy for this particular story.

“For me, it’s actually the most grounded performance I’ve ever had, but — wildly! — getting some of the biggest laughs of my career,” Byrne told IndieWire during a recent interview. That’s the product of a process Byrne has worked on for decades. But as seems to be the case with an actor who is just as gregarious and charming in an interview as you’d expect, it’s also because of the collaborations that really get him excited. That’s better than scene-stealing.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

IndieWire: You’re the kind of performer that, when you show up in a project, I’m like, “Oh, my God, I’m so excited to see him!” You steal scenes by making them better. You’re not chewing the scenery, you’re not stomping in, but you are adding this extra oomph to everything.

P.J. Byrne: I really believe all ships rise with the tide. If someone hogs the scene, or they want to get all the hits, it just goes south. I’ve just been doing this so long now, and it’s been my 10,000 hours. It started when Mike Nichols saw me and was like, “You need to go do whatever you want” [in “Charlie Wilson’s War”]. That gave me the fearlessness with Marty to make up my own monologue for [“The Wolf of Wall Street”] and just go crazy. I think all these great directors see, “You know what? He does the work.”

Before I start filming anything — and this sounds nuts — I try to show up two weeks before, and I literally just live in a hotel, almost to the point, I’m in my underwear, I’m getting food delivered, and I’m [looking at the script] like, “Where can I raise moments and how can I elevate this character and make this moment truly pop?” It’s not to win it from anyone else. I have to make sure it’s not trite, and it potentially could be zeitgeist-y, and it potentially is a tee-up for everybody else to do it. But I also know, if you’re going to improvise and add stuff, it has to be a nuclear weapon.

I always make the joke, my bio will be, “P.J. Byrne, Over the Shoulder, Out of Focus.” I know when the camera is coming to me. I know I get one shot. It better be a nuclear weapon, because then that gives me the freedom. Directors, like the Mike Nicholses or the Martys or the Damien Chazelles, they’re like, “Just go.” Peter was like, “Get the handcuffs off him. We’ve trust that he’s done the work and passed us knowing that character.” But it’s so important to me to take their vision, because after a while you realize what they really want, and then you can imbue your character perfectly into that and then share that with the other cast members. But that is a lot of work. It’s a crazy amount of work.

You cannot just show up on the day and be like, “Oh, here’s a line that I think that I can really put my signature on.”

Look, some people might have that gift. My gift is coming up with 10 amazing ones, calling friends, “Anything like that, whatever, how’s this one, whatever.” But don’t get me wrong, when the scenes happen, if you get one shot, I have my nuclear weapon. If we’re doing it a couple times, I’ve got four more to throw in the mix, and maybe the fourth wins. But that, to me, is the most fun on set. I’m so crazily prepared. I could still do probably all the lines of the movie now, or some of the [other movies] that I’ve done.

I did a small part in “Green Book,” and really, there are no small parts. I so believe that. Doing these small parts gets me into the world of all these people, and then that grows within that project, or I get a ton of repeat business. But that’s the best interview to ever do. It’s like, see me in action, see how I’m on the set, see what I can bring and try to elevate everybody. I’m never down, like a Friday night at 4:00 a.m., I’m still the Energizer Bunny. That’s a big part of me, because I just know it’s like we’re so lucky to be doing this. Then, I always say, “ABC,” always be classy. It’s so easy to be nice.

I know, it really is. And it makes you feel better. It doesn’t feel good to be a jerk or to be angry or to hold onto things.

It makes no sense to me. But if I see anyone sort of slacking, it makes me crazy, because I’m probably friends with the writer or whoever’s involved. They’ve put years of their lives into this. We don’t need any cancers. This is such a team effort. That’s why this movie in particular was so special, because everybody was there to crush.

The fact that Peter gave me this chance, and Rick Montgomery, I did a commercial with him years ago. They’re always like, “He needs a bigger part in a movie. P.J. needs a bigger shot.” Toby Emmerich, I did “Horrible Bosses” and “Final Destination 5” with him. They all were sort of rooting for me to finally get the shot. And because I had that, I saw it in Anthony. Anthony was getting his shot. It’s about giving Rocky a shot.

This film doesn’t work without you and Toby being an incredibly believable duo. How did you two build that bond?

Me, in this movie, is nothing without Toby. Anything positive is because of that beautiful, insanely good actor, the great Toby Kebbell. There’s so much truth. It’s an interesting thing when you show up at set like, “We have to have a 20-year relationship. I’ve just met you nine minutes ago, and action.” You know when you meet people, you’re like, “Oh, we’re going to be homies. We’re going to be friends forever”? We had a conscious effort of just looking at each other. I think it comes through. We’re having whole conversations just looking at each other, because that’s really what producers are. They don’t talk a lot. They just observe the world.

What did you know about this real story before you came on board?

All I really knew was that he demanded to play the part. I knew that what he was doing in his life, that he had no money. Those are the fundamentals. The crazy part to me is the fact that the studio wanted him to fail. We all know how hard it is to make movies, and when the studio is purposely waiting for you to die, essentially, that was an extraordinary moment. The fact that it turned out this way, with the insane low budget, and they’re doing one takes, and we find the Steadicam, thank God.

Did you know that the real guy showed up when we were doing the steps scene? The man that made that camera, Garrett Brown. When you watch football games and you see the cameras drop, he’s the camera master of making the Steadicam, and everything else. The shot you see in the movie of the girl running up the stairs, that is actual footage, that’s real footage of his wife from 50 years ago. And he’s from “Sesame Street!” It’s like, what a cute place for it to come from.

OK, so this is crazy. Let’s just say, I knew of him, because he produced “The Wolf of Wall Street.” I know the power of Irwin Winkler, because when we were doing scenes, and there’s a thousand people in a room, and it’s just craziness, Irwin Winkler walks on with Marty Scorsese and 1,000 people shut up. You’re just like, “Who’s this? What’s happened?” People are very quiet for Marty, but when those two were chatting on set, it was like 1,000 people are quiet. It’s like, “OK, that’s an interesting asset that this man has.”

When I knew this was coming, I was like, “I have to get a shot at this. I must.” Thank God, Peter and Rick, they’re like, “Put it down. Let’s go. Let’s see what you got, baby.” So then when I did get the part, Irwin said, “Come over to my house, and we’ll chat.” It’s like, “Oh, fuck.” I go over, and he lives in a mansion north of Sunset Boulevard, and he calls it “the house that Rocky built.” It is every magical thing that you can imagine. He’s so gracious, his wife’s lovely.

You go into this amazing old school office, and you’re just, “Can I write every script and take meetings and calls in this room?” What’s so intimidating is, everybody famous from 1960 to present day, there’s a picture of them on his wall with him staring at you while you’re like, “Hi, can I ask about…?” And then he has a film crew there doing a documentary, so they’re filming me asking him questions. It’s an intimidating thing, because he remembers 50 years ago like it’s 15 minutes ago.

I learned from our own interview with Anthony that, while Sly said for a while that he wasn’t involved, he actually met with Peter before the film was made. But Peter was like, “Can you not talk about this? We don’t want you to feel too involved.” And then he went too far to the loop.

Yes. Crazy. Crazy. Crazy. No, yeah, they both blessed it. They both blessed the script. It’s like they blessed us playing those parts separately.

When you are on set with someone like Anthony, who is about to have this massive breakout, what does it feel like for you?

This is super meta, it’s life imitating art. He’s just a kid from Long Island. You’ve got to remember, what is he, 24 when he’s auditioning? We’re shooting, he’s 25. Sylvester was 29, 30, doing this movie. He’s also a younger kid playing this part. He’s number one on the call sheet. This is his first gigantic movie. He’s got Tracy Letts and Matt Dillon, he’s got Peter Farrelly. So it’s very intimidating. This is the greatest part ever, where you have to do the thing of a real thing that happened in a movie.

But the fact that we are living, in the theme of Sylvester Stallone, let’s give somebody a chance, it played out through all of us. I say it all time, I’m so lucky to have been around extraordinary performances, like Leo in “Wolf of Wall Street.” Margot Robbie in “Babylon,” when they do the scene where she comes on the set, and she has to cry, and she does one tear and then two tears, that was real every time. You become an audience member. Even though you’re there and you’re saying your lines, a part of your brain is like, “We’re in the zone, it’s happening.” And that happened with Anthony.

At times, I felt like, “Did Sylvester Stallone travel through space and time and possess a 25-year-old kid’s body?” It’s so natural, and subtle, and soulful, and heartfelt. I would literally look at Peter, and I was like, “He is the greatest actor ever?” It can be an “SNL” performance; it could be a caricature; everybody does a version of him. And it wasn’t just that. It was soulful.

At what point did you realize this was going to become such a crowd-pleaser? I wasn’t at the TIFF premiere, but I went the next morning, and that screening was like being at a Super Bowl or something. Everyone was constantly clapping and cheering and yelling.

None of us thought it would be that. [The TIFF premiere] is the greatest viewing experience of watching a movie that I’m in that I’ve ever had. People are jumping up during the movie, screaming and missing lines because they’re clapping. That was the greatest thing. I was like, “They’ve got to watch it again!” The standing ovation at the end, they stayed up as we were walking on the stage. It was almost an out-of-body experience. It was pure and beautiful. And then, thank God, there were so many moments where I added stuff, but the moment that I didn’t know was going to get that big of a laugh was, you know when the boxing choreographer comes on?

I do. The best boxing choreographer in Hollywood!

That guy’s incredible, too, that guy is so sick. In the original scene, though, I didn’t come on where he gives me his jacket, we added that little thing: “Oh, I’ll take your jacket. … That was interesting.” Also, in that bit, my character, all he said is, “It’s a boxing movie.” I went to Peter, I was like, “There has to be something more, because at this point, he’s never boxed, he can’t box, Stephan [James, who plays Carl Weathers] can’t box.” I’m like, “Let me get the world’s greatest boxing choreographer,” because the job as a producer is to put out fires and lower risk.

I was so nervous about that night because it was the night before Thanksgiving. I know it was late shooting, so I’m like, “Am I going to add a whole bit here at the end of this goddamn thing?” But to Peter’s cred, he’s like, “Well, let’s see what you got.” All those little things that you add, it just shows, if you do the work, if you’re true to what the character is, you’re true to the essence of what the film is, moments like that happen.

If you prepare enough, you can make character choices that are informed. I hear this from a lot of performers: “If you know it enough, you have more freedom.”

But you have to have a director — and this is the big part — who is fearless. Meaning, again, Peter, Chazelle, Marty, Clint Eastwood. They’re just like, “This is what I’m doing. I know what I’m doing, and then I’m going to pass the keys to everybody.” When you have other people who are operating out of fear … they’re not wanting to be creative, everyone’s tight and tense, and you feel it on set, and there’s no room to grow or play. You’re just hitting speed bumps the whole way.

You are also in another movie this year that I love, “Coyote vs. Acme.”

We’re starting to see a push to have it recognized as an animated film, including at the Oscars.

Apparently, they’re technically allowed. It’s over 75 percent animation, so they are allowed to be put into that category.

What does that possibility feel like for you, after everything this film had to go through to even get released?

The director, Dave Green, is a legend. I lived this process with this beautiful human. He’s another one of the kindest, classiest people, the way he handled the whole process, always being calm in the storm. We all knew, and as we’re doing it, something special is happening. We can all feel it. He’s another guy who’s like, “Let P.J. run and [John] Cena go, let Will [Forte] go.” That was another big, important thing, just that this movie is out there.

But also the biggest part truly, in my heart, is Eric Bauza. He just passed away, and he was the nicest, warmest, loveliest human being you’ve ever met. I really believe he’s our generational talent for voiceovers. He is the guy of our moment. He was presenting an award at the 2024 Annie Awards — and the bulk of his income came through Warner Bros., that’s the bulk of this man’s income — and he was the first person, art over commerce, going, “Release ‘Coyote vs. Acme!’” Against the people that pay him!

Please, God, let this movie be nominated. The work, the music, the animation, there’s so many extraordinary things. To think that that was not going to see the light of day! The fact that the world loved it, it’s got 96 percent on Rotten Tomatoes. It’s just like, the world’s right. Every once in a while, the world is right.

Do you get recognized on the street? And if so, what do you get recognized for?

It’s like anything and everything. Sometimes, they’ll just be like, “You’re a great stand-up comic.” I’m like, “I don’t even know what that means. I’ve never done that before.” Sometimes people hear my voice, and they’re like, “Are you from that cartoon?” That stuff, God, it goes back years, too. I did a show 15 years ago called “The Game,” and if I’m in Atlanta, they’re like, “Let’s go. I hate you, but I love you!” People screaming at me. Sometimes it’s “Wolf.” Sometimes super cinephiles go crazy for “Babylon.” They go absolutely nuts, corner you. Anybody talking about me? I’m always happy. That means I’m working or doing something.

My last question is my favorite to ask of people who I feel like have already done so many different things: What have you not done yet that you really want to do?

God, I would love to do a “Hoosiers” and be a coach. No one’s putting me in a war movie, but if you look at it now, I’m kind of growing into the general role, or some higher officer role. I want to be a bad guy in “Star Wars.” I want to be like, “Let me see how someone spends $340 million.” I want to be the man in “Mission: Impossible” standing next to Tom Cruise, or being the other guy on a computer. All of the big massive movies, because I miss doing that stuff, and they don’t shoot in LA as much, those big monster, masterful movies.

Ultimately, I want to work with great directors who are fearless. That’s the real thing. The directors that go, “P.J., take the handcuffs off and go out there and play, let them throw the touchdown pass to you.” The quarterback’s the star, but I promise I will make a great play as the wide receiver. Whoever that person is, whoever’s doing that, I will show up, and I promise I will score for you.

An Amazon MGM Studios release, “I Play Rocky” will be in theaters everywhere on Friday, November 20.

#3399. How to Make Sure an 'Onion' Site on the Dark Web Is Legitimate

Thankfully, Tor Browser already has a cryptography-backed feature that can verify the authenticity of an onion site, by confirming whether it has end-to-end encryption and extended validation certificates. Here's how this feature works, where it falters, as well as what other red flags you should look for.

While phishing on the dark web works as it does on the clear web, scammers have a few unique advantages due to the secretive nature of the environment. Most importantly, you can’t just glance at an onion link to tell if the site is genuine. Normal website URLs tend to be short and memorable, while onion links are 56-character strings of alphanumeric text that look mostly like gibberish.

When you try to connect, Tor Browser verifies the URL against the originating website’s cryptographic key, which is how you know nobody has hijacked the address or tampered with it midway. But since this has the unwanted effect of making domains harder to recall, scammers have a much easier time generating lookalike addresses or creating website clones.

For example, many popular websites use “vanity prefixes” to make their onion addresses more easily identifiable or to add some branding appeal. That means their 56-character onion link starts with something like “facebook,” “bbcnews,” or “ciadotgov.” But scammers can use a free tool like mkp224o to generate lookalike addresses with the same vanity prefix as the legitimate website, which gives users a false sense of security.

Of course, most dark web users don’t type addresses directly into Tor Browser; they use dark web directories like the Hidden Wiki to find useful onion sites relevant to their search. Scammers will create fake search engines or link directories to point users to their fake websites, like when the Ahmia search engine discovered that a copy of its platform was directing users to 255 cloned services back in 2015.

Of course, it’s possible to orchestrate phishing attempts that don’t involve cloning sites at all. Researchers at Freie Universität Berlin describe a sophisticated technique where attackers serve the real website through their own reverse proxy, which lets them manipulate parts of the site or log your online activity without your awareness. In 2019, ESET even found a trojanized version of Tor Browser that replaced Bitcoin addresses on websites to direct payments to hackers. So both genuine websites and your browser itself are also vulnerable to manipulation if you download or access them from an unverified source.

There are a few best practices to avoid phishing attacks when using the dark web. None of them are foolproof on their own, but together, they considerably lower the risk of ending up on a fake or manipulated website.

On the desktop version of Tor Browser, you can access an onion site using a shortened version of its URL called an Onion Name. For now, this feature only works with SecureDrop, so newsrooms can establish tip lines with addresses like mysitename.securedrop.tor.onion, which would then redirect to the 56-character original onion address. This feature is in active development, so more platforms might support it in the future.

When you load up an onion site using the Tor Browser, you’ll see an onion icon on the address bar, which confirms that your connection is end-to-end encrypted. But you can also click on the onion icon to check if the site has an Extended Validation (EV) certificate, which tells you that its authenticity has been verified by a trusted certificate authority like DigiCert. While not every legitimate onion site will have an EV certificate, famous ones like Facebook tend to.

On the other hand, if you see a caution sign next to the onion icon, that means the site is using a self-signed or expired certificate that isn’t guaranteed by a trusted authority. It may also imply that the site is being served over an insecure URL. This doesn’t definitely tell you it’s a phishing site, but it’s a red flag to watch out for nevertheless.

Don’t rely on search engines, link directories, Reddit threads, or Telegram channels too heavily on the dark web. Once you’re sure you’ve found the onion address for a genuine site, bookmark it so you can access it directly the next time you want to visit.

If you realized that you’ve been the victim of a phishing attempt, the first step is to close the browser window with the fake site and access the real onion address to reset any account passwords you may have accidentally divulged.

Also, generally try to enable two-factor authentication and PGP logins on any dark web account that supports it for added security. And if you downloaded Tor Browser from anywhere other than the official Tor Project site, uninstall it now and grab a fresh copy from the official address.
