#3398. MacBook Neo 2: Here’s everything we know so far

Apple released the all-new MacBook Neo earlier this year, and it’s been a resounding success by all indications. Here’s everything we know so far about what’s next for Apple’s most affordable laptop …

The current MacBook Neo is powered by the A18 Pro chip, which is the same chip used in the iPhone 16 Pro. As reported by Bloomberg, Apple is working on a next-generation MacBook Neo powered by the A19 Pro chip.

In terms of performance, the A19 Pro is about 10-15% faster than the A18 Pro in single-core and multi-core CPU tests. The jump in GPU performance is even bigger, with benchmarks showing an up to 40% boost for the A19 Pro. This is because every GPU core in the A19 Pro has Neural Accelerators built in.

The A19 Pro chip is also used in the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone Air.

According to reporter Tim Culpan, Apple will likely use a “binned” version of the A19 Pro chip in the MacBook Neo. While the A19 Pro chip in the iPhone 17 Pro has a 6-core GPU, the MacBook Neo version of the chip will likely have a 5-core GPU.

One of the compromises of the MacBook Neo is that it has 8GB of RAM. The rest of Apple’s Mac lineup nowadays starts with 16GB of RAM.

The next-generation MacBook Neo won’t jump all the way to 16GB of RAM. Instead, it’s expected to offer 12GB of RAM thanks to the aforementioned A19 Pro.

As I wrote in my review, I don’t think it’s a huge limitation that the MacBook Neo has just 8GB of RAM. Still, an increase for the next-generation model is a great improvement.

The combination of the A19 Pro chip and 12GB of RAM upgrades should also unlock support for Apple’s more powerful on-device AI model announced at WWDC. This model enables a more accurate dictation experience and new options for customizing the Siri voice.

The current MacBook Neo doesn’t support this feature because of its A18 Pro chip and 8GB of RAM.

The MacBook Neo is available in an array of fun colors, including citrus, blush, indigo, and silver. Bloomberg reports that Apple’s plan is to “periodically” update the MacBook Neo with new colors.

There aren’t any details on which colors the next-generation MacBook Neo will be available in.

Apple released the current MacBook Neo in March. Tim Culpan reports that the A19 Pro version of the machine is slated for a release sometime in 2027.

What changes do you want Apple to make with the second-generation MacBook Neo? Are you a MacBook Neo user? Let us know down in the comments.

#3397. Clint Eastwood Nearly Directed A Star Is Born With Beyoncé

Bradley Cooper and Lady Gaga's chemistry helped make 2018's A Star Is Born a success, but its musical performances were just as important. Cooper made his directorial debut playing Jackson Maine, a country-rock musician dealing with alcoholism. Gaga played Ally, an undiscovered singer who catches Jackson's attention at a drag bar. Their romance develops alongside Ally's rising career, creating tension as Jackson's struggles worsen. Their performance of "Shallow" marks a turning point, as Jackson brings Ally onstage to perform her original song, introducing her talent to a much larger audience and helping launch her career.

However, the version audiences eventually saw was far from the only one being considered. Years before Cooper stepped behind the camera, Clint Eastwood was attached to direct his own remake of A Star Is Born, with Beyoncé set to play the leading lady (via Los Angeles Times). The pairing was an interesting one, especially given Eastwood's longstanding interest in jazz and Beyoncé's career as one of the biggest names in contemporary music (via Shadow and Act). It was also a serious project backed by Warner Bros.

Eastwood's remake never made it into production, and the project underwent several changes before Cooper brought his interpretation to theaters (via BAFTA). Although Eastwood's version would have followed the same basic story, his approach to the music and Beyoncé's involvement could have given the film a different identity. Each major version of A Star Is Born has reflected the entertainment industry of its time, and Eastwood had specific ideas about the music he wanted to explore. His plans for Beyoncé and the circumstances that eventually brought Cooper aboard reveal how differently the 2018 remake could have turned out.

When Eastwood signed on to direct A Star Is Born in 2011, Beyoncé had already been attached to the project for several years. According to TheWrap, the remake had gone through several potential directors before Eastwood became involved. Screenwriter Will Fetters had developed a version focused on a rising female singer and an older, fading performer, although the production had yet to secure its male lead.

Eastwood also had specific ideas about the film's music. In a 2012 interview reported by Shadow and Act, he discussed Beyoncé's interest in writing songs for the movie and his desire to introduce her to jazz. He even compared her vocal abilities to those of Sarah Vaughan and Ella Fitzgerald, suggesting a musical direction quite different from Cooper's eventual adaptation.

In Cooper's film, Jackson's country-rock sound contrasts with Ally's transition toward mainstream pop, capturing the growing distance between their careers. Eastwood's interest in jazz could have given the characters a different sound, especially if Beyoncé contributed original songs. Although the full soundtrack was never produced, his comments suggest he wanted to explore a different side of her talents.

Clint Eastwood's A Star Is Born faced several setbacks before Beyoncé officially departed in October 2012. Production was initially reportedly delayed by her pregnancy, while scheduling conflicts and difficulties securing a male lead complicated the project further. According to the Los Angeles Times, several actors were considered for the role, including Tom Cruise, Leonardo DiCaprio, and Bradley Cooper. However, the musical movie never moved forward with Eastwood directing.

Cooper had actually been approached by Eastwood about starring in the remake, but initially felt he was too young for the role. After working together on 2014's American Sniper, Cooper eventually became interested in developing his own version of A Star Is Born. Interestingly, Beyoncé remained part of his plans for a time. During a BAFTA career retrospective, Cooper explained that he had written his adaptation with her in mind before considering Adele.

Ultimately, Cooper found his leading lady after watching Lady Gaga perform "La Vie en Rose" at a cancer fundraiser. Impressed by Gaga's performance, Cooper approached her about playing Ally, and the two began developing the film together. Their collaboration ultimately brought A Star Is Born to theaters in 2018, with a different director, leading actress, and musical direction than Eastwood had originally envisioned.

#3395. Christopher Nolan and Guillermo del Toro Break Down ‘The Odyssey’ Monsters and AI’s Limitations with Production VFX Supervisor Andrew Jackson

With “The Odyssey,” Christopher Nolan ventured into the realm of fantasy for the first time, realizing a time of towering monsters, swirling whirlpools, and apparent magic. The production is a true showcase for his longtime collaborator, production visual effects supervisor Andrew Jackson, who began working on the film‘s elaborate set pieces far ahead of production.

“What’s essential is having the visual effects team be part of the main unit through prep, through the shoot, everything — and not treating you guys as somebody that’s going to come on afterwards and add to the film,” Nolan said, speaking with Jackson during a panel following a Visual Effects Society screening of “The Odyssey” at the IMAX auditorium of AMC Theatres’ Universal Cinema location in Los Angeles. The discussion was moderated by Guillermo del Toro. Related Stories ‘I Play Rocky’ Star P.J. Byrne Isn’t a Scene-Stealer — He’s Something Better ‘Elsinore’ Review: Andrew Scott’s Towering Performance as a Dying Actor Can’t Overcome AIDS-Movie Awards Bait Clichés

“What I’ve found through the years is to treat the effects as a remedial thing that is separate from everything is a big mistake,” del Toro added. “The beauty of it and the respect for the crafts is to integrate them early enough so that they are part of a physical solution as well as the post-production solution.”

The panel offered a detailed breakdown of several standout sequences in “The Odyssey,” including the early encounter with the Cyclops, which was realized with a mix of animatronic puppetry, digital effects, and a performance by clowning veteran Bill Irwin. Nolan shared that Jackson, who started as a model maker, is always one of his earliest collaborators — he was the first person to read the script for “Oppenheimer,” even. Integrating the various design elements of the Cyclops required a constant conversation from pre-production through the editing room.

“We were forced to shorten the time we had to build it,” Jackson began. Nolan then offered a joke: “I like the word forced. It’s good. I’m getting used to my crew members just vilifying me completely as we sit in these Q&As.”

“We both know that the result of being forced to trim away all the more complex parts of the plan resulted in a solution that was better than it would’ve been if we had continued with the original plan,” Jackson continued. “We basically just made a very, very simple marionette, which had still detailed solid components for the physical body, but just missed out on all the complicated joints and where the parts intersected. But the fact that it was simple and moved in a fascinating way that had a life of its own became really compelling.”

“I knew that one day you’d be sitting here and Guillermo del Toro would say it was perfectly integrated, so it’s all worth it,” Nolan said.

As with many industry Q&As these days, the topic of artificial intelligence’s impact on the filmmaking process, particularly on the field of visual effects, was addressed. Nolan, Jackson, and del Toro each emphasized the need for human oversight of the technology’s implementation, suggesting that “The Odyssey” could not have been realized without the conversations that happened across the film’s various departments.

“In an age with artificial intelligence looming — with synthetic creativity around us, or whatever — it’s actually very important to acknowledge the artistry that goes into the compositing process,” Nolan said. “My demand on the compositors and the animators is always to be using their eye rather than their brain, if you like, rather than simulating things or creating a simulation reality. I want them to look at it with an artist’s eye: the way matte painters who were working on glass paintings did, so that there’s an impressionistic quality in the composites.”

“The defense of the human touch and the defense of the craft is as urgent, if not more urgent, to VFX because it is the one that has gotten assailed the fastest by things like AI, which was not invented or demanded from any artist,” del Toro said. “It was demanded and created by people that were alien to that and appeal only to time and money mostly.”

“Well, time and money and also a misunderstanding of the process,” Nolan said.

“You’re absolutely going to need artists to know even whether the new tools have delivered things that you want. You need people to be able to assess that,” Jackson said.

At any given moment, Scott Simone has at least three books jockeying for his attention. He’ll never turn down a campus novel with a literary bent, nor will he hesitate to add yet another mystery to his Leaning Tower of Pisa-inspired to-be-read pile — which is built upon the bedrocks of too many short story collections, how-are-these-real true crime books, and classics waiting to be cracked open again. Topics that have him ripping through pages the fastest include closed-circle murders, unhappy professors, life-questioning philosophical deep dives, so long as they feature sharp sentences, a dark sense of humor, and at least a little malice.

He’s spent so much time in book shops over the years he is, to his wife’s chagrin, continuing to build a library that doesn’t quite respect the dimensions of the apartment meant to contain it.

When we think of sci-fi books, our imaginations conjure massive epics — doorstop novels that spend an immense amount of time building new worlds and introducing readers to entire civilizations. There are historical conflicts to understand and strange technologies to become acquainted with. Sometimes you're a hundred pages in and still trying to remember who rules which planet. But that's part of the appeal. Some of the best science fiction creates worlds so thoroughly imagined that we can lose ourselves in them.

And then there are those writers who pull off an even more unimaginable feat: They pack all that into a bite-sized read of fewer than 100 pages. Let’s stop just to imagine how some authors have been able to challenge our understanding of humanity — taking us to far-flung times and locales inhabited by extraterrestrial beings — in the space it’s taken others to simply introduce us to it all. There's no time wasted on elaborate histories or lengthy explanations, carrying an unheard-of burden to make every little detail matter. Some take us hundreds of thousands of years into the future; others imagine technologies or alien encounters that turn familiar human behavior on its head. Yet they don’t require you to sketch out family trees or create a running glossary to follow along.

The first surprise in H.G. Wells' The Time Machine isn't the contraption that gives the novel its name — it's the disappointment waiting at the other end. Wells creates a world hundreds of thousands of years in the future, where humanity has presumably enjoyed more than enough time to solve its problems. It should have overcome its limitations and become something truly remarkable. But no: The time traveler enters a civilization that’s accomplished little other than making itself comfortable.

The Eloi have no interest in work. That extends to any intellectual pursuits — or much of anything, really — that requires effort. They're pretty, and they’re pleasant. And they’re utterly helpless. Wells took the Victorian ideal of a life free from labor and made it look pathetic. But the patina of time has morphed the Morlocks into something even uglier. The class divisions of Wells' own era have become so entrenched that humanity has evolved into two separate species, each trapped by the circumstances its ancestors created. It's an unflattering assessment of the society that produced him. And as the Time Traveler ventures still further into the future, Wells begins stripping away whatever comfort we might find in the idea of human progress.

A person's face is usually a fairly reliable indication of who they are, but John W. Campbell Jr. makes that assumption impossible in Who Goes There? An Antarctic research team discovers an alien capable of perfectly imitating other organisms, and once the men realize the creature could be hiding among them, the most ordinary interactions feel sinister. A colleague asks a question. Someone offers an explanation. A man insists he's telling the truth. But all that is how an impostor would act, so everyday goings-on are no clue to who’s who.

The brilliance of Campbell's novella is in how he dismantles the group's ability to reason. And these are scientists we’re talking about — people who are more than a little accustomed to examining evidence and drawing conclusions. But the thing they're investigating makes any evidence suspect. Within that framing, the reader becomes just as distrustful as the characters, so Campbell doesn't have to rely on his monster parading around to frighten. The possibility of its presence is quite enough. By the time the researchers devise a way to identify the creature, we're so suspicious of everybody that even a promising solution feels shaky at best.

Nnedi Okorafor's Binti bastardizes the familiar coming-of-age story. It doesn’t ask its heroine to leave home and discover who she'll become — it questions just how much of herself she can take along for the ride. Binti is a gifted young mathematician who's earned a place at a prestigious intergalactic university. It’s an incredible opportunity, though it means leaving her Himba community behind. Binti is eager to make something of herself, but that doesn't mean leaving behind everything that makes her who she is.

And Okorafor shows how uncomfortable it can be when you're surrounded by people who regard your customs and your differences as something to gawk at. Take, for instance, how a fellow passenger feels entitled to touch Binti's hair, treating her appearance as something of a curiosity. Others view the reddish otjize she applies to her skin as strange, even primitive. Then a violent run-in with the alien Meduse threatens the journey. And now those very traditions become indispensable. Binti's knowledge of mathematics and harmonizing allows her to communicate with the creatures, while her otjize possesses properties that even she hadn't fully understood. That’s the central irony here: Okorafor gives us a galaxy filled with astonishing technological achievements, then reminds us how little progress people can make when they refuse to understand anyone unlike themselves.

Katya Gould knows the value of a good paper trail. In the future imagined by Mary Robinette Kowal, she makes her living selling authenticated objects and experiences to wealthy customers who want something genuinely original. It's an unusual way to make a living in a world where practically everything people do is recorded and stored away. There's little reason to trust your memory when you can pull up a recording of what actually happened, which puts Katya in a difficult position when something happens to her that she has absolutely no way of proving.

Katya has a strange encounter in the woods that leaves her disconnected from the network, and now she must remember what happened herself — no relying on any type of recorded history. Kowal’s prose is presented as a typewritten account. We get Katya’s spelling mistakes and corrections, even the occasional muddled sentence. Those little mistakes become as interesting as the story itself. We find ourselves picking apart Katya's account, wondering whether she's forgotten something important, gotten her facts mixed up, or isn't telling us everything. But there's also something reassuring about all those errors, as it humanizes her — surely none of us can perfectly recount every detail. And that's where Kowal gets us. We've become so accustomed to having proof of everything that we begin treating Katya's perfectly ordinary lapses in memory as reasons to doubt her.

There are many unsettling aspects in E. Catherine Tobler's The Necessity of Stars. There’s a dying Earth, an increasingly unfamiliar garden, an alien creature that seems to belong to neither the animal nor plant kingdom, but the one that lingers most is probably the most ordinary: a lapse of memory. Bréone Hemmerli is a 63-year-old diplomat whose mind has begun to betray her. Names slip away, and familiar experiences become difficult to place. She struggles to make sense of those changes unfolding more so than the world deteriorating outside her Normandy estate thanks to environmental collapse.

Tobler stretches this bit of personal uncertainty. She never gives a clear account of events, only to watch Bréone struggle to understand them. She similarly disorients the reader. Memories are never in sequence, and familiar details are tinged by a certain strangeness. Even the garden Bréone knows so well becomes almost unrecognizable. So when an alien presence shows up among its trees, the reader is hardly in a position of surety. We, too, question what we’re witnessing. And then the story takes on a whole different dimension: Bréone spent decades negotiating disagreements and navigating complicated relationships. It's a history that’s taught her patience and empathy. As humanity confronts a future it scarcely understands, Tobler places its prospects in the hands of someone whose own future has become increasingly uncertain.

Black Friday is still a couple of weeks away, with the big shopping event falling on November 27, but Amazon's early Black Friday sale is already bringing some worthwhile discounts on Soundcore's Nebula projectors. Prices start at $299 for the compact Nebula P1i and go up to $2,799 for the premium X1S 4K laser projector, with savings of up to $700 across the models we've rounded up. There's quite a bit of variety here, too, from battery-powered projectors you can take camping or move between rooms to more powerful 4K models designed for a dedicated movie-night setup.

The Soundcore Nebula P1i is down to $299 from $399, while the Nebula P1 is $699.99, down from $799. Both offer 1080p resolution and Google TV, but their speaker setups are what make them interesting. The P1i has two 10W speakers that flip out and rotate to direct sound toward your seating area, while the P1's speakers detach completely and can run wirelessly for up to 20 hours. The P1 is also brighter at 650 ANSI lumens versus the P1i's 380, though you'll need a power outlet for either projector since neither has a built-in battery.

Small enough to slip into a bag, the Nebula Capsule 3 and Capsule 3 Laser are worth considering if you want something you can easily take on trips or move around the house. The standard Capsule 3 is down to $399 from $529, saving you $130, while the Laser version is $649.99, down from $749.99. Both offer 1080p resolution, automatic image adjustments, and up to 2.5 hours of battery life, although the Laser model is a little brighter at 300 ANSI lumens compared with the standard model's 200.

Taking movie night outdoors is a little easier with a battery-powered projector, and both the Nebula Mars 3 Air and Mars 3 are designed for just that. The smaller Mars 3 Air is down to $519.99 from $599.99, offering 1080p resolution, 400 ANSI lumens of brightness, and up to 2.5 hours of playback. The larger Mars 3, now $899.99 from $999.99, steps things up with 1,000 ANSI lumens, up to five hours of battery life in Eco mode, and a more powerful 40W speaker. It also has a weather-resistant design that's useful for camping or backyard screenings, though its extra bulk might make it less convenient to carry around.

If you're ready to move beyond 1080p, the Nebula Cosmos 4K SE at $1,099.99 (originally $1,299.99) offers a more affordable way to get 4K resolution. Its hybrid LED and laser light source delivers up to 1,800 ANSI lumens, while its Dolby Vision support helps bring out more detail in compatible movies and shows. You also get Google TV and automatic image adjustments for easier setup, though it doesn't have a built-in battery, so you'll need a power outlet nearby.

At the premium end of Nebula's lineup, the X1 and newer X1S are designed for a more serious home theater setup. The X1 is down to $2,299 from $2,999, saving you $700, while the X1S is $2,799 from $3,299. Both use triple-laser technology with 4K resolution, Dolby Vision, and optical zoom, but the X1S has a considerable advantage in brightness, reaching up to 6,000 ANSI lumens compared with the X1's 3,500. That extra brightness is useful in rooms with some ambient light, but the tradeoff is louder fan noise.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

The best thing you can do is compare the prices with other retailers that have Black Friday sales. If that seems like too much work, you can just follow our Black Friday coverage (we're already doing all the searching and vetting for you). Some other tips are making sure you're not being sold an older or cheaper version and always reading reviews.

#3391. Hands-on: This 25W MagSafe charger is thinner than an iPhone: KUXIU K4 Air [Video]

When it comes to 3-in-1 travel chargers, I look at two main things: How fast it can charge my iPhone and how portable it is. I have tested plenty of travel chargers that aim to be as portable as possible by using lightweight materials or folding into a smaller footprint, but there usually seems to be some sort of compromise. But this new K4 Air by Kuxiu might be the most impressive option I’ve tested to date. This charger is just 8.5mm thin, weighs less than 120 g, and can wirelessly charge your iPhone at up to 25W. After spending a few weeks with it and traveling across the Atlantic, here is what you should know about the Kuxiu K4 Air.

Be sure to check out our hands-on video with the K4 Air to see it in action!

The biggest selling point of the new Kuxiu K4 Air is its design. When completely folded, this thing is barely thicker than an iPhone. For reference, my iPhone 17 Pro measures roughly 8.25mm thick, while the K4 Air comes in at just 8.5mm. That is insanely compact for something that can charge three devices at once. And even though they went ultra-slim, they did not really need to sacrifice any charging performance. You get:

One of my favorite things about Kuxiu has always been their price-to-performance ratio. While some brands and companies are removing charging bricks and even cables, Kuxiu is adding a ton of value here by including everything you need directly in the packaging. The build quality of the charger is also fantastic. It feels balanced, well-made, and extremely versatile because of all the situations you can use it in.

Kuxiu has also done a great job of bringing us a Burgundy color option that perfectly matches the new Burgundy iPhone color. I wish Apple would continue making the Cosmic Orange iPhone because the K4 Air in that orange would have been awesome.

I recommend watching our video to see my reaction when I pick up the K4 Air for the first time. I was shocked at how small it was. It was thin and lightweight, but still felt solid because it was made of metal and not plastic. The form factor and size make it incredibly easy to throw into any bag, pocket, purse, or even just leave it attached to your iPhone for when it is needed.

The charging experience is actually pretty straightforward. You unfold the charger, connect the USB-C cable, and you’re ready to go. The main magnetic charging surface supports your iPhone, while the second surface is for AirPods. They even added magnets to the AirPods charging pad to ensure they stay in place every single time. There is also a dedicated Apple Watch charger that folds down to charge any Apple Watch. I was charging my Apple Watch Ultra 4, and it fit perfectly.

But now the big question: how well does it work with the iPhone Duo? Personally, I charge my iPhone Duo on my nightstand charger when it is folded shut. So I have zero issues with it. But if you open the iPhone, place it on the charger in landscape mode, and then use it, it will tilt slightly to the left. But to my surprise, if you use the iPhone Duo and open it in portrait mode, it works great! The charger doubles as a stand and easily supports the iPhone Duo. Another cool piece that the form factor unlocks is that it can technically charge two iPhones at the same time, so if you are in a pinch, you can charge two iPhones at once,

So, regardless of which iPhone you are using, as long as it supports MagSafe, you are good to go. But how much does something like this cost?

The Kuxiu K4 Air is finally back in stock after a limited initial run. You can get it on Kuxiu’s website for $79. It comes in Space Gray and their new Burgundy color. As I mentioned above, you also get the charging cable, a 45W charging brick, and a carrying pouch.

Personally, I am a huge fan of how good the Burgundy color looks.

After using the Kuxiu K4 Air, it is just one of those accessories that makes sense. It is small, compact, lightweight, and extremely useful. It fits perfectly into the travel charger category. There are a ton of great 3-in-1 chargers, with new ones flooding the market daily, but very few combine this level of portability with all the features we discussed.

So if you are shopping for a portable 3-in-1 travel charger for yourself or as a gift, I would highly recommend giving this one a shot. It’s well-built, charges your big three Apple products, and looks fantastic.

#3390. DC Officially Releases First Image Of Batman's New Child

DC has revealed the first official image of Batman's new child, following the reveal that Catwoman is pregnant. The image has sparked debate among fans, raising more questions than answers.

The recent Absolute Batman #25 - from Scott Snyder, Nick Dragotta, Frank Martin and Tom Napolitano - ended with a pregnant Selina Kyle walking back into the Dark Knight's life, simply saying, "Bruce..."

Now, DC has revealed the cover for Absolute Batman #27, showing Bruce and Selina cooing over what appears to be their kid. The image has fans asking which character (if any) the Absolute Universe intends to adapt as Bruce's new child.

The cover - by Nick Dragotta and Frank Martin - was shared on social media, with the caption "Who says the Absolute Universe can't be cute?" The image shows a baby playing with Batman's cowl and cape while Bruce and Selina stand reflected in Catwoman's mirrored helmet.

Behind the baby is a repeated 'HAHA' motif suggesting the Joker/Jack Grimm's involvement, with the arc title 'THE DEMON CHILD' appearing alongside.

In Absolute canon, Bruce and Selina are childhood friends who grew up together, with a young Bruce Wayne working for gang lord Falcone at one point due to his threats on Selina's life. As adults, Bruce became a vigilante and Selina became a professional thief. The two recently met up, apparently conceiving a child during the period when Batman was fighting Bane.

Underneath DC Comic's Instagram post, fans have been debating the identity of the child. While some think it's Damian Wayne (Bruce's mainstream son with Talia al Ghul) others argue it's Helena Wayne, Bruce's alt-universe daughter with Catwoman, who grows up to become the vigilante Huntress.

The title 'The Demon Child' suggests it's Damian, with the 'al Ghul' family name literally meaning 'the demon.' However, Snyder previously said he wouldn't be adapting Damian, and the Absolute Universe - especially Absolute Batman - is built on wrongfooting fans. This is a world where Bruce is close friends with the Penguin and Two-Face and is hunted through the streets by his various Robins, so anything is possible.

The laughter on the cover image is a good reason for fans to be fearful. In this world, Joker is an immortal billionaire who carries out wide-ranging superhuman experiments, creating monsters including Mr. Freeze, Poison Ivy, Man-Bat and more. There are a LOT of ways Joker could be messing with Bruce. For instance, Absolute Clayface is a shapeshifter who has copied his genetic code - this may not even be Selina.

It's also worth noting that Absolute Scarecrow's introduction introduced a byzantine maze of bluffs and plans manipulating both Bruce and his family, including faking the survival of his father Thomas Wayne. Scarecrow would and could fake a Wayne baby, and while Selina doesn't have any direct ties to Joker, she's a professional criminal in a world where he wields immense influence.

Fans will find out the truth as Absolute Batman's 'The Demon Child' unfolds, but given everything Bruce has been through in the series so far, it's likely to be a bumpy, twisted ride.

Absolute Batman #25 is available now from DC Comics.

#3389. David Ellison on Elon Musk’s Skydance Investment, Trump and ‘Rush Hour 4,’ and Whether He Would’ve Made ‘Digger’

Though David Ellison has been around Hollywood for a while now, he’s undoubtedly our newest media mogul and still a fresh face when it comes to being the center stage headliner at fill-in-the-blank business media conference. There’s still a lot we don’t know about him and a lot of questions people have about his plans for Skydance, his politics, and his taste in movies.

So on Wednesday when he spoke with Andrew Ross Sorkin of the New York Times at the DealBook Summit on Wednesday, he had a chance to get candid about a whole range of subjects. It’s early days at Skydance, with changes to the C-suite coming daily, so he’s still keeping his cards a little close to his sport jacket. But we did learn a few things about what he envisions for Skydance. Related Stories Christopher Nolan and Guillermo del Toro Break Down ‘The Odyssey’ Monsters and AI’s Limitations with Production VFX Supervisor Andrew Jackson ‘I Play Rocky’ Star P.J. Byrne Isn’t a Scene-Stealer — He’s Something Better

“One of our guiding thematics has always been where entertainment is heading,” Ellison said. “It’s that great Gretsky quote, skate to where the puck is going, not to where the puck has been, and that’s been what’s guided the company.”

Following a report that the world’s richest man had invested $1 billion into Ellison’s Skydance, leading many to think there’s some bigger picture brewing between Skydance and Starlink, Ellison did confirm that Musk is an investor and shareholder, and though he couldn’t comment on anything on which they may be collaborating, he’s welcoming the opportunity.

“He’s the greatest entrepreneur of all time,” Ellison said. “He doesn’t invest in a lot of companies, so to have his vote of confidence and to have him as a shareholder is an honor and a privilege, and if there’s ever an opportunity to collaborate in the future, from our perspective it would be a privilege.”

Sorkin did double back and ask if Ellison will still allow Alex Gibney’s “Musk” documentary to air on HBO as been planned. He said that HBO has a Pay-1 deal with A24, so of course they would honor that agreement, and they “believe in independence and we don’t believe in censorship of any kind.”

One problem: A24 didn’t produce “Musk” as Ellison said. It’s a Bleecker Street film. So we’ll put a little asterisk on that answer.

Tom Cruise’s mega flop “Digger” has the ironic and unfortunate distinction of being the final movie released by Warner Bros. Discovery. And Ellison was asked “how risky” he would continue to be in the context of how much money “Digger” stands to lose. Ellison started by saying that Cruise is “one of the seminal artists of our time,” that Skydance has made eight movies previously with him, and they’re making a “Days of Thunder” sequel before (hopefully) heading into making “Top Gun 3.”

Ellison then described a long story that involved sleeping on Hans Zimmer’s couch before landing on the age old, “what’s the budget?”

“I spent the last 16 years of my life on the filmmaking side of this business. I have lived on set, I have slept on Hans Zimmer’s couch, I have been in editorial rooms for 20 hours non-stop, I do understand the creative process of this business,” Ellison said. “The goal has to be in any film that you make is how do you reach the broadest possible audience for that particular story? There is no one size fits all approach. We will make franchise movies, we will make original stories, we will make genre pictures, we will tell stories aimed at audiences from every single walk of life. What is important is that you size the budget to the potential addressable audience.”

Sorkin pushed Ellison hard about what his politics are and who he voted for in the most recent election. He still did not get an answer, but he would not let slide some of the reports that President Trump himself asked about Paramount requesting that the studio make “Rush Hour 4.”

“We are working with Brett [Ratner] on ‘Rush Hour 4,’ which is a sequel to an incredibly successful franchise,” Ellison confirmed. However, he said the first time he heard about the prospect of that movie was when film chief Josh Goldstine walked into his office and mentioned it, not that it came from Trump, and that “there’s a lot of made up stories” out there.

“Rush Hour” director Ratner as a reminder was in 2017 accused of sexual harassment and misconduct by six women as part of a Los Angeles Times report, including actresses Olivia Munn and Natasha Henstridge, claims that he denied. His most recent project was this year’s “Melania” documentary that was released by Amazon MGM.

One thing Ellison has been working with President Trump on is his desire to get passed a federal tax rebate for film productions in the U.S., and he told Sorkin his goal is to see the rebate passed by the end of this year, at which point the new Congress comes into office and a bill has to be reintroduced. He said he had three meetings with the late Senator Lindsay Graham about the problems of film production leaving the country.

Ellison was staunch in pushing back on some data from the Tax Policy Center as shared by Sorkin that while subsidies do influence where productions choose to shoot, it’s not the same as creating measurable economic growth and that it just pulls workers away from other jobs and tourism.

“Categorically that’s just not true. When you actually look at the rebate in the United Kingdom, it has been a boom to their economy, same is true in Canada, same is true in Australia. All those other countries have those rebates because it pencils out,” Ellison said. “If you look at Texas, Paramount was a part of building a 31 percent rebate for all of Taylor Sheridan’s productions. We had a meeting down there with the deputy governor that said, based on their own independent audit, for every dollar that was invested by the state returned $4.70.”

He also stressed that it’s a misnomer that Tom Cruise is the one getting a tax break but that really it goes to helping union, working class film professionals who benefit.

“You are creating jobs, you are helping small businesses, and every other country that has done this in the past has done this because it is economically sustainable,” he added.

Ellison on numerous occasions in earnings calls and in other appearances has expressed his fondness for artificial intelligence and how he feels it’s going to transform Hollywood. He elaborated on that view a little more on Wednesday, calling it not just a tool for artists but a “creative unlock.”

“Going back to the days of Pixar, the lesson was always be wrong as fast as possible…we’re going to be living in a world where you can make the movie not 10 times but 20 times before it gets put out,” Ellison said. “We’re also living in a world where a $750K movie made $500 million because the cost of production has boxed out new voices.”

He’s referring to “Obsession” there, but he also gave the example of the original “Terminator,” which Ellison said James Cameron made for $4 million but today would cost $70 million. He felt the AI tools would help people to make those original stories, and he’s fully on board.

“The relationship we basically have with talent, our understanding of technology and how those two things are fused together, it’s a feedback loop,” Ellison said. “It is the art challenges the technology, technology inspires the art feedback loop. That is what is necessary to meet this moment in time and build the entertainment company of the future.”

#3387. Apple’s Siri AI smart glasses are reportedly launching next year, here’s what to expect

Apple’s long awaited smart glasses, akin to Meta Ray-Bans but tailored to Siri AI and the Apple ecosystem, are almost here. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the product should be introduced at the next WWDC, and they should be on the market by the end of the year. Here’s what to expect.

First and foremost, Apple wants to rely on its deep app ecosystem to give its glasses a boost. While companies like Meta are undeniably leading in the agentic AI assistant game, the third party app integration just isn’t quite there.

Starting with iOS 27.3 beta, Apple is finally laying the groundwork for proper third party app integration within Siri, rather than just Siri Shortcuts. By the time the glasses release at the end of next year, there should be a plethora of third-party integrations to utilize.

That said, the glasses themselves won’t run apps directly. Everything will rely on a nearby iPhone, per Gurman. The glasses will still have Wi-Fi for apps to function if an iPhone isn’t nearby, but these will largely serve as an iPhone accessory.

According to the report, Apple’s glasses will likely be slightly thinner than a pair of Meta Ray-Bans:

Lastly, a big focus of these glasses is the audio quality. According to Bloomberg, engineers are describing the audio quality as “industry-leading.”

#3386. ‘Bedford Park’ Trailer: Sundance Winner Stars Moon Choi, Who Falls for the Other Driver in Her Mother’s Car Accident

The last person Audrey (Moon Choi) wants to share a ride with is Eli (Son Sukku), the other driver in her mother’s car accident. But when the New York physical therapist returns to her childhood home in New Jersey to care for her suddenly injured parent (Won Mi Kyung), Audrey finds herself carpooling with the local security guard — now without a car of his own.

Somewhere along the way, she and Eli start looking forward to their next argument. And part of the fun of Stephanie Ahn’s stunning debut, “Bedford Park,” is wondering which of them will catch on first.

Premiering exclusively on IndieWire, the film’s official trailer offers a tantalizing glimpse at the buzzy Korean American romance Sony Pictures Classics acquired out of Sundance this past January. “Bedford Park” won the festival’s U.S. Dramatic Special Jury Award for Debut Feature and later screened at Toronto and Busan. #3385. 10 Shows Like 'The Traitors' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

What started as De Verraders way back in 2021 has become a global reality phenomenon: Peacock in the U.S. hosts the American version with the sartorially supreme Alan Cumming, and also the earlier UK take as well as iterations from Australia, Canada, and New Zealand—but there are spin-offs in France, India, Germany, Ireland, Turkey, and more. Basically, throw a dart at a map and you're likely to hit a country with its own take on The Traitors. And yet! The addictive nature of reality TV means that we can't really ever get enough. In that spirit, here's more backbiting reality TV, and a couple of dramas that offer up similarly duplicitous thrills.

A reality show with a complex history as relates to The Traitors, the premise being so similar that it may well have served as an inspiration. Here, players participate in collaborative missions in order to build a prize fund. But it's not all fun and games: There's a secret double agent among the group (the mole, obviously) whose sole task is to undermine the ability of the rest of the group to earn money. Eliminations are done via quiz: The group is grilled on the information they've collected about the mole, and whoever knows the least gets the boot. Originally airing in the aughts, Netflix brought it back for a couple of seasons more recently, with the potential for more to come. Stream the most recent seasons of The Mole on Netflix.

If there were a prize for dramatic title (and set design), you could do a lot worse than this one. In this South Korean reality show, 12 celebrity contestants are challenged to build a prize pot through strategy games. Sometimes they're collaborative, sometimes entirely competitive, and sometimes a blend, but prizes come in the form of "Pieces" that can be won or lost (and that eventually combine to create their own final puzzle). Anyone who finds themselves without a single Piece is out. Pieces can be spent to buy advantages, and also traded, so the show turns on players forming alliances in order to build the prize pot and survive as long as possible. Stream The Devil's Plan on Netflix.

Here, a bunch of strangers are holed up in an apartment building, cut off from the outside world—and each other. Players can only interact via a custom app, and, thus, can portray themselves however they want, whether that means being 100% genuine (unlikely!) or creating a whole new persona. Players judge the competition based on their interactions, determining the "Influencers" who will get to decide on the eliminations. The show ran for seven seasons on Netflix, and is moving to Hulu for the forthcoming eighth. Stream The Circle on Hulu.

You show up at a fancy hotel, and someone hands you a suitcase containing one million dollars. It's yours to keep—as long as you can keep it a secret. In this one, all the contestants get a suitcase, and only one contains the money. Much as with The Traitors, the goal is to figure out who's keeping the secret, with challenges designed to help flush that person out. If the truth is discovered via a vote, that former millionaire is ousted and the money is concealed in another suitcase until the final contestants are given the opportunity to swap bags with someone who they think has the money. Easy come, easy go, I guess. Stream Million Dollar Secret on Netflix.

I'm a little more into the normies on Traitors myself, but there's no question that a big part of the appeal (for most seasons) is watching reality-show celebs go at it with cash on the line. So it is with House of Villains, a Big Brother-style competition with Joel McHale as ringmaster. The core premise is pretty simple: villains (Richard Hatch, Tom Sandoval, Jonny Fairplay, one-time Trump bestie Omarosa Newman, etc.) compete in challenges for rewards and for safety from the inevitable banishment. It's all mostly an excuse to watch some of TV's biggest personalities go for each other's jugulars. Stream House of Villains on Peacock.

This is not a reality show, but rather a drama about a reality show that may well slake your thirst for treachery while offering up consequences a bit more dramatic than the bruised egos and hurt feelings of The Traitors. Here, eight strangers are selected to compete in a game in which they're locked together in a building and sequestered on different floors each night. They earn money for each minute they last in the game, but all their provisions must be purchased with money they've won, at an extreme markup. At first, the contestants pool their resources so that everyone gets more money—until they learn that people on higher floors are getting more. Then things get nasty Stream The 8 Show on Netflix.

This one plays a bit like The Traitors in reverse: A $250,000 prize pot is, right off the bat, allocated to all 11 contestants who get to hang out in a luxurious villa. So the game isn't about winning money so much as it is about how much you'll keep and how much you're willing to share. Eliminations offer the opportunity to remove those who the others don't want to share with—though contestants don't have to actually ever vote anyone out. They can just keep their portion of the money and hang out, something that obviously does not happen. Challenges along the way force contestants to reveal embarrassing and sometimes ugly truths about themselves that may well put them on the outs with the others. There's only one season at present, though there's potential for more. Stream The Trust on Netflix.

Blending the Big Brother-esque social aspects of Traitors with Survivor's love of the great outdoors, this one drops four teams of four into the Alaskan wilderness (moving to Panama for season three). The contestants are all, by inclination, loners, but the game has only one core rule: Only a team (of at least two) can win, so while the game has the typical reality show eliminations, these wilderness enthusiasts must work together in order to take the money. In the same way that The Traitors creates a tension between competition and cooperation via its communal prize pot, Outlast sees its contestants forced to maintain relationships whether they like it or not. Stream Outlast on Netflix.

The tasks on Traitors aren't typically the most thrilling part of the show, which makes this James Bond-branded competition a solid match if you want more complicated and better developed challenges. In this one, nine teams of two visit exotic locations in each episode and compete in spy-themed activities with the ultimate goal of winning £1 million by making it to the end. It leaves out the bits where people sit around a castle strategizing, but it includes, like Traitors, a dapper Scotsman not afraid to camp it up—in this case, Brian Cox, serving as the spymaster who directs the teams in their missions. Stream 007: Road to a Million on Prime Video.

Squid Game: The Challenge would probably be a more reasonable choice for this list—given that it's a proper reality show and not a blood-chilling thriller. But I'm sticking with the original drama here since, as perfectly entertaining as that spin-off is, it feels like it misses the point. In the original (surprise smash hit) drama, 454 needy contestants are recruited for a new reality competition in which they're tasked to play rather simple children's games—with deadly consequences that are cheered on by the wealthy financiers who are willing to pay good money to watch both the poors go at each other, as people turn on each other to survive and to win the rather shockingly large prize. A bit like The Traitors if all of Alan's murder schtick were literally true. Stream Squid Game on Netflix.

#3384. 20 Years Later, Guillermo del Toro’s Dark Fantasy Classic Gets a Stunning 4K Release

Hannah covers horror, sci-fi, and games at Collider, where she writes news and features, reviews new releases, and interviews the people who make them. She’s helping build out Collider’s gaming coverage, with Pokémon as one of her specialties. If she isn’t writing about a monster, she’s probably watching one on a tape from her VHS collection.

One of the first things Captain Vidal does in Pan’s Labyrinth is correct the way a little girl shakes his hand. Ofelia (Ivana Baquero) has her books tucked under her right arm, so she offers him her left. He could take the books for her. He could let the whole thing go. Instead, he takes her hand just long enough to tell her she’s given him the wrong one. Guillermo del Toro gives Ofelia plenty of reasons to be afraid of her new stepfather, but that’s the moment you understand why she’d rather take her chances with whatever lives in the woods.

Ofelia has better luck with Mercedes (Maribel Verdú), the housekeeper who can walk through Vidal’s rooms almost unnoticed. To him, she’s the woman who brings dinner. To the rebels hiding in the forest, she’s the reason supplies keep reaching them. It’s one of the pleasures of revisiting Pan’s Labyrinth twenty years later. Once you know what Mercedes does whenever she leaves the captain’s sight, even watching her set his table becomes suspenseful.

Collider can exclusively debut a clip from the 20th anniversary edition of Pan’s Labyrinth featuring Cate Blanchett, Jessica Chastain, and Jacob Elordi. All three know what it’s like to play someone del Toro dreamed up. Blanchett had Bradley Cooper’s number from the moment he sat down in her office in Nightmare Alley, and Chastain made a cup of tea feel like grounds to leave the house in Crimson Peak. They join Frankenstein’s Elordi to discuss how del Toro writes women, something he has been consistently applauded for throughout his career. Watch the exclusive clip below ahead of the movie's 4K Steelbook and Blu-ray release on December 1.

Four franchises, four completely different ways of getting underneath your skin. This is the one built out of your particular fear, why it works so well on you, and what it would leave behind.

Your nightmare does not wait outside the door. It waits for you to close your eyes, which you are going to have to do eventually, because nobody has ever won that particular argument.

Your nightmare is not really the doll. It is the face of the person you tell, and the way they decide, very kindly, that you have imagined all of it.

Your nightmare has your number, knows your name, and has almost certainly been inside your house before. The worst part is that you already know them.

Your nightmare is not really about you. It is about the people asleep down the hall, and the feeling that whatever is here is not interested in leaving.

Del Toro oversaw the new 4K restoration using the original 35mm elements. The collector’s editions pair a new retrospective and contributions from actors and directors with the commentary del Toro recorded in 2007. That last feature makes for a good double bill with the anniversary material. You can hear what other filmmakers took away from Pan’s Labyrinth after living with it for twenty years, then go back to what del Toro wanted viewers to notice when the movie was barely a year old.

The restored movie earned more than $2 million during its theatrical return, and Cineverse says the anniversary edition had the biggest physical preorder launch in the company’s history. The Amazon-exclusive Steelbook sold out, but collectors have another shot at one on December 1, when a 4K + Blu-ray Steelbook with different cover art arrives at retailers nationwide alongside the Blu-ray Collector’s Edition. A separate 4K + Blu-ray Collector’s Edition follows on December 29.

Pan’s Labyrinth 20th Anniversary Edition is available to own on digital now and to rent beginning December 8. Stay tuned at Collider for more.

#3383. The new Apple TV has twice as much RAM as the previous model, but apps and games can’t use it

The new Apple TV 4K features an A19 chip inside with 128 GB storage and 8 GB RAM, twice the amount of memory as the previous version. Presumably, the supply crunch surrounding the memory chips is part of the reason this generation of Apple TV box jumped to a $299 price point as well.

However, although the specs have been upgraded, apps and games are not actually able to use more RAM for themselves. Apps on Apple TV are limited by the operating system to 2 GB RAM each, and that cap has not changed on the fourth-generation box.

Obviously, most of the apps you run on Apple TV are streaming service clients, which generally have much smaller RAM requirements anyway. However, ostensibly, Apple markets the Apple TV as a gaming device and RAM constraints matter much more there.

A hypothetically graphics-intensive game will easily hit the 2 GB RAM ceiling, and some fans had hoped that the new box with the new chip and double the internal memory would help here. Unfortunately, with the current tvOS software, that is not the case.

9to5Mac independently confirmed that an Apple TV app is force-quit by the system when it allocates more than two gigabytes of memory for its process. The developer API os_proc_available_memory function also reports a 2 GB limit to the app, the same value as the third-gen Apple TV.

It is unclear whether this is an intentional policy decision, or an oversight. Nevertheless, the 2 GB limit is the status quo. Tangentially, it’s worth noting that the 128 GB of onboard storage is also not usable by a single app or game; tvOS imposes app bundle limits of about 4 gigabytes with apps able to reserve about 20 GB extra for some assets.

Regarding the unchanged RAM limit despite doubling the internal memory on the chip, there is some speculation that Apple opted to reserve a portion of the system memory to help the performance of the Siri AI models. However, this doesn’t make too much sense to us. The most complex Siri AI features you can do on the TV offload to a connected iPhone or server backend anyway. The same Siri AI features are also available on the prior two generations of Apple TV hardware, so it doesn’t seem like RAM constraints are a meaningful factor.

One group of users hoping for more RAM in the Apple TV was the game decomp community, which use AI to get AAA studio games running on anything from an Apple TV to an iPhone. Some of their projects have run into the 2GB tvOS limit previously, and were hoping that the new Apple TV would alleviate that. So far, that is simply not the case.

#3382. 10 Most Memorable Jujutsu Kaisen Characters

Few shonen series have introduced as many unforgettable characters as Jujutsu Kaisen. From exceptionally powerful sorcerers and terrifying curses to students struggling to find their place in a dangerous world, Gege Akutami's manga has no shortage of personalities who leave a lasting impression. Some stand out because of their incredible abilities, while others become fan favorites through their relationships, personal struggles, or the emotional weight of their stories.

Of course, being memorable doesn't necessarily mean being heroic or even likable. Several of Jujutsu Kaisen's most recognizable characters are responsible for its cruelest moments, while others remain beloved despite the shortcomings of their storylines. Whether they changed the course of the narrative, delivered some of its most devastating moments, or simply became impossible for fans to forget, these characters helped make Jujutsu Kaisen the phenomenon it is today.

Jujutsu Kaisen introduces Mahito, an undeniably hateable villain, who is almost universally disliked by viewers. From his early appearances, Mahito is crafted to leave a lasting impression with each twisted action, becoming progressively more despicable. His manipulation of Junpei solidifies him as one of the most loathsome characters, but his defining moment comes during the Shibuya Incident arc.

During the height of this arc, Mahito had killed thousands of humans, including one of the most loved characters from the series, Nanami, and left the fate of the female lead, Nobara, hanging. The satisfaction of seeing Yuji finally end Mahito’s reign of terror makes this a pivotal moment, with Mahito brought to his lowest point, solidifying his place as one of the series’ most memorable villains for all the wrong reasons.

The deuteragonist, Megumi Fushiguro, is easily mistaken as the series protagonist instead, as the series intricately weaves many key narratives around him. Megumi possesses the traits commonly associated with shonen lead character, such as hidden abilities, a powerful lineage, and a father whose actions have deeply influenced his life. Unlike some other characters, Megumi has a clear and compelling motive for becoming a sorcerer, making him an intriguing figure to follow.

Here's a comprehensive guide of what happened to Jujutsu Kaisen's major characters in both the original series and the spin-off manga.

Additionally, Megumi has also become the subject of a lighthearted joke among fans, who note how quick he is to summon his trump card, Mahoraga, even in situations that don't seem to warrant it. His significance is further emphasized when he becomes a vessel for Sukuna, solidifying his importance in the series. With all these elements, there’s little doubt that Megumi will remain one of the most memorable characters in Jujutsu Kaisen.

While the Shonen genre often struggles with the portrayal of female characters, Jujutsu Kaisen takes this issue to another level. Nobara Kugisaki, the female lead, initially seemed poised to become one of the series’ strongest characters. However, as the narrative progressed, she was sidelined for almost half of the story. Her fate during the Shibuya arc was left ambiguous, and with no return in sight, fans had even accepted that perhaps the character is indeed dead.

Near the end of the series, it’s revealed that Nobara is alive, but by then, the opportunity to craft a compelling arc for her had long passed. Her portrayal feels oddly incomplete, and while she remains a memorable character, it’s for reasons that highlight the series’ missed potential in developing its female lead. Still, there's no doubt that Nobara ranks among Jujutsu Kaisen's strongest women.

Jujutsu Kaisen features several villains, but few are as compelling or memorable as Suguru Geto. The Hidden Inventory arc, which details Geto’s tragic descent into villainy, weaves a poignant and emotionally charged narrative centered around his deep bond with Gojo Satoru. The shock of seeing Geto, once allied with the strongest sorcerer, fall to the dark side and ultimately meet a heartbreaking end at the hands of his best friend makes his arc all the more impactful.

What makes Geto’s story even more intriguing is the revelation that Kenjaku, a millennium-old sorcerer, has taken over his body. Kenjaku’s centuries-old plans come to life, adding layers of intrigue and mystery to the narrative. With his extensive experience as a cursed user, Kenjaku emerges as one of the series’ most fascinating characters, arguably even more so than Sukuna, therefore it is a shame that the series fails to address this character's origin.

The strength of the characters in Jujutsu Kaisen is measured by the amount of cursed energy the characters possess. Therefore, for a character such as Toji, who possesses zero cursed energy, it instantly puts him at a rank of his own. With no cursed energy, Toji is blessed with a side effect that improves all of his senses with superhuman strength. His portrayal leans toward villainy, largely due to his complex relationship with the Zenin family, which led him down a dark path.

One of Toji’s most defining moments is when he nearly killed Gojo Satoru, the strongest sorcerer of the modern era, who possesses a vast amount of cursed energy and the Six Eyes. While Toji was essentially killed in this battle, he has become memorable for almost killing Gojo while not many could even touch the strongest sorcerer.

Yuta Okkotsu, often seen by fans as a more fitting protagonist than Yuji Itadori, does indeed meet all the criteria of a Shōnen protagonist. His portrayal in Jujutsu Kaisen 0 is especially compelling, largely due to the well-crafted narrative that surrounds him. Blessed with immense cursed energy, Yuta is not only able to hold his own in any battle but often comes out victorious. Jujutsu Kaisen 0's manga was also a prototype for the series as a whole, meaning Yuta was originally the series' protagonist before Yuji.

What sets Yuta apart is his unique cursed technique, which allows him to copy the abilities of others and even wield their weapons against them. This versatility, combined with his raw power, makes him a standout character. Arguably, Yuta is one of the strongest characters in Jujutsu Kaisen, and in a heavy-action battle series such as this, it already gives him an edge to be memorable.

Watching Jujutsu Kaisen for the first time will leave an impression on the viewers as if Yuji Itadori isn't the main character of Jujutsu Kaisen. The portrayal of Yuji isn't what is generally expected of a Shōnen hero, with the character even lacking a main motive to enter the world of the sorcerer. It was only after an incident that Yuji was pushed into this new world but since, Yuji has made a remarkable journey.

Born with an extraordinary body, Yuji was able to harbor Sukuna inside him and since then, has done his best what is expected of him. Over time, the series flirts with the "chosen one" trope, hinting that Yuji may share a deeper connection with Sukuna. However, it’s not just this potential destiny that defines him—it’s his inherent uniqueness. This quality makes Yuji not only a standout character in Jujutsu Kaisen but also a refreshing presence within the Shonen genre.

Essentially, Jujutsu Kaisen is Shōnen Jump's most battle-focused manga, so the popularity of the characters is rooted in how strong the characters are. Ryomen Sukuna, the series's main antagonist, is arguably the strongest character of the series, with a scale of power so high that even Gojo Satoru, deemed as the strongest, didn't stand a chance. It was only through the cumulative damage inflicted by various sorcerers and the fact that Sukuna had not yet regained his full strength that he was eventually brought down.

Jujutsu Kaisen has many sorcerers with overwhelming powers and insane cursed techniques, but only a few can be called the strongest in the franchise.

Every action Sukuna took throughout the series was driven solely by his own ambitions, and in the process, he sacrificed thousands without a second thought. Fans initially believed that Sukuna would play a role similar to Kurama from Naruto, aiding Yuji in some way. However, Sukuna’s purpose was singularly his own. Sukuna's ruthless nature and overwhelming prowess make him one of the series' most memorable and unique characters.

Amidst the characters wielding incredible supernatural powers and villains with centuries-old schemes, Kento Nanami stands out as the most relatable figure in Jujutsu Kaisen. His grounded presence introduces a sense of realism that naturally draws viewers to him. Unlike many characters with lofty dreams and aspirations, Nanami simply desires to live a good, uneventful life.

As Yuji Itadori's mentor, Nanami brings a heartwarming dynamic to the series, forming what is arguably its best duo. His reluctance to fully embrace the life of a sorcerer, due to the profession’s inescapable ties to death, makes his eventual fate all the more heartbreaking. Written with a relatable realism that resonates with Jujutsu Kaisen fans, Nanami is one of the most memorable and well-crafted characters in Jujutsu Kaisen.

Satoru Gojo, the strongest sorcerer of the modern era, also known as the 'Honored One' or simply, 'The Strongest,' goes by many names, and it’s hardly an exaggeration to say that his popularity is more than the whole series itself. From the series' commencement, the series depicted Gojo as the strongest, and since then, the fleets of the strongest sorcerers have been unachievable. Gojo's portrayal in Jujutsu Kaisen has become such an iconic element that his influence has affected fans to act in real life. Jujutsu Kaisen's creator also famously does not like Gojo, and has joked about it several times.

When Gojo was first sealed inside the prison realm, an X account (formerly Twitter) was dedicated solely to counting the real-time duration of his confinement. Whereas, when Gojo met his demise in the battle against Sukuna, fans in Chile even held a real-life memorial in his honor, tied to the series' promotion. These actions from fans demonstrate just how deeply Gojo resonates, arguably making him the most memorable character in Jujutsu Kaisen, perhaps even more iconic than the series itself.

Jujutsu Kaisen is a Japanese anime and manga series created by Gege Akutami. The story is set in a world where Cursed Spirits, born from negative human emotions, prey on humanity. It follows high school student Yuji Itadori as he becomes entangled in the world of Jujutsu Sorcery after swallowing a cursed talisman—Ryomen Sukuna's finger—and becomes the host for one of the most powerful curses. Yuji joins the Tokyo Metropolitan Magic Technical College to learn how to combat curses while searching for the remaining fingers of Sukuna to exorcise him permanently.

#3381. Five Things I Wish I'd Known Before Getting a Foldable Phone

The iPhone Duo might be the highest profile foldable phone to date, but it’s by no means the first. Personally, I’ve had my eye on the Google variant, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold—and recently I finally took the plunge. I thought I’d done my research to know how different having a foldable phone would be, but I still had a bit to learn. Here are some of the things I wish I’ve learned along the way after making the jump to foldables.

One of the most notable aspects of the iPhone Duo is how wide its screen is, even while closed. And there’s a good reason for that: The larger screen while open has exactly the same 1.41:1 aspect ratio as the smaller screen while closed. This has a ripple effect on how every app you use looks and feels—and whether you like Apple’s approach is largely a matter of personal preference.

Compare with my Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which features an extremely tall 2.17:1 aspect ratio when closed, but a nearly square 1:04:1 aspect ratio when open. On the outer screen, apps are a little less wide than on my old phone, but there’s plenty of space for reading books or articles on the inner screen.

I like the tall, thin display personally because it feels easier to reach buttons with my thumb, and the wider display is better for reading. However, this approach can occasionally result in some odd app layouts. Not every app is designed for tablets, especially on Android, and shifting the aspect ratio between the inner and outer display sometimes means re-rendering or even restarting an app entirely to load properly.

The iPhone Duo has a more consistent aspect ratio and general feel between the inner and outer display, but it comes at the cost of a really wide phone. Neither approach is better or worse on its own, but it might be worth going to a local store to get your hands on the phone you’re thinking about before buying.

For years, the screens on most smartphones have been made of increasingly tough and scratch-resistant glass. So tough that you might not even need a screen protector anymore. On a foldable phone, that can be true of the outside display, but it’s very much not when it comes to the inner, foldable display.

Screens might be foldable, but the strong, durable glass that makes your phone so scratch-resistant isn’t. No matter what foldable phone you use, the covering on the inner display will be more flexible, and thus softer. Apple uses a nano-texture polymer film that can be replaced, but the film on most foldable phones cannot. That means if they get damaged or scratched, those marks will be there for the life of your phone.

If you (like me) haven’t considered a screen protector in a while, it might be time to try one again, at least for the inner display. It’s also worth keeping in mind how rough you plan to be with your phone. Construction sites or factories might not be the best home for a foldable phone you plan to open a lot, but an office job should be a bit safer.

Similar to the screen protector issue, cases can be more of a headache. Most rigid cases will come in two pieces, and the piece that covers the outer display can be shockingly minimal—barely more than a frame, for some of the cases I looked at. A poorly made case can be brittle or pop off more easily, so it’s more important to get a high-quality one.

If you like to use your phone case as your wallet, it’s also important to be wary of cases that aren’t specifically designed for your model of phone (and maybe some that are). A lot of wallet cases are built to unfold to reveal your phone’s screen on one side, and your cards and ID on the other. But depending on how your foldable phone unfolds, it could be awkward to reach the inner screen.

The hinge also introduces more spaces for dust and debris to get into your phone. Despite the extra moving parts and gaps, most foldable phones still offer the now-standard IP68 dust and water resistance rating. That mainly applies to what can get inside and damage the components inside your phone. It’s still possible for hair and dirt to get gummed up in any pinchable spaces, so look out for any case that might provide even more nooks for dust to collect in.

I’ve set up most of my apps how I like them by now, but when I first got my foldable phone, I had to revisit some settings I thought I was done messing with. One of the most notable examples was my ebook apps: I was previously using a single-column, medium-font layout, but it looked ridiculous on the inner display. After switching to a two-column layout, it not only felt more natural, but a lot like reading a regular book.

Similarly, there were some uses for my calendar app that got a whole lot more useful. I’ve never really been able to use anything other than either the one-day or Schedule view if I want to make out anything, but on the inner screen, I can finally look at my week at a glance. But that meant tweaking some things—like showing reminders, which fit naturally amid my events in Schedule view, but become a cluttered mess when I saw 14 different reminders to take my meds at once in the Week view.

Most apps do a decent job of automatically adjusting to different screen sizes, but I found a few outliers that I had to figure out myself. As an example, Google Docs would default to a view with extremely tiny text when I first started using it. It took me a bit to figure out that this was due to a “Print layout” toggle in the document’s settings. This is, for some reason, enabled by default when opening a document on the larger inner screen. It can take some time to learn the eccentricities of all your apps, but it’s worth poking around when you can.

I know, it sounds so obvious, right? The outer screen is the one you’ll use most often, so how could you forget about it? But when you unfold the inner screen, the outer one is still useful in some surprising ways that I hadn’t even considered until I went poking around in some of my apps.

One of the most adorable examples is the Made You Look feature in the Pixel’s Camera app. When unfolded, you can take a picture using the rear camera and see a preview like normal, while the outer screen shows silly animations to capture the attention of a baby or toddler that you want to look into the camera. Admittedly, this is an older feature, but it’s a clever one. For adults, you can also use the outer display to get a selfie preview while using the rear-facing camera.

The outer screen is also just better for some things. YouTube is one of the few apps that has a unique layout designed for a partially folded screen, with the video playing on the tilted-up portion of the screen, and video controls on the bottom portion.

However, in my experience, it was a lot nicer to watch a YouTube video by just propping up the outer screen by unfolding the phone a bit, like a kickstand. My Pixel even detected when YouTube was in full-screen mode on the outer display and would be more forgiving of unfolding the phone without switching to the inner screen. The phone anticipated I might just want to prop up the smaller screen, which I thought was a nice touch.

#3380. Apple engineers ‘actively working’ on Face ID for iPhone Duo 2’s outer display: report

Next fall, Apple will introduce its second-generation iPhone Duo. It’s unclear what it’ll offer in terms of meaningful upgrades outside of the usual chip upgrades and camera improvements, but Apple engineers are reportedly attempting to bake Face ID into the device. That said, the feature might not make the cutoff.

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple has two priorities for iPhone Duo: Face ID and the Action Button. The latter might just end up being a new software addition to Camera Control that allows you to remap the hold action from Siri in Camera to an app of your choice.

As for Face ID, Apple engineers are ‘actively working’ on integrating the technology on the device, specifically on the outer display:

Other goals for the next couple of generations include adding a telephoto camera and making the device thinner and lighter overall. But Face ID is the top priority. I’m told that Apple has already developed prototypes of the iPhone Duo 2 with Face ID, and engineers are still actively working to integrate the facial-recognition system into the outer display of the second-generation model.

That said, the feature might not make it. According to Gurman, the timelines are tight here and it isn’t quite ready – so he isn’t reporting with certainty on whether or not this feature will make it. If it doesn’t debut with the iPhone Duo 2, it’ll likely be in the cards for iPhone Duo 3 in 2028.

Later down the road, the company wants to introduce an improved camera system for the iPhone Duo, including a telephoto camera. It also wants to make the device even thinner and lighter. The Duo definitely needs to be lighter, but making it even thinner would be an interesting feat.

While Face ID on the iPhone Duo would certainly be much appreciated, I’m not quite convinced that it’ll be super meaningful on only the outer display.

Being 8 years late to the foldable party, kinda makes you wonder why they weren't "actively working" on it during that time. They got it into the Air afterall.

If they magically make it happen for the Duo 2 then it looks like they held it back purposefully for yearly incremental improvement reasons as opposed to it not being possible.

I’m fine with Touch ID, but whenever it is bothersome, it’s usually on the inner display, where it can be hard to reach the button depending on how you’re holding the device. If I could only have Face ID on one display, I think I’d rather have it on the inner display.

Orientation can make a huge difference for how you reach Touch ID on the inner display, whereas you’re generally only going to hold the outer display one of two ways: upright in your left hand, or upright in your right hand.
