#3379. The Unexpected History of 'Black Friday'

Since the 1950s, Black Friday—once simply known as "the day after Thanksgiving"—has grown into a quasi-holiday in the United States marked by steep discounts, ceaseless shopping, and occasional violence. But more recently, Black Friday has also metastasized. It's not a day anymore. It's a week, a month, a veritable state of mind. (Speaking of which, check out Lifehacker's Black Friday coverage. We got all the deals, baby!)

While pre-dawn trips to the mall are waning as online shopping grows, in-person shopping on Black Friday is still a big deal in the U.S.—it’s estimated that around 80 million Americans visited a brick-and-mortar store on Black Friday in 2025. But how did Black Friday come about, and what does it all mean?

“Black Friday” in the United States originally referred to the start of the Panic of 1869, when the collapse of the price of gold devastated the national economy. “Black Friday” as a description of the day after Thanksgiving dates back to 1951; the term first appeared in the journal Factory Management and Maintenance, where it referred to the number of employees who skipped work on the day after Thanksgiving. Around the same time, the police in Philadelphia and Rochester started informally using “Black Friday” to describe the traffic and crowds that appeared in their cities as shoppers hit the stores on the day after Thanksgiving. The phrase gradually caught on. It was picked up by national press in 1975 when the New York Times used "Black Friday" specifically to describe the day after Thanksgiving and the shopping and sales it brings.

But even before it had a name, Black Friday was a thing. The day after Thanksgiving has been known by merchants as the start of the shopping season since the late 1800s. By the early 20th century, retailers sponsored Thanksgiving Day parades that traditionally ended with an appearance by Santa Claus, as if to say, “Now it’s time to shop for Christmas.” By unspoken agreement among retailers, Christmas-themed advertisements rarely appeared before Thanksgiving in our grandparents’ day. This informal bargain obviously no longer applies.

Referring to a day as “black” traditionally denotes a period of calamity or tragedy, leading some to suggest different names for the day. In the early 1960s, Philadelphia merchants suggested “Big Friday,” a name which did not catch on, leaving retailers with the weak explanation that the “black” in Black Friday refers to the black ink denoting profits in a ledger. Oft-repeated lore suggests that retailers are "in the red" all year, and only start making an annual profit at the end of the year, but big retail chains generally make money all year long.

A more modern issue with the name is that Black Friday sales now last for days or even weeks, beginning in early to mid-November and bleeding over into the following Saturday, Sunday, “Cyber Monday,” Tuesday, and beyond, leading people to say things like, “Do you want to go Black Friday shopping this Sunday?” So far, alternative names like “Five-Day Frenzy” and “The day I get to trample someone to save $8 on a Nespresso” haven’t caught on. But here’s hoping.

Beginning around 2010, an insatiable thirst for profits led many retailers to push the start of Black Friday shopping to Thursday (aka Thanksgiving Day). Kmart opened Thanksgiving morning. Toys R Us opened that night. By 2011, Walmart was opening its doors at 10 p.m. on Thursday. The trend led to widespread backlash, with many Americans appalled that employees were forced to work on Thanksgiving or angry that consumerism was encroaching upon a holiday meant to celebrate colonialism. By 2021, most major retailers had relented and elected to remain closed on Thanksgiving.

The term “Cyber Monday” describes the boost in online retail sales on the Monday after Thanksgiving, sparked by workers returning to the office and getting right to online shopping. The term first appeared on Nov. 28, 2005, in a Shop.org press release entitled “'Cyber Monday’ Quickly Becoming One of the Biggest Online Shopping Days of the Year," which may be the most influential press release ever written. Since its early 2000s birth, Cyber Monday has become the biggest online shopping day of the year. Americans spent $14.25 billion online on Cyber Monday 2025, according to Adobe Analytics. So is Cyber Monday bigger than Black Friday? Retailers really don't care: Analysts now tend to mash everything into the category of "Black Friday–Cyber Monday" (or even "Cyber Week").

If all this naked consumerism makes you a little squeamish, you're not alone. Anti-consumerists have named the day after Thanksgiving “Buy Nothing Day,” which you can celebrate by doing charity work, cutting up your credit cards, or simply not purchasing anything. Pioneered by artist Ted Dave and popularized by Adbusters magazine, the first Buy Nothing Day was celebrated in Canada in 1992.

It’s hard to measure the success of the alternative holiday. Both online and brick-and-mortar retail sales have increased sharply since 1992, suggesting Buy Nothing Day’s effect is negligible. On the other hand, maybe big retailers are losing millions because someone on Bluesky reminded you not to shop. Sure.

Depending on how you measure it, Black Friday has resulted in between one and 17 deaths. Jdimytai Damour is the only person killed directly due to a Black Friday sale: The 34-year-old worker was trampled to death by a surging crowd at a Long Island Walmart on Black Friday in 2008. If you include car accidents, shootings, retail worker suicides, and fatal heart attacks, Black Friday’s death toll balloons to 17, with 128 reported injuries.

Black Friday violence has even inspired a horror flick: Eli Roth's 2023 holiday-themed slasher Thanksgiving opens with a hilariously brutal Black Friday riot at a big box store, setting off a chain of events that involve a lot of people being murdered by a dude in a Pilgrim mask.

I mean, yeah, of course. Critics of Black Friday point out that there are arguably better times to buy a new TV (like the week before the Super Bowl), not to mention plenty of other goods. Savings from Black Friday shopping are often illusory—big-ticket “doorbuster” items generally sell out quickly, leaving behind goods that are, by and large, priced the same as they would be at any other time of year. Some retailers even mark up products ahead of Black Friday so the discounts look bigger. If you're buying online, your browser history, location, and cart contents can tweak the prices you see on Black Friday, as they can on any other day.

Yet despite protest holidays, the unpleasantness of shopping when stores are overcrowded, and the frustration of hunting for bargains that often aren't that great to begin with, Black Friday stubbornly remains an unofficial holiday, celebrated by over 100 million Americans in one way or another. What that says about our country's relationship with capitalism is unclear, but personally, I’m going to continue my own day-after-Thanksgiving tradition of eating pie for breakfast and thinking about going for a walk, but then watching The Quick and the Dead instead. I'm not protesting anything; I just don't need the hassle.

#3378. Here’s one small change that could improve iPhone Duo’s unoptimized apps

iPhone Duo has been out for about 3 weeks now, and I’ve happily been using mine since launch day. Many people have made a big deal about the app situation, but I’d largely say most apps I rely on are updated for iOS 27.0 at least.

That said, a fair number of apps are still from iOS 26 and earlier, and those apps have letterboxing. In my time since trying the phone, I feel one quick adjustment could make the letterboxing a lot less of an issue.

Right now, on the home screen, iPhone Duo allows you to long press an app and open it in Split View. All iPhone Duo apps allow Split View, even if the developer hasn’t compiled it for iOS 27 or 27.1.

One of the beautiful things about iPhone Duo Split View is the fact that you don’t have to decide what you’re splitting right away. On the other half of the display, you’ll see your home screen, and you can later decide what app to open.

So, given the fact that a non iOS 27 app will only occupy around half of the inner display anyways, I feel like it’d make sense to have an option to open every non-optimized app in Split View by default – rather than needing to select it every time. Or, better yet, toggle certain apps to always open in Split View.

Certain apps, even if they’re optimized for iOS 27, don’t quite feel right spread across the wider inner display of iPhone Duo – so it’d be nice to always have them in a half split without needing to think about it.

This would be a small UX improvement that I feel would go a long way, so if Apple could implement this on iPhone Duo – it’d certainly help out the app situation. While they’re at it, it’d be nice to have Slide Over on the iPhone Duo, for when you want to quickly see a smaller app on top of your full screen app.

#3377. 10 Classic Rock Songs That Are Perfect for Thanksgiving, Ranked

As far as music goes, Thanksgiving gets the short end of the stick. Christmas has its carols and Mariah Carey, Easter has countless hymns, St. Patrick's Day has pub-drinking songs. Thanksgiving has, well, what exactly? There's only so many rhymes for "turkey," after all. But the theme of the holiday is being with family and friends, giving thanks for the many wonderful things – and even the not so wonderful – that we've been blessed with over the years. With that in mind, the pool of music suddenly becomes much larger, like the turkey pants you have at the ready. Here are 10 of the best.

Arlo Guthrie's "Alice's Restaurant Massacree" is one of only two songs that are legitimately about Thanksgiving. Only Guthrie's 18-plus minute tune is about much, much more. The story behind it begins on Thanksgiving Day in 1965, when 18-year-old Guthrie and a friend were staying in the home, formerly a Trinity Church, of Ray and Alice Brock in Stockbridge, Massachusetts. A number of guests were coming for dinner, so the pair offered to haul a big pile of garbage accumulated over time in a Volkswagen microbus. That rather innocuous task sparked a turn of events that would be recounted in Guthrie's comically absurd, largely true opus, recounted in a deadpan blues song. There's also an element of protest against the Vietnam War draft and bureaucracy for good measure.

Kiss is no stranger to songs about perseverance, with tracks like "Crazy Crazy Nights" and "I," the latter from the much-maligned Music From "The Elder." Then there's "God Gave Rock and Roll to You II," the band's contribution to the Bill & Ted's Bogus Journey soundtrack. It is, in a nutshell, a song about being thankful for music, a gift that is there to help one persevere over life's hardships, a gift for everyone. Paul Stanley's vocals are engagingly upbeat, as always with songs like these, and sell the hope behind it. As you might suspect, if there's a II there must be a I, and so there is, from Argent in 1973. Only Kiss modified the lyrics to the point that "II" seemed more appropriate. Fun fact: there's also a 1.5 (I.V?), with Christian rock band Petra covering it in 1977.

ZZ Top's cover of Sam & Dave's "I Thank You" is as simple a Thanksgiving track as you're going to get, a straightforward expression of thankfulness, with lyrics like “You didn't have to love me like you did / But you did, but you did / And I thank you.” Being ZZ Top, the sentiment is told in that contained driving, Texas blues-rock sound that is distinctly their own. Being ZZ Top, the lyrics definitely skew towards innuendo, not quite as family-friendly as they are upon first listen. You've been warned.

A standout track from the 1997 album Nine Lives, "Full Circle" is an impossibly catchy song from Aerosmith about making peace with the past, being grateful for the journey, and valuing the time and people you're with right now. It has a pub sing-a-long vibe to it, one that calls for a toast to those very things: "Raise your drinking glass / Here's to yesterday." Here's to "Full Circle."

Arguably the least Led Zeppelin-sounding track on Led Zeppelin II, "Thank You" is a quiet, mellow acoustic number that is a complete 180 from the heavier tracks on the record. Written by Robert Plant as a touching homage to his then-wife Maureen, "Thank You" is filled with gratitude for love, trials and tribulations; honest reflections on the past and present. There's an optimism to it that, unfortunately, wouldn't last, given the couple would divorce 14 years later. Thankfully, they remained friends.

Full disclosure: there's nothing about The Beatles' "Come Together" that expresses any feelings of thanks and gratitude, short of its plea to "come together." Hey, whatever gets the Beatles on a top 10 list of any sort works. "Come Together" has a slow, blues-rock vibe, which pulls together a litany of odd, surreal lyrics (seriously – "He wear no shoeshine, he got toe-jam football / He got monkey finger, he shoot Coca-Cola"). But at Thanksgiving, family and friends do "come together," and presumably give thanks for the Beatles.

"Drove my Chevy to the levee, but the levee was dry."

Thanksgiving is a time to show people you love and care for them, to be thankful for togetherness, to focus on both "thanks" and "giving." Supertramp's "Give a Little Bit" is about taking the time to show people you love and care for them, to be thankful for togetherness, to focus on both "thanks" and "giving." Doesn't get simpler than that. And it doesn't come across as a directive, but rather as a shared, communal effort between band and listener to harvest connections, in a warm, acoustic feel.

Sly and the Family Stone's "Thank You (Fallettinme Be Mice Elf Agin)" ("thank you for letting me be myself again") is a funky cry of gratitude for finding one's authenticity, one's "self," with the love, acceptance and support that comes from loved ones. It's an earned gratitude, one of defiance that says, even amid the societal tensions of the late 1960s, I am still who I am, and grateful that hasn't been lost. The song is also the first time Larry Graham utilizes his famed slap-bass technique ("thumpin' and pluckin'"), and if there's anything one should be thankful for, that's it.

We've gone through 8 songs to this point without mentioning the one thing that Thanksgiving is really about: food, and lots of it. And while tradition dictates that pumpkin pie is the dessert of choice, might we suggest "Cherry Pie" instead? Warrant's infamous "Cherry Pie" is about the dessert in the same way that Aerosmith's "Big Ten-Inch Record" is about a vinyl record. Still, it's one of the greatest hair-metal anthems of all time, and Grandma doesn't need to know of its rather saucy intent, right?

We'll wrap up this list with a "true" Thanksgiving song, and we'll end it on one: Adam Sandler's "The Thanksgiving Song." Sandler introduced the song during the Weekend Update segment of Saturday Night Live's 18th season in November 1992. It is, more or less, a love letter to turkey, in Sandler's semi-falsetto manner, with lyrics expressing how he "loves to eat turkey" and "I wish turkey only cost a nickel." And in between, well, it's Adam Sandler. Nothing in the song makes any real sense whatsoever: "Wrap the turkey up in aluminum foil / My brother likes to masturbate with baby oil"; "Love to eat the turkey at the table / I once saw a movie with Betty Grable"; and so on, referencing Daryl Strawberry, Elvis, Sammy Davis Jr., and his big brown shoe. Inane, yes, but then Thanksgiving should be filled with laughter (which I only thought of after).

#3376. Walmart’s 2026 Black Friday and Cyber Monday Sales Are Now Live

If you're thinking of picking up any big-ticket items—whether for yourself or as a gift for someone on your list— I would advise you not to sleep on Walmart's sale. Walmart is the first major retailer to announce and kick off its Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale for 2026, and they're actually holding three major shopping events between now and the December holidays.

Walmart will hold three sales between Nov. 12 and Dec. 2, as outlined in a recent press release. The sales will be both online and in-store, and will target a mix of Walmart+ members and general shoppers.

The events will take place on three different dates:

Walmart's Black Friday Deals Event 1: Nov. 12–15

Available online and in stores starting at 6 a.m. local time

Walmart+ members get six hours of early access beginning online at 12:01 a.m. ET on Nov. 12

Walmart's Black Friday Deals Event 2: Nov. 23–29

Online only: Nov. 23 starting at 12:01 a.m. ET

Online and in stores: Nov. 27 starting at 6 a.m. local time

Walmart+ members get six hours of early access online beginning Nov. 23 at 12:01 a.m. ET

Walmart's Cyber Monday Deals Event: Nov. 30-Dec. 2

Walmart's physical stores will open at 6:00 a.m. local time on Nov. 27 for their Black Friday events. Of course, they will start online earlier, so make sure to check their website as well.

Walmart says that they will have discounts on electronics, toys, fashion, beauty, home goods, gifts, and everyday essentials. Although the company doesn't provide much in the way of specifics in its press release, last year's sales included discounts on TCL TVs, Dyson vacuums, Dreo appliances, and toys from LEGO.

Walmart's first sale already features plenty of good deals; you don't need to wait for Nov. 27 to start to find some products going for their lowest prices ever. Here are some of the best ones I've found so far:

No. But if you are a Walmart+ member, you'll get early access to the sale. You can sign up for a free 30-day Walmart+ subscription and cancel it afterwards or get the annual plan for $98 ($8.17/month).

Deals will be both online and in the physical stores. There might be deals online that you won't see in-store and vice versa.

The holiday season will see major sales from the same list of retailers that compete for your dollars throughout the year—namely, Best Buy, Target, and Amazon. Each will have its own version of Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales. So far, only Walmart has revealed its plans.

In short, yes. Though they aren't quite as impactful as they once were, Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales offer discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. Whether it's a major purchase you've been saving up for or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts, especially on items like appliances and electronics. Last year's sales included categories such as tech, home improvement, and fitness.

Black Friday used to be when major retailers offered their best deals on expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Now, however, the distinction is almost meaningless: Every major retailer offers sales on both days, which means the smart move is to know what you want, use price trackers to monitor the deals, and refer to our Black Friday coverage, where we do all the searching, curating, and price tracking for you.

#3375. Michael B. Jordan's Involvement In New Prime Video Boxing Series Clarified By Creator

EXCLUSIVE: The Greatest creator has cleared up how involved Michael B. Jordan was in the making of the new boxing series.

Earlier this month, The Greatest premiered on Prime Video, chronicling the life of heavyweight icon Muhammad Ali. While Jaalen Best performed the man originally named Cassius Clay, Jordan, who has experience playing a boxer character thanks to the Creed movies, worked behind the scenes as an executive producer. Ben Watkins, who created The Greatest, opened up about how the Adonis Creed actor contributed to the series.

In an interview with ScreenRant's Brandon Zachary, Watkins recalled how Jordan was already a producer on The Greatest when he came aboard. The two men had “crossed paths many times before” and previously worked together on Burn Notice, though when the time came down for them to meet and discuss Watkins’ “approach” to The Greatest, it had “been a while” since they last talked. Regardless, Jordan was immediately receptive to Watkins’ ideas and promised that he would “protect” his “vision for the show,” feeling that “there was nobody else who could tell the story.” The showrunner continued:

That started our journey once I joined, and then the second time was when there was a moment where this show was on the fence about whether it was going to get greenlit or not. We knew we had a big meeting coming up with Prime Video executives, and we had a great presentation planned. We touched base with Mike, and he knew it was coming, and he was in the middle of a press tour or in production. Whatever was happening, he dropped everything and came to L.A. so he could be in that meeting in person and help seal the deal. Then we had a green light.

Then the bigger stuff was the support over time as a producer. He couldn't be in the trenches with us because he had so much else going on, but he could weigh in at very key times, and if it's push a button here, nudge something here, do this email, it was just really great to have someone like that. I've had really powerful entities in projects before, but I haven't had one that really put their ego to the side and said, 'What's best for the project? I know at this point I'm one of the biggest stars in the world, but what I'm right here right now is just this producer on this show trying to help you get your vision realized.’

While Jordan is best known for his roles in movies and TV shows like Friday Night Lights, Parenthood, Black Panther, Just Mercy, Without Remorse, and Sinners, he also has a sizable amount of producing credits on his resume. That includes TV shows like Gen:Lock, Raising Dion, and 61st Street, though like the latter series, he doesn’t appear on camera in The Greatest. As Watkins laid out, while Jordan couldn’t contribute to the Prime Video TV show on a day-to-day basis, he was nonetheless instrumental in making sure that the project turned out just the way Watkins wanted.

Michael B. Jordan has been a part of two franchises that have had critical and commercial success and in between, he's had fantastic smaller roles.

Best is joined in The Greatest’s main cast by Omari Hardwick as Cassius Clay Sr. Dana Gourrier as Odessa Clay, Kai Parham as Rahaman Ali, Giovanni Ribisi as Angelo Dundee, and Amin Joseph as Sonny Liston. The series has earned primarily positive critical reception, boasting an 85% Tomatometer on Rotten Tomatoes based off 20 reviews. Watkins also shared his hope that The Greatest will return for two more seasons to explore other chapters of Ali’s life.

The Greatest season 1 can be streamed in its entirety on Prime Video. Jordan will next be seen starring in The Thomas Crown Affair, which he also directed and executive produced, and releases in theaters on March 5, 2027.

#3368. 5 Greatest Thanksgiving Episodes of '80s Sitcoms, Ranked

Thanksgiving is just around the corner, and what better way to get into the holiday spirit than with a few classic Thanksgiving episodes? The 2000s had How I Met Your Mother's Thanksgiving mishaps, while the '90s gave us the iconic turkey-on-the-head disaster in Friends. But the '80s had their fair share of memorable holiday moments, too.

There's something nostalgic about sitcoms from that decade, when Thanksgiving often meant a big family dinner, plenty of laughs, and a little chaos along the way. Of course, things rarely go smoothly in sitcom households, and these episodes are no exception. From an unexpected food fight to spending the holiday in jail, here are the greatest Thanksgiving episodes from '80s sitcoms, ranked.

Thanksgiving at the Huxtable household gets off to a chaotic start when bad weather delays travel plans, prompting Denise (Lisa Bonet) to invite Paula (Victoria Rowell), her husband Martin's (Joseph C. Phillips) ex-wife, to join the family for dinner. Meanwhile, Clair (Phylicia Rashad) keeps sending Cliff (Bill Cosby) into the pouring rain to pick up forgotten ingredients, including canned pumpkin, fresh nutmeg, eggs, and tomatoes. Each trip leaves him more soaked and miserable than the last, while the family tries to navigate the awkwardness of having Paula at the dinner table.

The Cosby Show makes great use of its ensemble cast here, giving nearly every family member a moment to shine. Cliff's increasingly miserable grocery runs provide most of the laughs, but there's plenty happening back home, too. Vanessa complains about sitting at the kids' table, Sondra (Sabrina Le Beauf) and Elvin (Geoffrey Owens) get into a little spat, and Olivia (Raven-Symoné) steals the show with her adorable Thanksgiving song. The episode also gives Paula more depth than the typical sitcom ex-wife, allowing her to bond with Denise over their shared connection to Olivia. It's a nice change from the usual drama surrounding former spouses.

Thanksgiving in Family Ties doesn't go as planned when Steven (Michael Gross) and Elyse (Meredith Baxter) decide to attend an anti-nuclear weapons protest instead of celebrating with the family. Their kids aren't happy about it, especially Alex (Michael J. Fox), whose conservative views often clash with his parents' activism. Things get more complicated when Elyse's parents arrive for the holiday, only to find out that they have been arrested at the demonstration. The couple refuse to sign a waiver promising not to protest again, so they end up spending Thanksgiving in jail. Rather than leave them there, the rest of the family brings Thanksgiving dinner to the jailhouse so they can celebrate together.

The episode is at its funniest when the Keatons' very different personalities start clashing. Alex is embarrassed by his parents' activism, while Charlie isn't exactly thrilled that their arrest has thrown his holiday plans off track. Kate is more sympathetic, though, and isn't afraid to defend Steven and Elyse when Charlie gets annoyed with them. It's a fun family dynamic that keeps the episode from feeling too heavy, even when the disagreements get heated. And instead of wrapping things up with everyone suddenly agreeing, the episode lets the family remain divided on certain issues. They don't have to share the same opinions to put those differences aside and enjoy Thanksgiving together.

Thanksgiving at the Conner household gets messy when both sides of the family gather for dinner. Roseanne (Roseanne Barr) is already exhausted from preparing the feast when her parents, Beverly (Estelle Parsons) and Al (John Randolph), and Dan's (John Goodman) parents arrive. Meanwhile, Jackie (Laurie Metcalf) reveals that she's joined the police force, but Beverly is far from supportive of her decision. Things get even more uncomfortable when Dan's father, Ed (Ned Beatty), makes advances toward Crystal (Natalie West), prompting Dan to confront him. As tensions rise around the dinner table, Roseanne makes one final decision: her parents will be spending the night at a motel rather than taking over her house.

Thanksgiving is supposed to be about appreciating loved ones, but Roseanne flips the script by showing just how exhausting family can be. Beverly's reaction to Jackie's career choice exposes her lack of trust in her daughter, while Dan's confrontation with Ed over his behavior toward Crystal brings another uncomfortable family feud to the dinner table. Still, Roseanne's decision to send her parents to a motel is easily the episode's funniest running gag. After getting up at five in the morning to prepare dinner, she has absolutely no interest in putting up with Beverly's criticism for another night. Honestly, anybody could sympathize with her decision.

The Tanners are spending their first Full House Thanksgiving without Pam, and Danny (Bob Saget) wants to make sure his daughters still have a special holiday. When his mother gets stranded in Tacoma due to bad weather, Danny, Jesse (John Stamos), and Joey (Dave Coulier) are left to handle Thanksgiving dinner themselves. With D.J. (Candace Cameron Bure) and Stephanie (Jodie Sweetin) helping out, the family tries to keep Pam's holiday traditions alive—unfortunately, not to much success. Amid the kitchen chaos, Danny and Jesse also struggle with how much they miss Pam, giving the episode a bittersweet touch.

Grief doesn't take a holiday, and celebrating Thanksgiving without someone you love can make an already difficult time of year even harder. That's what makes Danny's determination to give his daughters a happy holiday so touching. Thankfully, the episode knows when to lighten the mood, balancing its emotional moments with plenty of classic Full House shenanigans. Between the frozen turkey, the ruined pumpkin pie, and Joey getting his tongue stuck in a bottle, there's never a dull moment in the kitchen. But beneath all the laughs is a sweet reminder that Pam's memory is still very much part of the family. The Tanners may never get back the Thanksgivings they shared with her, but they can still make new memories together.

Thanksgiving isn't looking particularly festive for the Cheers gang, as everyone struggles to find somewhere to spend the holiday. When Diane (Shelly Long) discovers she's been invited to her professor's Thanksgiving party as domestic help, she opts to attend Carla's (Rhea Perlman) potluck dinner instead. With the entire gang gathered around the table, things quickly go awry when Carla's turkey refuses to cook, and tempers begin to flare. The next thing they know, the gathering soon descends into an all-out food fight.

There's no better company for the holidays than your dysfunctional friends from the bar. Cheers shows that family doesn't have to be bound by blood. Sometimes, it's simply the people who choose to spend the day together. Most of the sitcom takes place inside the Boston bar, so moving the action to Carla's apartment gives the gang a more intimate setting to let their guards down. Of course, they're still an imperfect bunch, and even the pettiest disagreements can spiral into something ridiculous. The result is one of the most memorable Thanksgiving scenes of the '80s, completely throwing off the picture-perfect idea of what the holiday is supposed to look like (admittedly, the food fight did attract some criticism, given that the episode aired during the Stop World Hunger campaign).

The regulars of the Boston bar "Cheers" share their experiences and lives with each other while drinking or working at the bar where everybody knows your name.

#3367. X-Men Officially Kills Two Founding Heroes, And It Highlights One Massive Marvel Problem

The X-Men franchise just ended a years-long storyline, and it went out with a bang, not a whimper. A climactic fight scene put a pin in one X-era, or maybe pulled the pin is a better way to put it, while setting the course for the next one. There's a lot to process, including the apparent deaths of two OG X-Men, and a lot to look forward to for X-Men fans heading into 2027, but not everyone is going to be happy with the way Marvel handled things.

For some fans, the franchise's latest big twist is a huge red flag. At the very least, it is an example of Marvel leaning into a creative impulse that leaves many readers frustrated. Is Marvel struggling to give its stories authentic dramatic stakes? Or is it keeping up with the changing landscape of superhero storytelling, and encouraging everyone to keep up too? Those are the critical questions that stem from the final pages of DNX #5, the final issue of Marvel's big X-Men x Fantastic Four crossover.

Everything comes down to a fight between Cyclops, the X-Men's longtime leader, who has been straining under the pressure of trying to avoid making the same mistakes as Charles Xavier, and the original version of his teammate Beast, who has become a villain and embraced a warped version of Magneto's mutant supremacy.

Marvel takes a big swing with how the fight between Beast and Cyclops ends. The problem, though, is the follow-through on that swing.

Wow, you think as you read the climax of DNX #5. They really did it. They really killed off Cyclops. It is an X-Men comic, so you know the character has died before, and that he will be back. Still, it is always a big decision for Marvel's X-Office to take one of their top mutant heroes off the board for a while. So, good for them, you think, for finding a good endpoint to Scott Summers' story for now. Blowing himself up to take out the corrupted version of his old friend Hank McCoy. A classic heroic sacrifice.

Then you flip the page. There's an advertisement for next month's X-books, and an in memoriam page for Daredevil writer Roger McKenzie, who passed away recently. After that, you're surprised by an epilogue page. This is where it gets divisive. The epilogue reveals that, in fact, Cyclops and the Chairman (evil Beast's current moniker) are alive. "You and I, we have work to do," the Chairman says to Cyclops, waking him up in an undisclosed location.

Professor X has made many questionable decisions as leader of the X-Men, but his biggest mistake almost led to a worldwide catastrophe.

On the one hand, it is a good hook. The overarching story of Cyclops vs. Chairman Beast isn't over after all. It is just entering a new phase, starting a new "season." At the same time, it is an almost parodically fast walk-back of not one, but two major character deaths. That could be a breaking point for some readers who have already felt frustrated with the X-Men franchise's creative direction over the last several years.

DNX #5 "ends" (before its surprise epilogue) with Jean Grey screaming back to Earth, drawn from her solo mission out in deep space by the psychic disturbance of Cyclops' seeming demise. As the X-Men's current field leader, Psylocke assumes temporary command and tells the team they have to get ready, because Jean is going to be pissed. "The Phoenix is going to want answers for the death of her husband," she says bluntly.

Marvel had already teased that the X-Men would be voting for a new leader to replace Cyclops. Taking the character out of the equation feels like a dramatically rich opportunity for X-Men canon. Yet because Marvel wasted no time revealing Cyclops was still alive, it seems likely that the series will continue to be very much his story, at least in parallel to what is happening with the rest of the team.

As a powerful X-Men hero unlocks a new frontier of their powers, a founding member finally has an equal... and an endgame romantic partner?

So, then the lingering question becomes, how long are the X-Men going to think Cyclops is dead? Again, this isn't a bad story arc in a vacuum. The problem is that it is the latest, most egregious, example of the fact that Marvel has become totally unwilling to kill off major characters, even temporarily.

Ultimate Iron Man's 2024 death was reversed after one issue. Major deaths at the end of last year's One World Under Doom crossover were swiftly undone. Ultimate Spider-Man's death earlier this year lasted like two whole issues. In the recently wrapped up Avengers: Armageddon event series, which promised a superhero body count, the one alleged hero casualty was revealed to be alive after one issue, in an epilogue akin to DNX #5's big swerve.

It is a noticeable trend. Marvel loves character deaths as cliffhanger moments, but has approximately zero interest in even the illusion of "permanence." It is the full 180-degree turn from when former Marvel Editor-in-Chief Joe Quesada instituted a hard "dead is dead" policy in the early 2000s. The problem isn't that one approach is better than the other, it is that Marvel continues to struggle to find that "Goldilocks zone" between the two.

By and large, the X-Men franchise is telling good stories right now. Better than it often gets credit for. It is worth keeping up with the feud between Cyclops and Chairman Beast, which has become the backbone of main X-Men continuity over the past year. In a way, it is an arc that is too good to end so soon. Yet it is also fair to be critical of the complete lack of chill Marvel has when it comes to these fake-out deaths.

Could the reveal of Cyclops and the Chairman's survival have waited an issue? Three issues? Six? The next year's worth of X-Men plot might, in retrospect, tell readers no, it couldn't. The same goes for whether Marvel could have really gone through with killing the characters off. The job of X-Men now is to prove why fans wouldn't have wanted that.

DNX #5 is available now from Marvel Comics.

#3363. New camera sensor coming to the iPhone 20 Pro’s main camera, says leaker

The biggest improvement to iPhone photo quality that Apple could make would be to give the device a larger sensor. There have been two reports suggesting this is on the way, although with a potentially rather large catch.

A leaker today says that the iPhone 20 Pro is getting a new and more sophisticated sensor for the main camera, but details are unclear …

There are two main reasons people still buy standalone cameras despite having an iPhone in their pocket wherever they go. The first is lens quality: iPhones have small plastic lenses compared to the far larger and more sophisticated glass lenses used with dedicated cameras.

The second is sensor size. All other things being equal, a larger sensor will capture more light and provide a higher quality image. Current smartphone sensors are absolutely tiny compared to those used in even mid-range consumer cameras.

We’ve seen two previous reports suggesting that a larger sensor is on the way for future iPhones. One of these suggested that it would be coming in 2027 or 2028, although a later one suggested the latter date was more likely.

The reports were not without a catch, however, suggesting that the larger sensor would only be for the telephoto lens and would have a 200MP resolution. Squeezing more pixels into a given sensor size tends to sacrifice low light capabilities in return for higher resolution. This is less likely to be an issue with a telephoto lens, which is normally used outdoors rather than inside.

What I’d really love to see is a significantly larger sensor for the main camera, with no increase in resolution. This would improve low light performance and overall image quality.

A brief report from leaker Ice Universe suggests that the iPhone 20 Pro will get a new and more sophisticated sensor for the main camera.

iPhone 20 Pro to feature a new sensor using 17nm logic process for its main camera next year.

(Under Apple’s current naming system, next year’s iPhone Pro would be the iPhone 19 Pro. However, it’s widely expected that Apple will jump to the iPhone 20 nomenclature in order to mark a significant design upgrade for the 20th anniversary of the device.)

There are no further details, so we don’t know whether the size of the sensor will be increased or remain the same.

#3360. Shameless: Lip's Greatest Love Interests, Ranked

When it comes to Lip Gallagher's girlfriends in Shameless, the show took a revolving-door approach as Jeremy Allen White's character grew up across the show's 11 seasons. All of Lip's girlfriends were markedly different people from different walks of life, a contrast to Fiona's toxic relationships, which all seemed to blend together messily after a while. The eldest Gallagher son didn't seem to have a "type", and there was no common theme linking every single one of Lip's girlfriend. Instead, some of Lip's relationships had a huge impact on his life and arc as a character, while others just provided momentary distractions.

However, each of Lip's girlfriends added to his story and showed Shameless viewers how the character handled the various situations he found himself in throughout these personal entanglements. Some of them changed him for the better, while some of them led him to some of the worst decisions Lip made during Shameless' 11-season run. While there was the occasional girlfriend Shameless had to work at making sense of, Lip's other romances had audiences rooting for an endgame. Despite the fact that Lip's stories weren't always about romantic love, his relationships provided some of the most intense stories during Shameless' run.

The worst of Lip's relationships in Shameless comes in the season 7 episode "Be A Good Boy. Come For Grandma". After his affair with Helene falls apart, and he loses Amanda and his dorm room, Lip seems to be having some sexual performance issues. He's seen unsuccessfully trying to sleep with the many sorority girls surrounding him in his newly acquired living arrangement as the sorority houseboy.

After some interesting intervention involving his feet and Queenie, Frank’s free-spirited girlfriend, Lip seems to be cured and wastes no time testing this, ending up in a foursome with sorority girls by the end of the episode. This hook-up might not be significant in the grand scheme of Lip's character, but it does demonstrate how much he ties his worth and success to his relationships.

When Lip joins Debbie and Mandy in their mission to bring down the local sex offenders in the community in Shameless season 3, he gets more than he bargained for when he ends up at ex-teacher Blake's house. When he tries to prove that she's an offender, she falls into his plan and seduces him, and he is able to snap a picture of the encounter. Instead of turning her in, he has sex with her and keeps the photo to himself. Mandy takes matters into her own hands, scaring away the teacher by digging a grave in her yard.

With Lip's girlfriend in season 3, Shameless wasted an opportunity for him to do the right thing. Blake Collins was portrayed by actress Justine Lupe, and her acting career has really taken off since appearing in the series. She did a few one-offs on series like The Good Wife, Younger, and Alone Together, but had a long arc on Cristela as Maddie and appeared in A Midsummer Night's Dream as Flute. She played Astrid Weissman on The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel, but her biggest credit was during her time on Succession as Willa. She's currently on Nobody Wants This as Morgan.

Lip slept with Tami's sister, Cory, in Shameless season 9 after finding out that Tami slept with her ex, Boone. Tami was able to move past the act pretty fast once Lip pointed out that they were even. This proved that Lip wasn't really over Tami, and that they should give an exclusive relationship a try.

And Tami taking Lip back, even after he slept with her own sister, proves that she is willing to accept him for who he is, which becomes important later on. So Cory was important to Lip's story, though she wasn't ever meant to be more than a one-night stand. While Corey doesn't really count as Lip's girlfriend, as they don't date, Shameless still uses the encounter to further his narrative arc.

Cory Tamietti was played by actress and aspiring director Maddie McCormick. Before appearing on the Showtime drama, McCormick starred in a series of TV show one-offs and films. She got her start in the industry by appearing in an episode of Bucket and Skinner's Epic Adventures before appearing in Wal-Bob's as Allie. She played Spencer in The Dead Girls Detective Agency and appeared in Little Fires Everywhere as Jen R. She headlines The Secret Life of Amy Bensen, and previously directed an installment of Sh*t Girls Used to Say.

Eddie was intense both in and out of the bedroom, though their fling was more of a distraction for Lip in season 8. Although it wasn't the craziest relationship on Shameless, it was clear the two were never going to lead to anything meaningful. Eddie shows her flakey side and disappears without warning, leaving behind her orphaned little sister. Lip takes care of her until she leaves with her sister in season 9. Her abandonment of Xan may have reinforced Lip's desire to be a father, but it broke any chance of Lip ever seeing Eddie as a love interest.

In terms of Eddie being Lip's girlfriend, Shameless made it clear from the get-go that she wasn't his soul mate. Eddie was played by actress Levy Tran, and it seemed like her arc, albeit small, really boosted her career. Directly after, she had a role on The First Purge as Roenick and then starred in The Silk Road as Haruko. Tran then played Trish Park in The Haunting of Hill House before starring in the MacGyver reboot series as Desi Nguyen.

When viewers first met Amanda, it was as Lip's roommate's controlling friend with benefits. However, it isn't long before she sets her sights on Lip, proceeding to schedule out every aspect of his life, their sexual interactions included. Things take a turn when Amanda's parents offer Lip money to stay away from her.

Despite having a negative arc, Lip's girlfriend in Shameless season 4 saw her doing a lot of nice things for him, buying him clothes and a new phone, and making sure he has food. But her intentions seem to be more swayed towards fabricating the perfect boyfriend than authentically helping him. Eventually, Lip gets distracted by Mandy, and then Professor Helene, leaving Amanda behind. But she doesn't leave quietly, causing him to get kicked out of the dorms as revenge for leaving her for Helene.

Actress Nichole Sakura portrayed Amanda, who was a memorable girlfriend for Lip due to the strangeness of their relationship. Most probably recognize Sakura for playing the bubbly Cheyenne on Superstore, but she's also played Louise in the TV show Maggie, and Jessica in the series Ghosts. Sakura also does a lot of voiceover work, playing the title character in Suzume and playing roles in Kiff, Central Park, and Star Wars: Visions.

Shameless places Lip in the trope of the student falling in love with the Professor, though it does give it a little bit of contrast by flipping the typical gender roles. However memorable she was though, Helene is still, out of all of Lip's girlfriends, a toxic partner. By choosing her, he loses everything he had worked for up until that point. Due to his unwillingness to let the relationship go and the excessive alcohol use that follows their breakup, Lip gets expelled from the University.

He goes home with his tail between his legs, all because of the mysterious, mature Professor who did not seem to lose much sleep over their end. Through Lip's girlfriend in season 5, Shameless gave him an intriguing, albeit sad, arc that changed his character's trajectory forever.

Professor Helene Runyon was portrayed by actress Sasha Alexander, who is mainly known for embodying one-half of the crime procedural duo Rizzoli & Isles as Maura Isles. Alexander had another long stint on a procedural, as she played Caitlin Todd on NCIS. Some may know her for her short arc on Dawson's Creek as Gretchen Witter, or possibly for playing Melissa in Mission: Impossible III. She most recently voiced Adeline in Deathstroke: Knights & Dragons - The Movie.

Karen was Lip's girlfriend in Shameless seasons 1 and 2. She shared his love for sex, and they certainly shared hatred towards their respective father figures, but she proved to be more than Lip was willing to put up with. Among the many shameless things she does is taking advantage of a drunk Frank and filming it as revenge towards her dad in a Shameless season 1 forgotten moment, and not only lying to Lip about him being the father of her baby, but having a complete disregard for the child when Hymie is born.

Karen is run over by Mandy and the resulting brain trauma changes her personality completely. She leaves the show shortly after being released from the hospital, so it's clear the two will never be an item again — although this may have been true with or without the brain injury given how unhealthy their relationship was. Laura Wiggins played the infamous Karen on Shameless, and she's mostly played bit roles on TV or appeared in indie flicks ever since. Wiggins has had roles on shows like CSI, Chicago P.D., and Intelligence. She played Jordan in Along Came the Devil 2 and Maddie in InstaPsycho.

Lip met Sierra at Patsy's Pies where she waitressed under Fiona's management, and she becomes Lip's girlfriend in season 7. She befriends Fiona and starts to date Lip, but Lip is still healing from his college mess and Sierra has an ex who still comes around. She also had a child, which was a first for Lip. In the end, he does the honorable thing and helps her ex get sober and win her back. In Lip's girlfriend in season 7, Shameless saw the character taking a turn for the better, and learning a thing or two about responsibility.

Sierra was great for Lip, but he just wasn't at the right time in his life to be with her. Actress Ruby Modine played Sierra in Shameless, and audiences may recognize her for taking on the role of Lori Spengler in the Happy Death Day franchise. She's since appeared in a few horror flicks, including Satanic Panic and Fear. However, she's also had roles in The Survivalist and On Our Way.

Under different circumstances, Mandy and Lip would still be together. However, in Shameless, Mandy chooses a path that leads into some risky situations and away from being Lip's girlfriend. Until Tami came along, audiences still held on to a small hope that Mandy would come back, and the two would rekindle their romance. Mandy will always be the girl that Lip was the most himself around, and she seemed to have only the best intentions for him, submitting college applications in his name and behaving defensively on his behalf. Some of Shameless' best episodes feature the couple.

While Mandy's time as Lip's girlfriend was a highlight of the show, her arc in Shameless ultimately meant the two couldn't end up together. Mandy Milkovich was recast in Shameless, but when she was Lip's girlfriend she was played by actress Emma Greenwell. The actress had a short stint on True Blood as Claudia before playing Charlotte in Holy Ghost People. She then moved on to playing Caroline Bingley in the horror comedy Pride and Prejudice and Zombies, followed by Catherine in Love & Friendship. Greenwell had a long stint as Mary Cox in The Path and played Abbie in Rattlesnake.

Out of all of Lip's girlfriends, Tami turned out to be the one he settled down with. Tami and Lip have an odd but fitting meet cute in season 9's first episode, having sex during Brad's wedding to her sister. Due to his need to prove how much better in bed he is than the experience shows, he pursues a second chance with her and this leads to the two dating.

Some viewers wondered if it would have made sense for them to stay together if it weren't for the child she ends up becoming pregnant with, but in the context of the show, it seems Tami is a good fit for Lip since she makes him happy and gave him the family he's been wanting. Finally, through the last of Lip's girlfriends in Shameless, he finds a life and family that he's always wanted, properly closing out his arc for the Shameless ending.

Tami was portrayed by Kate Miner, who had quite a long history of TV series bit roles before starring in Shameless, appearing in Drake & Josh, Ugly Betty, CSI: Miami, Scandal, Two and a Half Men, and more. Since starring in Shameless, Miner has had roles on NCIS: Hawai'i, Nora, and FBI: International. Miner's upcoming roles include two TV movies, Festival of Trees and A Podcast to Die For, as well as the headlining horror thriller Stay Safe.

#3358. Microsoft outage saw 80% of servers fail – here’s what happened

Last week saw a truly epic outage to Microsoft 365, with a huge number of users unable to send and receive emails. The company has now admitted that at the worst point, more than 80% of its servers were unresponsive.

Microsoft has now explained what went wrong, stating that the mistake that led to the failure was actually made all the way back in July without being detected …

The company said at the time that it was a technical issue and not a cyber attack, and that it was working hard to fix the problem, admitting that it was taking longer than expected. Microsoft also denied that it was related to the thousands of layoffs announced the previous month.

Users were understandably unimpressed at the scale of the outage and the time taken to fix it, although meme creators were having fun.

Sorry but you have to be change the name now. Thems the rules pic.twitter.com/5UttZ8nt9f

It certainly points out that when you base your business on cloud services, you also take the risk that comes with that.

Platform head Charles Lamanna admitted the severity of the problem.

In less than two hours, the previously unknown defect was encountered across our fleet and rendered them unresponsive. At its lowest, more than 80% of servers were unresponsive.

He said it resulted from a combination of two issues. The company maintains two independent network gateway systems, one of which failed, meaning that the remaining gateway took the full load. That wouldn’t have been a problem on its own, Microsoft stating that each one has enough capacity to handle all traffic. However, a mistake made back in July led to a cascading failure.

A latent defect caused servers to become overwhelmed and unresponsive under certain load conditions. This was due to lock contention inside an internal process which caused the machine to become unavailable. This defect was the result of a fix that was prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers […]

The initial change in behavior first started deployment in July of this year. The update went through safe deployment and saturated globally over several weeks, during which time no issues were observed. For more than three months, the change was deployed worldwide without impact. Our normal load testing did not detect the latent issue because the different traffic and SKU mix used in our test labs. The contention issue is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware; whereas our load testing tended to focus on our weaker hardware SKUs with fewer cores.

In other words, the update wasn’t tested under the conditions in which it was most likely to fail.

While the company claims that the incident is unrelated to laying off staff and replacing them with AI systems, I find myself extremely skeptical. It seems inconceivable that a company of Microsoft’s size could make what appears to be a schoolboy error of this magnitude unless there were insufficient engineers working on the update. Please share your own thoughts in the comments.

#3357. Microsoft Officially Apologized for Yesterday's Outages

If you were having trouble accessing certain services like Microsoft Teams or Outlook, you were not alone. Early Thursday afternoon, many of Microsoft's biggest apps and services were experiencing downtime. According to Downdetector, which tracks user reports of issues with websites and platforms, Microsoft 365, Teams, Copilot, Teams, and OneDrive were all experiencing issues. As of Friday afternoon, Microsoft has restored service to many users, and has officially apologized for the outages.

When I first published this article on Thursday, I couldn't even load Microsoft 365's status page. (I've reported on many service outages, but I can't recall a time when a service's status page was also down.) Even as of Friday afternoon, the page still says "Service degradation on Microsoft 365 (Business or Enterprise)," and Microsoft says the following services may be affected: Exchange Online, Microsoft 365 admin center, Microsoft 365 apps, Microsoft 365 Apps Admin Center, Microsoft 365 Education, Microsoft Copilot 365, Microsoft Defender for Office 365, Microsoft Defender XDR, Microsoft Fabric, Microsoft Graph, Microsoft Intune, Microsoft Planner, Microsoft Power Apps, Microsoft Purview, Microsoft Teams, Microsoft To Do, Power BI, SharePoint Online, Universal Print, and Windows 365.

Looking specifically at Outlook, Microsoft's email service had hundreds of thousands of user reports Thursday afternoon, signaling a major issue somewhere in Microsoft's pipeline. The reports did "slow down" throughout the day, but Downdetector still showed over 50,000 reports coming in every 15 minutes when I checked Thursday afternoon.

While the root cause of the issue was a mystery throughout Thursday's outage, Microsoft confirmed the problem in an apology on Friday. According to the company, "This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI [or] agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions."

Microsoft says it is "deeply sorry" for the disruption to its customers and partners. The company says the fix rolled out slower than some might expect, since it wanted to restore service gradually to evaluate stability at each stage. It also says it will release a full post-incident report once it completes a review.

During the outage, the company had confirmed that some of its infrastructure was experiencing elevated load, which it said was likely contributing to the issues. Microsoft then said it was pausing all deployments and moving traffic from affected infrastructure, and that it found that a number of its servers were unexpectedly unavailable after failing health checks. The company then thought a specific component responsible for processing server health may be the reason the system is failing health checks. Microsoft said an alternative service health check method successfully restarted some of the affected servers. The company was then actively restarting and validating affected servers to bring them back to service.

#3356. Michael Jackson's Former Friends Sue Lawyer Bryan Freedman, Claim He Misled Them

Michael Jackson's former friends -- the Cascio family -- are suing attorney Bryan Freedman ... claiming the lawyer didn't tell them he represented MJ's estate in certain matters when he got them to sign a settlement agreement with the estate several years ago.

Frank, Edward, Dominic and Aldo Cascio, plus Marie Nicole and James Porte, have filed a complaint against Freedman claiming he committed legal malpractice. They say he claimed to be representing their interests with respect to their sexual abuse claims against Michael, which had not been made public yet ... but claim Freedman failed to disclose he actually worked for the estate in other cases.

The Cascios say Freedman approached them with an investigator after the MJ estate wanted to proactively address possible claims of sexual misconduct against Michael ... and they say Freedman told them he was advocating for their interests against the estate -- and told them they didn't need their own attorney.

However, the family says -- unbeknownst to them -- Freedman represented MJ's estate in a lawsuit against HBO over the documentary "Leaving Neverland," which focused on claims of abuse made against the late pop star by two other alleged victims.

After they signed a settlement with the estate -- one which the Cascios claim they didn't have a chance to get independent legal advice about or read carefully -- they say they learned about the contract's confidentiality, non-disparagement, penalty provisions to clawback money, and mandatory arbitration clauses.

They say if they'd known about that before signing the contract, then they never would've signed it.

The Cascios are suing Freedman -- who has represented numerous high-profile clients, including Justin Baldoni in his legal fight against Blake Lively -- for legal malpractice, breach of fiduciary duty, fraud, and negligent misrepresentation.

#3355. The 8 Greatest Cold War Books of All Time, Ranked

The second half of the 20th century was defined by the Cold War. The decades-long conflict shaped international politics, fueled devastating proxy conflicts, and brought humanity frighteningly close to annihilation. Unsurprisingly, these tensions provided fertile ground for novelists, particularly those interested in espionage.

The result was a deep and diverse body of work exploring the Cold War from every angle and perspective, covering many genres and introducing some of literature's most timeless settings, narratives, and characters. This list looks at some of the very best of them, from meticulously researched military thrillers to character studies about compromise and disillusionment.

"Why don't you pass the time by playing a little solitaire?" Many people will be familiar with the classic film, but The Manchurian Candidate actually started out as a novel. It focuses on Raymond Shaw, an American soldier who returns from the Korean War as a decorated hero after supposedly saving the lives of his fellow servicemen. However, the truth is considerably more disturbing. During his captivity, Raymond was subjected to an elaborate brainwashing experiment designed to transform him into an unwitting assassin.

Meanwhile, his former commanding officer, Bennett Marco, begins experiencing troubling nightmares that suggest their official recollections of the war are false. Building off that setup, the book becomes a chilling political thriller, as well as a striking time capsule for the paranoia and ideological hysteria of the 1950s. The cynicism and satire have aged surprisingly well.

"An alarm clock is a strange thing in a submarine." Shifting gears, we have Tom Clancy's breakout book, which turns Cold War tensions into a suspenseful, blockbuster entertainment. In The Hunt for Red October, Soviet commander Marko Ramius takes control of the Red October, an advanced nuclear submarine equipped with a revolutionary propulsion system that makes it exceptionally difficult to detect. When Ramius unexpectedly changes course toward the Atlantic, Soviet authorities launch a massive operation to intercept him.

Meanwhile, CIA analyst Jack Ryan becomes convinced that Ramius intends to defect to the United States, placing him at the center of a potentially catastrophic international confrontation. There is mystery and action aplenty here, but it's elevated by Clancy's meticulous research and attention to detail. He gets granular with the descriptions of submarine warfare, sonar systems, naval tactics, and the bureaucracy of intelligence operations.

"Sometimes the most important battles are fought without weapons." Winter of the World is the second entry in Ken Follett's sweeping Century Trilogy. It's a masterful historical epic that charts the major events of the 20th century through the eyes of a few families. The first book was all about the Great War and, here, the focus is on World War II and the early stages of the Cold War.

The sprawling cast includes characters from Britain, Germany, the Soviet Union, and the USA, whose personal ambitions and relationships become entangled with the major social forces of their time. Through them, the book brings many crucial historical moments to life, rendering them all in accessible prose and compelling plotting. As a result, a fairly weighty book winds up being quite a page-turner. Not for nothing, Winter of the World hit number one on the New York Times bestseller list.

"It was the beginning of his life." This is a gripping psychological thriller by Atonement's Ian McEwan. Set in Berlin during the 1950s, The Innocent centers on Leonard Marnham, a young British telecommunications technician recruited to assist with a secret Anglo-American intelligence operation. His assignment involves helping construct and maintain a tunnel beneath Soviet-controlled territory, allowing Western intelligence agencies to intercept sensitive communications.

However, Leonard's life changes dramatically when he begins a relationship with Maria Eckdorf, a German woman whose troubled past introduces complications far removed from his professional responsibilities. From here, we get an unusually smart and character-driven espionage story, expressed through McEwan's dependably brilliant prose. The Innocent gets pretty deep with its themes, too. Indeed, the title refers to the deluded belief that nations or individuals can engage in covert power struggles without getting blood on their hands.

"Some things are too important to be left to the intelligence services." This one is the opening entry in a trilogy (which itself is the first of three trilogies) about Bernard Samson, an MI6 officer who has spent much of his career operating in Berlin. Having grown up in the city, he understands the divided society intimately, as well as the complicated relationships between Western intelligence agencies and their Soviet counterparts.

His latest assignment involves extracting a valuable British agent from East Germany, but the operation becomes increasingly dangerous when evidence suggests that a Soviet mole has infiltrated British intelligence. Refreshingly, the book portrays spycraft as a grimy profession divided by personal rivalries and conflicting loyalties rather than glamorous adventures. Likewise, the protagonist is cynical and sarcastic, in stark contrast to the suave super-spies of classic espionage fiction.

"Innocence is like a dumb leper who has lost his bell, wandering the world, meaning no harm." This is one of the defining works by English novelist and journalist Graham Greene, who also wrote The Heart of the Matter and the novella that became the movie The Third Man. Set in Vietnam during the final years of French colonial rule, The Quiet American revolves around Thomas Fowler, a cynical British journalist who has become emotionally attached to the country despite his insistence on remaining politically neutral.

He then crosses paths with Alden Pyle, an idealistic young American whose enthusiasm for political theories contrasts sharply with Fowler's more experienced understanding of the conflict. Through these two men, the book examines the dangers of imposing ideological solutions on complex societies, especially as an outsider. It's something governments continue to fail to take to heart.

"The first one was a woman." One of the strongest James Bond books. The story begins with the Soviet counterintelligence organization SMERSH devising an elaborate operation to destroy 007. Their scheme involves Tatiana Romanova, a young cipher clerk who is instructed to pretend that she wishes to defect to the West. As an additional incentive, she offers to provide British intelligence with a valuable Soviet decoding machine. Bond is subsequently dispatched to Istanbul, though the true objectives of the operation are concealed from him.

Intriguingly, the entire first third of the novel doesn't feature Bond at all, instead detailing the inner workings of SMERSH in Moscow. All in all, From Russia with Love is a typically enjoyable mix of intrigue, espionage thrills, and juicy narrative switcheroos. Some of the series' most memorable supporting characters also appear here, particularly the resourceful Turkish operative Darko Kerim and the terrifying assassin Red Grant.

"What do you think spies are: priests, saints, and martyrs?" When it comes to quintessential Cold War books, it's hard to top The Spy Who Came in from the Cold, John le Carré's magnum opus. In it, we meet Alec Leamas, a disillusioned British agent whose network of agents in East Germany has been systematically dismantled. Following the death of his last remaining operative, Leamas is recalled to London, where his superiors devise an elaborate operation intended to undermine a powerful East German intelligence official.

To make the deception convincing, Leamas must appear to have become a bitter, alcoholic willing to betray his country. However, as the operation progresses, the line between calculated manipulation and genuine betrayal becomes increasingly blurred. The result is a hard-edged, world-weary spy story that captures the grimness of the Cold War in the 1960s, forever changing the genre in the process.

#3353. 10 Books Like ‘A Court of Thorns and Roses’ You Should Read Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Sarah J. Maas’ lush, romance-soaked series A Court of Thorns and Roses has blossomed into a sprawling, complex fantasy series with millions of dedicated fans, and with good reason. A complex heroine who keeps discovering new depths in herself, fascinating supporting characters who shift from antihero to antivillain in unexpected ways, creative and beautifully rendered world-building—the series has it all, while also being unapologetically romantic (and steamy).

The story of a huntress who is kidnapped by a fae prince and brought to the Spring Court as a prisoner, only to become a key player in all that fae drama, ACOTAR is special, but Maas can only write so fast. If you need more books with the same lush feel, here are 10 to get you started.

It’s no shock that one of Sarah J. Maas’ other series would be recommended for fans of A Court of Thorns and Roses, but there’s a specific reason you should jump into her Crescent City series, especially the third book, House of Flame and Shadow. The most recent ACOTAR book, A Court of Splintered Harmony, revealed that the events of House of Flame and Shadow tie directly into the events in Splintered Harmony, particularly with regard to the character of Feyre’s sister, Nesta. In other words, if you read Splintered Harmony and wondered why Nesta was being so weird, there’s a whole other book series you should dig into immediately.

If Feyre’s grit and determination are your favorite aspect of ACOTAR, Julie Kagawa’s Iron Fey series (starting with The Iron King) will be your next obsession. Meghan Chase has never felt ‘normal’ in her life, and she’s been haunted by her father’s disappearance since she was a child. When her brother also vanishes, she goes on a quest for answers, learns that she’s actually the daughter of a faerie king, and finds herself in a magical world that blurs in elements of Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream. Meghan is determined to save her brother (and herself), but a certain ice-cold fae prince captures her attention, even though he’s as dangerous as he is beautiful.

If you’re looking for some serious romance in your fantasy, Jennifer L. Armentrout’s A Blood and Ash series is a must. Poppy was chosen at birth to be the kingdom’s Maiden, isolated and untouched in order to be ready for her Ascension to ensure the land is protected from the evil force that took her family. But it’s a lonely existence—until Hawke is assigned as her sworn protector. Golden-eyed and beautiful, Hawke offers Poppy the connection she’s craved. When chaos erupts around her, Hawke takes the opportunity to spirit Poppy away. But Hawke has a secret, and Poppy is soon in danger of losing both her heart and the favor of the gods themselves.

If you love how A Court of Thorns and Roses takes the “enemies-to-lovers” trope and builds it into a deep, complex mesh of emotions and plot twists, you’ll love Shelby Mahurin’s Serpent & Dove series. When witch Louise le Blanc flees her coven, she takes shelter in the city of Cesarine, where magic is forbidden, and witches are unceremoniously hunted and burned. Louise’s life gets infinitely more complicated, dangerous, and steamy when she’s trapped into an unwanted marriage with Reid Diggory—who happens to be a huntsman of the Church, charged with tracking down and eliminating witches. And then Louise starts to realize that Reid is actually pretty darn hot.

If you’re looking for a romantasy that’s broadly similar to ACOTAR while being its own thing, read A.K. Mulford’s The Five Crowns of Okrith series, starting with The High Mountain Court. Remy is a red witch, which means she’s in hiding and ready to make a run for it if the fae get near. So when a group of fae shows up at her tavern, she makes for the exit—only to be captured by Prince Hale of the Eastern Court. Instead of striking her down, however, Hale asks Remy for help—he needs to locate two ancient magical artifacts created by red witches, and he needs her red magic to find them. Hale promises to set her free and even reunite her with the red witches still living. More importantly, Remy finds Hale irresistible and has a primal urge to stay with him, no matter what the cost.

Looking for a romantasy with a slightly different vibe from ACOTAR? Variety is the spice of life, after all—and The Fourth Wing delivers. Rebecca Yarros’ Empyrean Series made a huge splash when it debuted, and for good reason—it has everything, from a capable, intelligent heroine thrust into a dangerous scenario (in this case, a dragon rider academy where failure can be deadly) and forced to navigate alliances, conspiracies, and her own heart, which is pushing her towards a romance that might be as dangerous as the dragons themselves.

Love the moral complexity of ACOTAR, where everyone has at least a touch of darkness? Check out The Folk of the Air series by Holly Black. When Jude was a child, the father of her half-sister, the faerie Madoc, murdered her parents and took her back to the Faerie world with him. Raised as part of the gentry, Jude lives in a world where her mortal nature is hated and despised, but she battles for her place at court anyway while struggling with her love-hate relationship with her adoptive father and a growing bond with the titular prince, a relationship that is strictly forbidden. Jude is a fierce and extremely morally gray character, and one that fans of Feyre will adore.

Looking for more smart women at the center of beautifully-rendered fantasy stories? You’ll love Princess Lucero-Elisa de Riqueza of Orovalle, star of this series-starter by Rae Carson. Elisa was chosen for “Service” as a baby, when a godstone was placed in her navel by the gods, signaling that she was destined for greatness. But as a young woman, Elisa is self-hating and miserable. She’s never done anything even remotely great, and spends her time isolated, overweight, and reading military strategy books. One day she’s shocked to discover she’s been married off to the king of a distant land on the brink of war—and suddenly all that rage and book learning becomes invaluable as she struggles to survive an unfamiliar court and help her new homeland survive a dangerous onslaught.

If you loved Feyre’s journey as she discovered unknown reservoirs of power and courage inside herself, you should read Leigh Bardugo’s Grishaverse novels, starting with Shadow and Bone. As a child, Alina was tested by the Grisha and found to possess no magical ability. As an adult, she serves as a cartographer in the army. Charged with guiding the Darkling—the most powerful of the Grisha—across the dangerous and terrifying Shadow Fold, Alina is unexpectedly revealed to have incredible powers and is packed off to train with the Grisha. There, she must determine who her friends and enemies are, even while falling under the spell of the charismatic Darkling.

Emilia di Carlo and her sister Vittoria are very different—Emilia is bookish and shy, Vittoria outgoing and brash—but they share a secret: They’re both streghe, and have spent their lives learning to use magic. In this version of Italy, the Malvagi (the seven princes of Hell) haven’t been seen in a long time, but a terrifying accident summons the Prince of Wrath and leaves three witches dead, including Vittoria. Emilia swears to use her power to avenge her sister, but when her revenge is delayed and she’s forced to work with Wrath, unwanted feelings begin to tick up the spice level to an uncomfortable degree.
