#3352. After Netflix's 95% RT Time Travel Series, You'll Never Watch Another Sci-Fi Show The Same

One Netflix sci-fi series managed to perfect the Mystery Box formula and, in the process, the show ensured viewers would never be able to watch any other entry into the genre the same way again. Although Lost is often called the first Mystery Box TV show, David Lynch and Mark Frost’s twisty murder mystery Twin Peaks and the classic ‘90s sci-fi series The X-Files helped shape the genre with their complex mystery plotting and elaborate mythology, respectively.

Twin Peaks introduced a level of serialized narrative complexity and obscure, esoteric symbolism that hadn’t been seen on network TV before, while the multi-season mytharc of The X-Files offered viewers a more focused, clearer conspiracy to sink their teeth into during the show's entire original run. That being said, the narrative complexity and experimental arrangement of Lost remained an important moment in the genre’s development.

Since Lost’s divisive finale, everything from HBO’s The Leftovers to Yellowjackets, to Prime Video’s video game adaptation Fallout, to Jonathan Nolan’s Westworld reboot has vied to become the next great Mystery Box show. However, while some of these shows are superb, it is Netflix’s three-season hit Dark that truly deserves this title, since the show’s unique sci-fi story structure changes the way viewers encounter any new series in the genre.

On the face of it, Dark might sound a lot like Netflix’s earlier sci-fi hit Stranger Things. After all, Dark also blends sci-fi plot elements and small-town character drama in the story of a multi-generational group of characters unearthing a bizarre, otherworldly supernatural mystery on the outskirts of their shared community after a local young boy goes missing. However, the differences between the two shows are pivotal.

While Stranger Things was a wild ride that grew progressively bigger in scale and scope with each season, Dark told a truly focused, self-contained story. The tale of the town of Winden and its secret cave that facilitates time travel was utterly unique, as viewers were expected to carefully follow multi-decade time travel cycles, casual loops, and intersecting timelines. Essentially, Dark was less like Stranger Things in Germany, and more like a version of Lost that made perfect sense.

Of course, this glib assessment is a little unfair on Lost, but the fact remains that Dark’s story truly did cohere in a way few Mystery Box shows do. This meant that new viewers could arrive at the show’s story with everything spoiled and still enjoy the experience, since what made Netflix’s Dark great was how events came together, rather than the specific shocks of finding out the next twist.

Much like Nolan’s Person of Interest, Dark was a sci-fi show of real intellectual depth that actively encouraged viewers to revisit its storylines and see how everything slotted together across its timelines. The satisfying clockwork mechanism of Dark’s storytelling was a refreshing change from the typical Mystery Box approach, where certain questions are never answered, and certain mysteries are simply left unresolved.

Here, thanks to Dark’s ingenious time travel mechanics, the show’s character work was as effective and grounded as anything from Lost, but its storytelling was as airtight as Shane Carruth’s infamously complex indie sci-fi Primer. This allowed Dark to fuse heart and head in a Mystery Box mix that gave even HBO’s masterpiece The Leftovers a run for its money.

Almost ten years after Dark’s 2017 debut, there is just one issue with the breathless 24-episode story of Winden’s time travel and its myriad unpredictable outcomes. For viewers who had the pleasure of seeing Dark and re-watching the complex sci-fi show, every new show in the genre tends to feel comparatively underwritten and ill planned.

#3346. These Are the Best Ways to Encrypt Your Email

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

As this in-depth explainer from Adaptive Security describes, most emails are encrypted in transit via Transport Layer Security (TLS), which prevents anyone from reading your message as it travels from server to server. However, encryption is temporarily stripped at each server: content is received and processed in plaintext and then re-encrypted when it leaves, meaning it could be read, logged, and distributed by the server provider.

Emails are also typically encrypted at rest—for example, while sitting on Google's servers and in a Gmail recipient's inbox. But this only prevents someone with physical access to the server hardware from reading messages, as Google still holds the encryption key and can access stored data. And, as PCMag points out, Google is scanning your messages to a degree, and it (along with other email providers) can and will hand emails over to law enforcement and government agencies in some cases.

If you have an account with a major email provider like Gmail, Outlook, or Apple Mail, you can add a third-party tool that layers an encryption protocol like OpenPGP on top of your existing account. PCMag recommends PreVeil, SecureMyEmail, and Virtru (which is limited to Gmail users in Chrome) for those who want to keep their current emails. Mailvelope is a browser add-on (and therefore a desktop-only tool) available in Chrome, Firefox, and Edge, though it can also be installed on other browsers, like Brave, that are built on the same architecture. FlowCrypt integrates with Gmail and Google Workspace on desktop and mobile.

Note that enterprise users of Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 have access to true end-to-end encryption without third-party add-ons. Gmail's Confidential mode and Outlook's Encrypt feature, available to all users, are not E2EE equivalents, as Google and Microsoft, respectively, still manage the keys.

For those who are willing to start fresh with a new email address (or who have a custom domain), providers like Proton Mail or Tuta offer native end-to-end encryption. The caveat: by default, this is only between users on the same service, so from one Proton user to another. If you want to send an end-to-end encrypted email from Proton to a Gmail user, for example, you have to set up password protection (and share the password via another secure channel) or use a PGP-compatible tool like those listed above. You can also Proton's Gmail integration does allow for end-to-end encryption, but only if both Gmail parties are using the Proton integration.

#3342. 10 Privacy Hacks Every Mac User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Enabling the macOS Firewall (which is off by default) adds a layer of protection against external devices on your wifi network, as well as unauthorized apps from initiating a connection to your device. Turning on Stealth Mode prevents your Mac from even responding to these requests, essentially making it invisible to anything that's scanning a network you're connected to. This makes it more difficult for hackers and malware to know your device exists, much less attack it. This can interfere with certain essential activity when you're on your home network, but it's a valuable security setting when on public wifi. You can leave Firewall on all the time and enable Stealth Mode only as needed. Go to Settings > Network > Firewall, flip the toggle, then hit Options to manage Stealth Mode.

Images and screenshots contain metadata, such as timestamps, device and hardware details, and, in the case of photos, physical location. Much of this information is stripped automatically when you share files to social media or via encrypted messaging apps, but if you're sending them via text or email, posting to forums, or sharing over AirDrop, metadata remains intact. You can easily remove metadata from your images right on your desktop. Select the file and hit control + click to bring up an options menu, then go to Quick Actions > Convert Image. Uncheck the box next to Preserve Metadata, then hit Convert. (This is also useful for quickly converting HEIC to JPEG without opening a separate app.)

If you're using iCloud to store photos, files, and device backups, your data is encrypted on Apple's servers and in transit. Apple still holds the decryption key, which is useful if you somehow get locked out of your account and need help recovering it, but for sensitive data—including device backups—end-to-end encryption is the most secure way to ensure no one but you can gain access. Advanced Data Protection is an opt-in setting for iCloud that encrypts your information end to end. You'll need to set up an alternative recovery method, such as your device passcode with two-factor authentication, a recovery contact, or a recovery key. Be careful, though: If you lose access to this recovery method, you will lose your data. You can enable Advanced Data Protection on your Mac under System Settings > [Your Name] > iCloud > Advanced Data Protection > Turn On. Note that some iCloud data, including passwords and payment methods, are already end-to-end encrypted by default.

#3339. If Your Google Pixel's Camera Is Suddenly Broken, Here's the Fix

Updates are generally good for your devices. The latest Chrome update, for example, patches an actively exploited security vulnerability, while Apple's latest updates stop people from seeing iMessages they shouldn't have access to. In most cases, it's beneficial to update your tech to the latest software version whenever possible.

Sadly, updates aren't all perfect, as Google Pixel users are discovering this week. As reported by Android Authority, Google's November update apparently shipped with a bug that breaks some Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 cameras. Seeing as Pixels are rather famous for their shooters, this is a decidedly unfortunate glitch.

Here's the situation: Following the November update, some users are opening their Pixel Camera apps to find an error that reads, "Something went wrong. Close and open the Camera app again," with a "Learn More" link to, well, learn more. Others aren't receiving the error, but are instead running into a blank Camera viewfinder, as if the lens is totally covered. What's more, some users are reportedly saying that the issue is present on third-party camera apps, not just the Pixel Camera app. That would imply this is an issue with the camera system-wide, not just the Pixel Camera app itself.

To be clear, it doesn't seem like this is a universal issue. It's not like all Pixel users are now running with broken cameras. But based on the forum complaints Android Authority discovered, it seems reasonable to assume that this glitch isn't limited to just a handful of unlucky Pixel owners.

Luckily, there is an apparent workaround here, though it's not totally obvious. Some users are having no luck restarting their Pixels, while others report that a factory reset wasn't enough to restore camera functionality.

What does appear to work, however, is shutting your Pixel down and waiting five minutes or so. It's not clear why, but giving your Pixel a chance to "breathe" seems to shake the glitch and bring back your camera. As Android Authority reports, that fix comes from "Diamond and Gold product experts" on Google's Support forum.

If your Pixel's camera is giving you grief following the November update, this workaround is definitely worth a try—especially since more drastic measures don't actually seem to do anything. As the issue does seem to be rather widespread, I wouldn't be surprised to see Google issue a patch in the coming days. But until then, turning your phone off for five minutes may be a decent compromise.

#3336. After 85 Years, Wonder Woman Officially Quits Being A Hero

Batman and Superman have hung up the cape multiple times before, but Wonder Woman's decision to throw the tiara is even more shocking. Superman is the most powerful and important superhero in the DC Universe, but even he has repeatedly stepped away from his role or been forced out of action. His most famous absence followed his fatal battle with Doomsday in Death of Superman. Beyond death, Clark Kent gave up his powers to marry Lois Lane in Whatever Happened to the Man of Tomorrow?, spent a year powerless after the Infinite Crisis, traveled across space during Warworld Saga and New Krypton, and retired from public heroism in Kingdom Come.

Batman has endured an equally dramatic history of physical breakdowns and self-imposed retirements. His most iconic defeat took place in Knightfall, where Bane broke the Bat's spine and left Jean-Paul Valley to patrol Gotham. Years later, Darkseid’s Omega Sanction seemingly killed Bruce in Final Crisis, stranding him in the distant past until his return in The Return of Bruce Wayne, while amnesia wiped away his memories entirely after Endgame. In alternate futures like The Dark Knight Returns and Batman Beyond, old age and a near-fatal heart scare finally pushed Bruce to hang up the cape for years at a time.

Wonder Woman's long lifespan allows her to be much more resilient than the World's Finest, but even a nearly immortal Amazon has a breaking point.

The weight of endless war finally drives Diana Prince to remove her iconic golden tiara and attempt to walk away from her superhero mantle altogether in Wonder Woman #39. She voices her frustrations with having to be the perfect hero, even more steadfast than Batman and Superman, and confesses to Steve Trevor that her immortal life feels like the endless torment of Sisyphus. Fortunately, Steve Trevor is there to remind Diana Wonder Woman that her willingness to endure exhaustion without ever losing her compassion is what makes her "the greatest superhero in history" and convinces her not to give up.

In true Wonder Woman fashion, Diana Prince not only drops the idea of quitting her superhero duties, but she returns to the battlefield even stronger than before as she unites the entire Wonder Family, joining forces with Donna Troy, Cassie Sandsmark, Yara Flor, Nubia, and Trinity to make a defiant final stand. The assembled Amazonian heroes confront a powerful group of villains led by Matriarch and the Sovereign, including Doctor Psycho and even Kite Man. Wonder Woman even gets to land a satisfying punch on Matriarch's face before Tom King and Daniele Sampere's Wonder Woman run concludes with issue #40.

Wonder Woman almost hung up her tiara in Wonder Woman out of sheer exhaustion, frustrated with her superhero duties. This is the perfect foundation for DC's third "For The Man Who Has Everything" story. In Alan Moore and Dave Gibbons’s 1985 masterpiece, the parasitic Black Mercy traps Superman inside an idealized hallucination of a utopian Krypton where he lives a peaceful ordinary life free from superhero responsibilities, which ultimately forces him to tear himself away from paradise to return to real life and save his friends. Earlier in 2026, Detective Comics 2026 Annual #1 delivered Batman’s dark counterpart when Bruce Wayne rejected the fantasy of his living parents outright.

Explore 5 unique stories that drastically reinvent Wonder Woman's character and origins over the years.

Now that Wonder Woman has openly confessed how weary she is of her Sisyphus-like immortal duties, Diana Prince is primed for her own deeply personal encounter with the Black Mercy to complete this Trinity trilogy. Unlike Superman, who had to mourn a family he never knew; or Batman, who immediately dismissed the illusion of a peaceful life, Diana’s greatest temptation would be a quiet mortal life alongside Steve Trevor and her daughter Lizzie. A "For The Woman Who Has Everything" story starring Wonder Woman would force Diana to face the same choices as her fellow Trinity heroes.

#3335. Five Hacks Every Apple Watch Series 12 User Should Know

The latest Apple Watches have a lot of new features that older watches don't, so I figured it was time for a new list of hacks. While our general Apple Watch and fitness tracking hacks are still golden, Series 12 devices offer new features like native step counting, a Readiness app, an upgraded heart rate sensor, an AI-based version of Siri, and "audio intelligence" that can replay and summarize real-life conversations, within limits. Here's how to get the most out of them.

The Series 12 can finally count steps natively, a task that for some reason is only arriving now, and is restricted to just the newest Apple Watch models. Enjoy it! To add a step counter to your watch face, long-press on the clock screen to edit it, tap on a complication (that’s what Apple calls those little icons and numbers that appear on some watch faces), choose Activity, and then tap Steps.

You don’t need this creepy feature listening in to everything, but it can be nice to have it as a backup on occasion. A button in your Apple Watch’s Control Center can turn the feature on and off. Keep it off except when you have a structured conversation that you’ll want to refer to later. This feature is currently in beta (which you can try now if you want to), but is expected to be available to everyone later this year.

It's worth turning off the default setting not just because of the creepiness factor, but also because the recaps work best when there is a single subject of conversation, with a clear start and end, and just one context. If you leave recaps running all the time, your doctor’s appointment will get mixed in with your grocery shopping, YouTube watching, and everyday chatter.

To finish off a recap and make it useful, take a look at the recap shortly after the conversation, tap the three-dots menu, and hit Edit. You’ll be able to adjust the notes and add your own important details. Siri won’t identify speakers and seems to shy away from including certain details, like people’s names. You can add in what it missed and also create your own bullet points so that everything gets noted down while it’s still fresh in your mind.

This one isn’t specific to the Series 12, but if you haven’t gotten on board with the pinch and wrist flick gestures yet, now is a great time.

First, the wrist flick: If a notification is on your screen, or you’re otherwise looking at something you’d rather be done with, just flick your wrist away from you and then back toward you, as if there were a crumb on the watch face and you wanted to knock it off. This will bring you back to the watch face and close whatever you were looking at.

The double pinch is another useful one, although Apple calls it double tap. This is confusing because you aren’t double tapping the watch, you’re tapping your thumb and forefinger together while wearing the watch. You don’t need to touch the watch face at all. So, when you get a notification or a call, look at it on your watch, and pinch your thumb and forefinger (of the watch hand) together twice. The watch detects the pinch from subtle movements in your wrist, and it will open the notification. You can then use the wrist flick to close the notification. Performing a double pinch when no notification is on screen will bring up your smart stack. You can then double-pinch to move to the next card in the smart stack, or single-pinch to open that card and see its details.

If you want to learn even more gestures, go into the Watch app, and select Accessibility and then Hand gestures. You can remap a whole-fist “clench” to do the same thing as pressing the digital crown, for example, or to open the control center or Siri.

A little rude, perhaps, but helpful: With the new AI-based Siri, sometimes answers to questions can be long-winded. If Siri launches into a novel-length response and you’re not interested in hearing all that, just put your palm over the screen. You’ll instantly be transported back to your watch face, and the Siri response will stop.

If you still want to see those longer responses without having Siri read the whole thing to you, you can set this up on your phone, and the settings will carry over to your watch. On your iPhone, go to Settings and tap Siri, then Responses. Select Silent responses instead of Spoken responses. You can then read through her answers, or skim them, as you prefer.

#3332. 10 Hacks Every watchOS 27 User Should Know

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

watchOS 27 introduces a solid set of upgrades to your wrist—assuming your Apple Watch supports it. While the newest update isn't Apple's most feature-filled, it does include a number of changes that improve the way you exercise, track your health, and locate missing items. That's especially true for anyone with the latest Series 12 or Ultra 4. If your Apple Watch supports watchOS 27, you should know about these 10 hacks:

With watchOS 27, Apple changed what double-pressing the Digital Crown does. Instead of opening the app switcher, it now triggers Audio Intelligence—if you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4. If you don't have access to those features, the gesture now does nothing.

It seems Apple realized the mistake, however, as evidenced by watchOS 27.2. When you're using an app while running this latest update, press and hold the bottom part of the watch's screen, and you'll trigger the app switcher. You can now jump to a different app, or close an app that isn't working. Sadly, this only works when you're already in an app, and not when you're on the Home Screen, but it's certainly better than nothing.

While you can load up multiple complications on your Apple Watch, they aren't exactly dynamic. That's why I'm a big fan of the Smart Stack widgets on the Apple Watch, which update dynamically to show contextual information. Now, with the new Siri Modular Face, you can access dynamic widgets on the Home Screen. If you've just parked your car, for example, you'll see a widget showing its location; likewise, if you have an upcoming calendar appointment, it will be front and center.

To use the Siri Modular watch face, tap and hold on the screen, go to the end of the list, tap the Plus button, and find and add the Siri Modular watch face. Once you do, you'll start seeing dynamic widgets when you wake up your watch. Don't expect much personalization from this watch face, however. You can customize the colors and add three small complications, but that's it.

The double-tap gesture is one of my favorite Apple Watch features. By tapping your thumb and index finger together twice, you can do things like answer a call or reply to a message. In watchOS 27, Apple took the gesture one step forward. You can now use the double-tap gesture to scroll through your widgets; if you perform a single tap, it then opens the highlighted widget or the shortcut. This means you can open and browse the weather app, or start a workout, without ever touching your Apple Watch's screen.

Your Apple Watch's new Music Recognition app has native Shazam integration. What's more, Shazam will record your request even when you're offline and away from your iPhone. The moment you reconnect, the service will identify the songs, which you can see in the Shazam app on your iPhone or Apple Watch.

It seems like Apple has a library of songs it uses for offline recognition, because in my testing, it was able to recognize a Coldplay song instantly, even when in Airplane mode. To use it, you can either open the Music Recognition app, or you can add the widget for faster access. Scroll up on the Home Screen, go to the bottom of the screen, tap the Edit button, then the Plus button, and add the Music Recognition widget.

Apple Watches have traditionally lacked a live step count widget or complication. To find your step count, you had to go to the bottom of the Activity app, or rely on third-party apps. But even still, these apps never showed live data. You’d always have to wait a couple of seconds to see the updated stats.

Now, if you own the latest Apple Watch Series 12 or the Ultra 4, you can add a live step count widget or complication to the Apple Watch face or the Smart Stack. This will show you your precise step count at all times. To use it, go to the bottom of the Smart Stack, tap the Edit button, then tap the Plus button. Here, find and add the new Step count widget.

Siri is no longer a voice assistant that you use for one-off tasks. With Siri AI, you can now carry on multiple conversations with context and memory. It's not as robust as ChatGPT or Claude, but you can use Siri AI for brainstorming, researching, and jotting down ideas for later.

The Siri AI app on the iPhone shows all your conversations, and so does the Apple Watch. This means you can continue your Siri AI conversations and view past chats on your Apple Watch. To use it, press the Digital Crown once, then tap the Siri app icon in the center. This will open up all your conversations instead of calling upon Siri. Tap a conversation to continue your chat on the Apple Watch. Of course, anything you do here will be reflected in the Siri app on your iPhone.

The new Find My app on the Apple Watch shows a single map for finding people, devices, and items. This means you can now locate your family members who are sharing their location with you, as well as AirTags or other Find My items from the watchOS app.

After opening the app, you can use the Digital Crown to zoom in or out of the map. Use touch to pan around. The map doesn't show all items and people at once, though. Tap the Menu button at the bottom-right corner, and then switch between People, Items, or Devices. If you have multiple items, you can scroll through them using the Digital Crown.

While it's not a Whoop-level feature, the Apple Watch now includes a Readiness score. Instead of individually looking at your training load, sleep score, and vitals, you now have one number that gives you the whole picture.

The Readiness score ranges from 0 to 10 and is based on your recent fitness activity, sleep data, and background health monitoring. If you have a score of 8 to 10, your Apple Watch thinks you can push yourself, or "go for it," as it says; if it's below 5, the watch thinks you should consider lighter activity. This feature, though, is only available on Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. You can use the new Readiness app on your Apple Watch to see this data, but you can also access it on your iPhone in the Fitness app's new Readiness section.

Low Power Mode isn't your only option when it comes to extending the battery life for your Apple Watch. watchOS 27 offers a special Max Extended Workout mode just for long workouts. With it, your Apple Watch disables some features, like splits and alerts, and reduces the frequency of GPS and heart rate readings, in the hopes of extending your battery throughout your entire exercise. To use it, go to the Workout app and select the workout you want. Tap the Goals button in the top-right corner, and choose the Extended option. Then, switch to the Max Extended option and start your workout.

The Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 come with a set of Audio Intelligence features that use the microphones on the Apple Watch, paired with AI models (both local and cloud-based), to identify sounds, music, and record conversation. Thanks to this new feature, one of the iPhone's accessibility features also makes its way to the Apple Watch.

Sound Recognition can alert you when it hears sirens, alarms, doorbells, and more, even when your iPhone isn’t around. To set this up, go to the Settings app on your iPhone and navigate to Accessibility > Sound & Name Recognition > Sound Recognition. Here, enable the sounds you want to monitor, and make sure to turn on the Detect using Apple Watch toggle.

#3329. I Analyzed the Seven Biggest AI Chatbots to Determine How Safe They Are for Kids

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

AI safety for both adults and children is under greater scrutiny than ever before, with a growing number of questions and concerns appearing around how beneficial or otherwise these conversational bots actually are for our mental well-being—even without considering their energy use, ethics, or economic implications. At the same time, an increasing number of apps and services are becoming age-gated in a growing number of countries around the world, as governments realize that letting kids loose on AI apps, social media platforms, and the web at large might not be the best idea for their ongoing development and prosperity.

The big AI apps, such as ChatGPT and Gemini, are right in the center of these trends, and the companies behind them are taking steps that they promise will keep children safe. If you want to know what youngsters in your family may be getting exposed to, and what you can do about it, here's the rundown.

OpenAI's ChatGPT has one of the more comprehensive setups in terms of parental controls. The minimum age for users is 13, and if you're under 18, you need to have parental consent to open an account—age is predicted via several signals, including what times of day you use ChatGPT and what you talk about.

Accounts for under-18s automatically become ChatGPT for Teens accounts. There's more of a focus on learning and study (with a dedicated study mode), as well as "age-appropriate safeguards to help reduce exposure to sensitive or potentially harmful content." There are built-in protections for "harmful topics," including sexual, romantic, or violent roleplay, graphic violence, and self-harm. These work on top of the safeguards for all users that limit chats about physical harm and illegal activity.

These ChatGPT for Teens accounts can also be linked to a parental account—but while parental consent is required for under-18s to use the service, ChatGPT clearly says that teens do have the option to break the link if they want. If you do persuade your kid to keep your accounts connected, you can set time limits on when the AI bot can be used, and tweak some of the sensitivity settings. However, you can't view any conversations.

To set up parental controls from ChatGPT on the web, click your profile icon (bottom left), then Settings > Parental controls > Add family member and follow the instructions. It's also worth bearing in mind that ChatGPT app can also be used for free, anonymously, in any web browser, though OpenAI says users accessing the AI this way are subject to the default under-18s limits (and can't save chats or access an archive).

Gemini is tied into everything else Google does, and follows the broader rules for Google accounts: No under-13s, unless you're part of a family group and using an account managed by an adult. You can manage your family through the Family Link portal on the web, though as far as parental controls specific to Gemini go, you can only enable or disable access to the AI (settings like screen time apply across all enabled apps).

For all under-18s (partly identified through age estimation), whether or not they're part of a managed family group, Google applies some additional protections. They include preventing the AI from taking on a persona, guarding against emotional dependence on the AI, and discouraging bullying and other forms of harassment. There are also safeguards to limit chats about age-restricted substances like alcohol or vapes, and mental health issues like eating disorders.

These protections for minors are applied in addition to the usual guardrails in Gemini for everyone. The guardrails should lead you away from conversations about self-harm, suicide, violence, and illegal activities, and offer quick links to support in times of crisis. However, Google itself admits that these filters aren't perfect.

As with ChatGPT, there's a loophole of sorts in that anyone can start chatting with Gemini, for free inside a web browser, with no checks at all. These conversations can't be saved and come up against usage limits fairly quickly, but they're only protected by the general restrictions for all accounts, not the ones specific to minors.

Meta AI will show up in several apps that young people and children are likely to use, including WhatsApp and Instagram, as well as having its own separate app on the web and on phones. The standard restrictions for Meta's social media accounts apply to its AI too: A minimum age of 13, and restrictions for all under-18s. Like many other platforms, it uses some AI magic to flag up accounts being used by minors.

If you're under 18 and on a Meta Teen account, you'll come up against blocks if you try to get Meta AI to engage in sexual or romantic roleplay, or discuss alcohol or substance misuse. Chats on topics such as eating disorders and self-harm will prompt the AI to offer guidance towards relevant support services.

Meta offers a comprehensive parental control setup for its apps, including Meta AI, but connecting a parent account isn't compulsory for teens. This is handled through the Meta Family Center portal, and parents can get reports on the general topics that kids are chatting about with AI—though they don't get the exact transcripts or prompts. Any self-harm or suicide discussion can trigger an alert to the connected parent account.

All users, under 18 or over 18, get support and crisis intervention responses when chatting about suicide and self-harm, and there are strict limits on discussing illegal and harmful acts, including drug use and cyberbullying, as well as sexual and adult content.

Apple users have to be 13 or over to have an account, which is required to access Siri AI—anyone younger needs to have an account created for them by an adult, and these accounts can only get at the basic, older Siri. Date of birth must be declared when opening an Apple account, with tighter checks rolling out in many parts of the world.

Anyone over the age of 13 can have an Apple account and use the Siri AI app, with or without a connected parent account, as it stands in most U.S. states. This means the well-being safeguards are essentially the same for teens as they are for adults: There are safeguards around self-harm, suicide, sexual and violent content, and illegal commands. It's one of the more conservative AIs when it comes to what it will talk about.

The new and improved Siri AI can be managed to some extent by the new parental controls available in iOS 27 and Apple's other software updates for 2026—Apple has clearly seen the way the wind is blowing—but this is optional for teens. It depends on whether or not you can corral your kids into a Family Sharing group.

If your teens are in your family group of users, then the standard Screen Time rules apply for controlling app usage limits and device access (in iOS Settings, tap your name, then Family to get at them). There are also options for disabling certain Siri AI features, such as the writing tools or the image creation capabilities.

Like Gemini/Google and Apple/Siri, Copilot is tied into the wider Microsoft ecosystem, and access for under-18s can be managed through it. Users must be 13 or older to hold a Microsoft or a Copilot account—and again, there's some underlying tech in place to detect anyone who might be deliberately lying about their age.

If you've got a teen using Copilot, you can manage their access through the standard Microsoft Family Safety portal. You're able to enable or disable Copilot access, set times during which Copilot can and can't be used, and disable certain features like image generation or voice mode. Parents can't read the Copilot chats of their kids, though.

Parental supervision is optional—a teen aged 13–17 can use Copilot without linking their account to an adult one. Microsoft says users identified as under 18 won't see personalized results or ads, and will get age-appropriate responses regarding risky or harmful content, though there's not much detail on what that entails.

More generally, content around self-harm, violence, adult content, harassment, and harmful or illegal activity is banned on the AI platform. Any prompts about suicide or drugs will bring up support options rather than answers, whether you're an adult or a young person using the service.

Out of the bigger AI chatbots out there, Grok is very much the worst at protecting minors. It can be accessed through X or as its own standalone app, and while its terms of use indicate there's a minimum age requirement of 13, a recent report by Common Sense Media says the platform's age checks aren't effective.

Ultimately that means that minors have the same access to Grok as adults, if they want it—an AI platform that combines "weak safety guardrails" and "a range of extremely harmful content" that includes "explicit sexual content, mental health risks, violent content, and inappropriate responses to... offensive content" (that's the Common Sense Media Report again).

Yes, this is the AI chatbot that has previously had a problem with deepfake porn imagery, and which has traditionally taken a rather casual attitude towards safety concerns, led by SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk. While illegal and harmful content is supposedly banned from Grok, its own FAQs admit that certain chats can result in "dialogue that may involve coarse language, crude humor, sexual situations, or violence."

There is actually a Grok Kids Mode that limits the kind of content that can be shown and the conversation topics that can be added, but it requires users to self-declare themselves as minors and is easy to bypass. The advice from Common Sense Media seems to be the way to go with Grok: Do not let your teens access it.

Claude's approach to child safety is straightforward: You can only register for an account if you're over 18. It is possible to lie about your age when signing up, but like the other platforms, Anthropic looks at various "signals" in behavior to spot minors—if your account gets flagged, you have to verify your age using an option like face age estimation or Yoti.

There's no free web access to the chatbot, like there is with ChatGPT and Gemini, so if you're under 18, you're locked out from the service unless you know the behavioral tricks to get past Claude's detection systems.

In terms of more general well-being protections on Claude, any chat around self-harm or suicide will guide users towards helplines and other resources for support. Conversations about illegal activities, disallowed speech, and explicit sexual content are banned from the platform. In recent months, Anthropic says it's also reduced AI sycophancy.

That's something of a whistle-stop tour of the big seven AI chatbots, but if you're a parent, it should give you some idea of what's out there and how easy it is to access. Besides the parental controls built into these AIs (or not), you also have the settings available at the platform level—Android, iOS, Windows, macOS—to restrict the use of any potentially harmful apps.

Update, 8:41 p.m.: The Federal Aviation Administration announced it has ended the ground stop.

On Friday afternoon, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop for all airports in the United States. If you're planning to fly this afternoon or evening, or you have friends or family doing the same, you're likely concerned about tracking flight statuses. While there's still a lot we don't know, there are tools to help track flights at this time:

There are a number of options for tracking flights, whether you have your flight number or not. If you have the flight number, the fastest method is to Google it: Google will display a live tracker of your flight at the top of the results page. You can also head to the airline's official website to track your flight: United Airlines, for example, has a flight tracker where you can either enter your route information or your flight number. Most, if not all, airlines will have a similar tool you can use.

Alternatively, you can use a site or service that tracks all flights. FlightAware is one such site and has a flight tracker that lets you search flights—so long as you know the origin and the destination. If you have the flight number, your iPhone can help: You can enter your flight number into Spotlight search to see a live tracker, or you can text a contact your flight number, then tap the link that appears under the number to see a tracker of the flight.

At this time, the exact reason isn't totally clear. According to the agency, “The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” but the FAA hasn't said what caused those communications issues or when they expect to lift the grounding. The grounding order comes one day after a massive Microsoft outage that disrupted service for users of Outlook, Teams, and other Microsoft products. It also comes one day after Ars Technica reported that the FAA was rolling out an AI-powered tool to help manage air traffic across the country.

This is only the third time in U.S. history that the FAA has made such an order—once after 9/11, and again in January of 2023 due to a pilot alert system issue; the latter ground stop lasted around 90 minutes.

#3324. Apple reveals how iCloud+ increases Siri AI and Apple Intelligence usage limits

iOS 27.3 beta 2 is now available, and Apple is adding the ability for users to unlock higher usage limits for Apple Intelligence and Siri AI via iCloud+. Here’s everything you need to know.

From the start, Apple has said that some Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features have usage limits because “they rely on powerful server models.” The company previously outlined that increased access would be available across most iCloud+ subscription plans, and now we have the full details on how this will work.

Apple says the new system applies to several categories of Apple Intelligence features, including:

The usage limits are per device, not per account. This means your iPhone, iPad, and Mac each have separate allowances. Apple isn’t disclosing specific limit numbers. Instead, it says that limits can vary based on the feature, request complexity, system demand, and more.

As you near your limit, you’ll see an alert within whichever feature you’re using. For example, if you are using Image Playground, a message will appear telling you that you’ve almost hit your usage limit for the day. Once you hit the limit, you’ll be prompted to wait for it to reset or upgrade your iCloud+ plan.

If you hit your limit, basic Siri requests will still work. This includes things like setting timers and alarms. Requests that require Siri to understand personal context and perform more complex, multi-step actions, however, are subject to the limits.

For example, asking Siri to find the details of an upcoming dinner reservation in your email and add them to your calendar would count toward your daily limit.

Additionally, each device uses its own standard daily usage limit first. After that, it can tap into the additional capacity included with an eligible iCloud+ subscription:

The usage unlocked by iCloud+ is shared across all devices signed in to your Apple Account, as well as family members sharing your iCloud+ plan. The shared usage is available on a first-come, first-served basis

All limits will reset daily at the same time, and limits don’t roll over. In most cases, limits reset around midnight in your current time zone.

Apple has published a support document with more details.

In a new lawsuit filed Wednesday and first reported by Rolling Stone, Frank Cascio and his siblings Dominic, Marie-Nicole, Edward, and Aldo allege that Freedman “exploited the family’s vulnerability and trust” to persuade them to sign a 2019 agreement with Jackson’s estate. Freedman was already representing Edward and Marie-Nicole’s husband in separate legal matters at the time, according to the complaint.

The siblings allege Jackson’s estate was seeking to contain fallout from the 2019 documentary Leaving Neverland, which featured allegations of sexual abuse against the late pop star, when it purportedly enlisted Freedman to “silence further victims from coming forward.” They say Freedman reached out and ultimately managed to “deceive [them] into signing a hush-money agreement.” According to the lawsuit, Freedman assured the siblings he was acting in their best interests. They say he discouraged them from hiring their own lawyers while concealing his alleged conflict of interest.

#3320. macOS 27.3 includes new privacy controls for Full Disk Access and more

With today’s new macOS 27.3 beta, Apple is implementing several changes as part of this.

In a post on its developer website last month, Apple said some developers are “using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems.” As such, it said that it would “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”

In macOS 27.2, “Device Control and Data Access” is a unified toggle in System Settings, where Apple says that apps with that level of access can “view and send email, edit contacts and photos, monitor your keyboard, track websites, record your screen, control any app on your Mac, and more.”

In macOS 27.3, Apple is splitting “Device Control and Data Access” into two categories:

For the latter, users will be able to specify which apps an automation tool can access rather than granting it unrestricted control. For instance, you could give an app access to the Mail app, but not Messages.

macOS 27.3 also adds an option for users to require an app to request permission every time it needs access, rather than granting it access indefinitely.

Apple is also introducing a new menu bar indicator that will provide additional transparency when an app is controlling another app with System and App Protection Override. This is designed to let users know when an automation tool is interacting with apps and information in the background.

Crucially, Apple isn’t removing the ability to give an app Full Disk Access. If you deem it necessary, you can still give an app Full Disk Access. However, Apple is redesigning the approval process to make the implications of that decision more obvious.

macOS 27.3 will display a more detailed explanation about the protections being bypassed and the types of personal information that could be exposed.

Users can also choose to grant an app access to specific folders instead of their entire Mac. For example, an app that only needs to work with files in a particular folder won’t get unrestricted access to everything else.

Any app you’ve already given Full Disk Access will still have that access. Previously granted permissions will remain in effect, and those apps will continue functioning as they do today without any approval required.

Apple has published a new support document detailing the Full Disk Access updates.

macOS 27.3 now warns you before giving an app full disk accessThat warning prompt is pretty scary! pic.twitter.com/J2qCKVWJRx

Apple says the underlying APIs aren’t changing, but developers will need to update their apps to account for situations where users grant limited access rather than unrestricted permissions.

Finally, Apple says developers of backup apps and assistive technologies can request entitlements that allow them to maintain the same experience for new installations as before macOS 27.3. Apple has already identified popular apps that rely on these permissions, and those apps will continue working as expected without requiring an entitlement.

Developers can read more on Apple’s Developer website.

#3318. Google Killed Its Dark Web Report, but You Can Still Monitor Data Breaches

Google’s Dark Web Report used to be the only consumer-focused platform that let users scan major data breaches, dark web marketplaces, and private forums to see if their personal information had ended up in the hands of hackers. But the company discontinued the service at the start of 2026, with new scans stopping on Jan. 15 and all accounts deleted on Feb. 16.

Google says it sunsetted Dark Web Report because, although the information it provided was generally useful, the service failed to provide “helpful next steps” for users whose data was found on the dark web. Google promised a new service that would provide more actionable intel, but that service has yet to materialize, and there haven’t been any further announcements about it yet.

Dark Web Report may not have been perfect, but it was the only early warning system of its kind that was available for personal use and let users run scans free of cost. Now that it’s gone, however, there are plenty of other services that offer the same service at varying costs and levels of effectiveness. Let’s talk through the nature of the insight that Google's reports offered, how it collected that information in the first place, and what options exist in the market to replace it.

Google launched the Dark Web Report in March 2023 as a premium feature available to Google One users, but later extended it for free to anyone with a Google account and moved it to the "Results about you" dashboard.

You'd set up a monitoring profile with your name, date of birth, physical address, phone number, emails, and Social Security Number if you lived in the U.S. After that, you could head to the dashboard anytime you wanted to run a free scan across dark web forums and marketplaces, publicly disclosed corporate data breaches, and other hidden online spaces to see if any of your personal information had shown up there. It was easy to use—but not a lot of people knew it existed in the first place.

It’s unclear what prompted the internal decision at Google, but in the absence of concrete next steps, it is reasonable to think the reports could create panic for the uninitiated. There’s no way to remove your information from the dark web once it’s already in circulation there. Still, having an early warning so you could reset 2FA or self-lock your SSN isn’t without merit.

But perhaps more importantly, most people with Google accounts didn’t know and hadn’t heard of the Dark Web Report’s existence. Google has likely taken it as a hint that users want more active remediation tools than simple alerts, which is why it’s now directing users to the Password Manager, Passkeys, and “Results about you” dashboard instead—though, again, the company hasn't followed through on a direct replacement for Dark Web Report, despite teasing such a feature.

Many of the top dark web scanners draw from the same well of information, scanning against major data breaches and dark web spaces. Several also offer breach notifications that send you email alerts when your details show up in a periodic scan. However, none of that is worth paying for because Have I Been Pwned or Mozilla Monitor cover those features quite well for free. Even the default password managers from Google and Apple come with some ability to monitor leaked credentials.

There isn’t an easy way to scrub your information from the dark web once it ends up getting leaked. But you can take steps to protect sensitive information or financial data once you know there’s been a leak. If a password has been compromised, reset it immediately. Also, enable 2FA on the affected account for added security. Even better, switch to a passkey if that account supports it. If not, authenticator apps are a safer way to receive 2FA codes than standard SMS.

If your Social Security number has been leaked, freeze your credit with Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion. You can do this by contacting each agency separately. Freezing your credit will prevent unauthorized credit withdrawals and protect your credit score from abuse by attackers. If one of your credit or debit card numbers has ended up in a breach, call your bank to freeze transactions on that card immediately.

Finally, get in the habit of using email aliases instead of sharing your actual email address with every platform and service provider. Addy.io and Proton’s SimpleLogin are both popular services that let you generate temporary email aliases that point to your inbox.

#3317. iOS 27.3 adds new face unlock feature for iPhone Duo

In today’s iOS 27.3 beta release, Apple is introducing two changes for iPhone Duo users. Most notably, it adds a new face recognition option that lets you unlock your iPhone Duo by looking at it.

Apple is also adding an option to have your iPhone Duo lock when you close it.

You can enable the new option to unlock your iPhone Duo with the front camera in Settings, under Touch ID & Passcode, after updating to iOS 27.3. When enabled, your iPhone Duo will unlock after recognizing your face.

Use the front camera, along with a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication, to quickly unlock iPhone Duo when it’s closed. Face recognition data never leaves your device.

This isn’t Face ID. This new option on iPhone Duo uses the front camera on the outer iPhone Duo display to recognize your face. The iPhone Duo doesn’t have the hardware needed for Face ID.

Because this isn’t as secure as Face ID, Touch ID, or your passcode, Apple has implemented a few guardrails. First, the setting only works to unlock your iPhone Duo. To use Apple Pay, access your passwords, unlock apps, and do other things that require authentication, you’ll have to use Touch ID or enter your passcode.

This face recognition feature also has a time-based limitation. After 45 minutes of inactivity, you have to authenticate with Touch ID or your passcode. That is, if you go 45 minutes without unlocking your iPhone Duo, the facial recognition feature is disabled until you enter your passcode or use Touch ID.

Finally, this new feature also doesn’t work when using the iPhone Duo unfolded. When unfolded, you still have to use Touch ID or your passcode to unlock the device.

Second, iOS 27.3 adds an option to lock your iPhone Duo when you close it. You can enable this in Settings, under Display & Brightness. Once enabled, your iPhone Duo will lock when you fold, rather than transition from the inner display to the outer display.

Many iPhone Duo users (myself included) have said Apple should do this. Personally, I’ve been using a shortcut to mimic this behavior, but I’m glad to see that Apple has listened to user feedback and added a default setting for it.

#3316. Snoh Aalegra Turned Heartbreak Into an LP With the Help of Stevie Wonder, Janet Jackson, and More

Snoh Aalegra is very honest about where she’s been in the five years since her last album, Temporary Highs in the Violet Skies. While fans were clamoring for her return to R&B, the Iranian singer, who was born and raised in Sweden, was in an emotional prison of unrequited love.

“I had so much love in me and nowhere to put it… this person wasn’t so receptive. He wasn’t in the same space as me,” Aalegra tells Rolling Stone. She had to find a new vessel, so she poured all her yearning into the studio.

The result is Legendary Love, an album that relies on both her extreme vulnerability and strength. She worked on the 13-track offering in Los Angeles with close collaborators, including Joel Compass, Mustafa, and Daniel Caesar. She also tapped songwriters who were newcomers into her world, like Josh Grant, and legends like Raphael Saadiq, Babyface, and Nile Rodgers. The latter was extra special: He added a nice varnish to the album after making all the classics that Aalegra says “gave my life a meaning.”

Legendary Love feels like a time capsule. Aalegra’s glittering voice accentuates deeply poetic lyrics as synths and basslines transport listeners into sonic spaces that feel like what Prince and Janet Jackson built in the Eighties. While some artists have referenced that decade because of its trend appeal, Aalegra says she explored it with intention. “The connection I had with the person [the album is about] felt so ancient and karmic and deeply layered, and it kind of took me back to the era of music that I grew up on as a kid,” she says. “I have such great reverence for that era and the artists that made me want to become an artist.”

Days before the album’s release, and seemingly healed from the tumultuous years that resulted in so much new music, Aalegra broke down several songs from Legendary Love. She also discussed getting a Stevie Wonder sample approved, her friendships with Janet Jackson, Mustafa, and Caesar, and how films like Pretty Woman helped set the mood in the studio.  Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

It was the first song I made with Josh [Grant]. I would say it feels like the end credits of this movie. I chose to start the movie with the ending because some movies do that. “Run Free” is about acceptance. It’s me acknowledging that I love very deep, and I have to always make my own mistakes. I have to always live them. I’m not going to listen to someone that might have lived my mistakes before me and listen to their advice. I have to go through it and I have to be hurt and then move on.

The reason why I repeat “I Love You” so many times [in this song] is because me and this person, over the course of four years that we were on and off, we never said “I love you” to each other. We were never in a real relationship or a committed relationship. So I kind of just wanted to scream it. But I’m not screaming it. I’m saying it very gently, but I’m saying it like 20 times in the song. I hadn’t heard someone, a man, tell me they love me in so many years. When I wrote this song, I felt like I wanted to say it. It’s also a beautiful song. I feel like someone can sing to their child. You can say it to your partner. It’s a wedding song. Essentially, it’s a celebration. It’s a celebration of love, and it’s the ultimate, most simple three words.

Nile Rodgers has this unmistakable rhythmic signature. You just hear when it’s him. I think you hear it even more when he plays on the second hook of “Supernova.” It was fun watching him try to search for what he wanted to do. Raphael too, so cool and so smooth.

“Karma” is not [a] true story. It’s a theory. I chose to hone in on the theory of what a karmic healer told me [about] what might have happened between me and this person. I was told we had 16 lives together, and that four of them really stood out. That we played very significant roles in each other’s lives. But in the previous [life], apparently I betrayed him, and I left him for someone else. And I’m paying for it in this lifetime. I would say “This That” is kind of like one of the core signature sounds of Joel Compass. Obviously I wrote the song with him, but he brought that jam and that rhythm and that pocket, and I was just like, “What is this?” Of course, it’s nostalgic, but it’s new. I loved it so much, and it also reminded me of Janet [Jackson], and just the way we layered my voice felt really fun. It’s like my 2026 version of “Nothing To Me” (from 2019’s Ugh, Those Feels Again). It’s just like my sassy song.

I love so deeply. I’m really like a ride-or-die kind of girl. So I mean it. I will give you my world, the world, whatever I have when I’m with someone. So that’s really what that song is. It took me to a lot of places nostalgically and in a contemporary way. Almost took me back to some Jai Paul kind of rhythms. I felt a lot of things when I heard that one.

Daniel Caesar produced it. I love how he adapted to the world I was making. I brought in some keyboards that I wanted him to use and then he ended up by the grand piano in Westlake [Studios] in the studio room where Michael Jackson did Bad. [Me, Mustafa, and Daniel] wrote that song together.

I opened up for Daniel Caesar on his first tour in early 2018, when I dropped my first album. And all these years, we never worked together, but we stayed friends. We’ve seen each other in passing, and we’re all cool. And Mustafa, who I also met during that tour, became one of my closer friends in life. This was a good moment to work together. Daniel plays every single instrument.

That song, to me, is about taking accountability in regards to this connection I had with this person, taking accountability for running back and forth to him. I kept going back, and so I’m dissecting myself and talking about how I kept choosing him when I maybe shouldn’t have.

[This song] was a little bit of a defeat, like “I give up, and it’s cool.” If I’m not good enough, then I’m not good enough. But I love myself, and this is me. Don’t be with me if you’re not gonna go all the way.

I’m very hard on myself. I’m a Virgo. I am a psycho. Every flaw, before anyone wants to even mention it to me… It’s like, “Trust me, I know already.” For a moment, I was very okay and proud of myself, and loved myself. I had that for a moment on this recording. So it is kind of like a reminder that I was able to feel that way, and it makes me emotional sometimes when I hear it back. That song is really special to me. It’s like a sacred, private moment and feeling that I chose to share on a song.

Babyface is one of the greatest of all time, one of the greatest songwriters to ever exist, and it’s been a lifelong dream to write with him. This was the perfect timing. This song is about my first and my second date with this person, and I love how Babyface helps me really tell that story very vividly. When I listen to it, it takes me right back to that first and second hangout.

It was really beautiful to write this with Babyface, and it was so much fun, just him on his guitar and just like hearing him even hum anything. I was just fangirling. I’ve always wanted to do this signature Babyface ad-lib that he has every artist do: “Yes, it was.” And I got to do it on “Timeless.” Later on I started producing it with No ID and Josh Grant and Raphael, and it really became so beautiful.

I told No ID I wanted to have a Stevie Wonder sample in here. I tend to do this Stevie Wonder nod sometimes in my songs, I did it in “I Want You Around” (“All I want to hear is ‘Innervisions’ on replay / And sit right next to you”). I was so happy when Stevie approved.

I did this one with Dahi. I wrote this one almost three years ago, finished it almost three years ago, then I revisited it again, rewrote some stuff from the verses with Joel. Right before almost mastering the album, Jimmy Jam played some stuff on this record, so that was cool to see him in the studio doing that. I think what he put on the song really uplifted the song and the whole bridge section and the modulation. Everything was really significant for the song. I actually played it for Janet [Jackson] and she really loves it.

I actually really wanted her on that song. So I played it for her. It’s cool that she approved. She came to my show some years ago in London, and we’ve been keeping in touch. She’s actually a friend of mine now, which feels crazy to say, but she’s incredible and so warm and humble and nice. It’s been really cool to be able to talk to her and have that connection with her.

That was one of the first songs I made from my album. I made that song almost three years ago with Christian Rich. They did “Nothing Burns Like the Cold,” and then they did a song called “Just Like That” on my last album, and now this one. They’re incredible. Two brothers from Chicago.

I would say it’s harder for me to write an up-tempo happy song. They come every now and then. Even when I wrote 2019’s “Woah,” I wrote that song in one hour, and I didn’t think much of it. And I was like, you know what? I’m gonna finish the words for the hook later. The “da da da da?” They’re supposed to be words. It feels like Stevie.

I mostly thought about my gratitude to the inner light and the universe and God when I made “Supernova.” That song is about God and trusting that whatever is meant for you will not miss you, and you know it will happen in due time.

‘Legendary Love,” “Supernova”, and “Greatest of All Time” are the first three songs I made for this album. I think this song truly embodies the theme of the album. It’s like the, “What if we didn’t even try, we were not even in a real relationship. We didn’t give it a true chance. What would have happened if we did?” You know, it’s a legendary love. The legendary love that never happened. But the feeling of limerence. This is true limerence.

I was very inspired by Roxette, “It Must’ve Been Love.” I was watching “Pretty Woman” in the background, Julia Roberts, Richard Gere, just like, over and over.

I had this song in my possession for a long time. I had to kind of keep updating it as I was forming this album. I definitely thought of Whitney Houston, for sure. I can’t escape it. She’s my number one female vocalist inspiration, you know, in the world — the first voice that I heard that gave me goosebumps as a kid.  Trending Stories CMA Awards 2026: The Complete Winners List Pearl Jam Plan ‘Big-Boy Conversation’ About New Drummer John Mulaney Enlists Stepfather-in-Law’s Country Band to Play ‘Kimmel’ The Man Who Broke the Texas Democratic Party to Save It

#3314. Four Things You Can Do With Google Maps' New 'Ask Maps' Feature

Google has given its AI-powered "Ask Maps" feature a major upgrade, adding tools for trip planning, real-time route guidance, appointment finding, and saved-list search. The updates begin rolling out today on Android and iOS.

Google launched Ask Maps last March as an AI assistant designed to handle questions and requests more complicated than simply searching the word "bar" or "groceries." Instead of performing simple keyword searches, the idea behind Ask Maps is that you can describe several specific requirements at once, and Maps will find places that match them all. For example, you could ask for a restaurant with outdoor seating for a certain number of people, and "Ask Maps" will factor in your past searches and give you results. Of course, AI assistants have a habit of making things up, so even with today's roll-out, you'll want to double-check your sources before you drive an hour to the wrong restaurant.

To me, this is the most useful new feature launching today. Whether you're planning a day trip for holiday shopping or something more ambitious, like a three-day road trip with coastal hikes and oceanfront dining, Ask Maps will put together a day-by-day schedule. Each plan includes insider tips and numbered map pins for every stop, so you can see the whole route at a glance. Once you're happy with the plan, you can share it with friends and family or export it to Google Docs on desktop.

When it's time to head out, you can ask Maps to pull up your itinerary, or look for the "itinerary" badge in your chat history. You'll see real-time details such as live traffic conditions, whether a place is currently open, and even the vibe at your next stop.

Plans can change on the fly, too. Ask Maps to add a scenic viewpoint or a lunch spot along the way, then tap to get directions to your next stop straight from the itinerary.

Here's what else you can use Ask Maps to do, starting today.

Pulling up directions now surfaces "Know Before You Go" tips for your route. These include where to park or charge your car, along with real-time conditions like weather, potential delays, and tolls.

Ask Maps is also gaining some agentic capabilities. Allegedly, you can just ask, “Find me a 4 p.m. nail appointment near me,” and Ask Maps will show you open slots across nearby businesses. In addition to finding appointments, Google says this agent will be able to call local businesses on your behalf—stay tuned while I wait for the upgrade and test this one out myself.

If you keep lists of saved places, Ask Maps can now search them for you. Ask something like, "Which spots saved in my lists have availability for 5 in the next 30 minutes?" Ask Maps looks across your lists and checks live availability, so you can pick a place and go.

These updates start rolling out today on Android and iOS. Travel itineraries and saved-list search are available everywhere Ask Maps is offered. "Know Before You Go" route tips and appointment finding are launching first in the U.S., with more regions coming soon.

#3311. Taylor Swift Is Getting a Museum of Fine Arts Exhibit in Boston

There’s a good chance Taylor Swift fans might be planning their next vacations.

The Museum of Fine Arts, Boston announced Wednesday that they’ll be showcasing a Taylor Swift-themed exhibit, based on the singer’s 12 albums and Eras. “Taylor Swift: The Eras Collection” will only be shown at the Museum of Fine Arts and will run from April 10 to Aug. 15.

“Every era of Taylor Swift’s career introduces a new sound, a new look, a new glimpse into the mind of an artist who has mastered the craft of reinvention,” the announcement read. “Presented at the MFA, a museum renowned for its collections of fashion and musical instruments, “Taylor Swift: The Eras Collection” takes visitors on a journey through Swift’s genre-defying career—exploring how she combines songwriting, performance, and visual storytelling to continually surprise and connect with audiences around the world.”

Opening April 10, the exhibit will include over 50 outfits, sketches, instruments, and more; all themed around performances, music videos, and tours throughout Swift’s discography. This will include her custom red Alberta Ferretti gown from folklore and evermore, the 2022 Midnights bedazzled bodysuit from Zuhair Murad, and the tinsel fringe jacket Swift wore during the “Karma” finale of the Eras Tour. (Swift was wearing the brightly colored jacket when she famously changed the live “Karma” lyrics in 2023 to a Travis Kelce nod: “Karma is the guy on the Chiefs / Coming straight home to me.”)

The exhibition will also include instruments from Swift’s famous performances, including the Deering banjo she used during the 2010 Speak Now World Tour, a green Gibson J-180 acoustic guitar she played during the 2017 Reputation Stadium Tour and its accompanying concert film, and the grand piano she played “Lover” on during her 2019 American Music Awards performance.  Trending Stories CMA Awards 2026: The Complete Winners List Pearl Jam Plan ‘Big-Boy Conversation’ About New Drummer John Mulaney Enlists Stepfather-in-Law’s Country Band to Play ‘Kimmel’ The Man Who Broke the Texas Democratic Party to Save It

“This is the first exhibition in the MFA’s history devoted to a musician, and we’re thrilled to invite visitors for an up-close look at the fashion and instruments of one of the most influential cultural figures of our time,” said MFA director of public programs Kristen Hoskins in a statement. “I’m excited to welcome audiences across generations to this unique experience at the Museum.”

Tickets for Taylor Swift: The Eras Collection are $40 and will go on sale Dec. 13 — the singer’s 37th birthday.

#3310. iOS 27.3 gives Apple’s Calendar app new design updates

iOS 27.3 beta 2 arrived today, most notably giving the iPhone Duo a face unlock feature. The update also includes some design updates for Apple’s Calendar app.

When you open Apple’s Calendar app in iOS 27.3, the interface will look largely familiar to what was there before. But there are some key design changes that make the app better suited for one-handed use.

Most notably, the buttons for search and for adding a new event have both been moved from the top of the screen to the bottom.

This is a welcome change for anyone who uses their iPhone one-handed a lot, as both important buttons were previously in the top-right corner. I normally use my iPhone in my left hand, so they were especially hard to reach before.

Additionally, Apple has moved the current month to the top-center of the screen and added the year too. Because the year is now always prominently visible, Apple removed it from the back button in the top-left.

Finally, the ‘Today’ button that takes you back to the current day has been changed to always show the actual date. So right now, it reads ‘Mon 16.’

You can reference the full side-by-side in the image above. Overall, these are relatively minor changes but they could make a big difference in everyday use.

What do you think of Apple Calendar’s design updates in iOS 27.3? Let us know in the comments.
